title: Building a software factory for AI SDK
description:
The AI SDK is one of the most popular open-source AI projects in the world. It serves over 20 million npm downloads a week and the repo has over 26,000 stars. Maintaining the codebase means tracking four moving targets at once:

  • Model providers: new providers, new capabilities, and new bugs

  • UI frameworks: bindings for React, Next.js, Svelte, Vue, and others

  • Sandboxes: the execution environments agents run code in

  • Harnesses: adapters for Codex, Claude Code, Pi, and others

After multiple years of growth, the repo was getting 100+ new issues every month, and when Anthropic's Opus 4.6 model was released, PRs hit an inflection point. By late June, that compounding had accumulated over 1,000 open issues and almost 800 pull requests.

That backlog is not a discipline problem. No maintainer, however good, can close that gap by working harder, and because generating code is cheap, it will only grow.

Instead of trying to scale ourselves, we built a software factory. Four weeks in, it authors between 25 and 35% of PRs we merge and closes 70-80% of issues.

Deciding what type of factory to build

Before we built anything, we had to answer three questions:

  • Why our existing approach using agents wasn't enough

  • What level of automation fit a project like the AI SDK

  • How to align automation and human effort to risk

Why not add more agents?

The best maintainers are already using agents aggressively. Mitchell Hashimoto runs Ghostty with the goal of an agent always working, and encodes every agent failure in AGENTS.md so it never repeats. Simon Willison runs four coding agents in parallel, and review bots like Vercel Agent and CodeRabbit sit on millions of repos. Other maintainers like Daniel Stenberg have opted to block AI-generated submissions to curl.

All of it helps, but none of it solves for the core constraint: every one of these solutions still routes every change through one human's attention. We believe that human accountability is still the core of trust in agentic engineering, so we knew our factory needed to solve for reviewer efficiency as a first principle.

What kind of automation fits AI SDK?

Software factories sit on a spectrum. At one end is full automation, where agents write, ship, and deploy without a human ever reading the code. In the middle are harnesses like Codex and Claude Code, where a person steers an agent or fleet of agents. At the far end is software you barely want to automate because the risk is too high, like firmware in a pacemaker or self-driving vehicle.

The AI SDK needs to operate closer to the careful end. It is foundational AI infrastructure with millions of applications built on top, so quality and security are non-negotiable, and a human needs to have control over what ships. We needed our factory to heavily automate the lifecycle around the human, without removing them.

How do we align automation and effort to risk?

For a given change, the depth of human review needed scales with risk.

Centralized roadmaps with detailed feature specs can define risk up front and directly shape the work going into a software factory. But open-source projects like AI SDK also get issues and pull requests from the community, and there is no guarantee they align with the goals of the project, or that changes are safe to make. Higher risk means human judgment is an even more critical part of the system.

To optimize our factory for that judgment, we knew agents had to go beyond generating code based on a request; they needed to evaluate full units of work in the context of the entire project.

Our goal was for the factory to generate a comprehensive assessment of each change for both fit and risk, including a full chain of documented evidence, making it easy for reviewers to apply the right amount of effort:

  • Docs fixes get a quick glance for verification

  • Well-defined provider changes get focused validation

  • A new public API gets deep review

What we built

ai-sdk-factory is a software factory that autonomously processes incoming issues and pull requests for AI SDK. Agents in the factory perform specific, reviewable tasks, like reproducing bugs, implementing features, and creating backports for older SDK versions. A human stays in control throughout the entire process, including merging every change.

We didn't ship the factory in one swing. We built it incrementally, starting at the beginning of the process with classification of issues as bugs, features, or documentation updates. That first step not only gave us more visibility into the shape of the backlog, but also passed helpful context to the other specialized agents we built later.

We prototyped multiple ways to build each new type of functionality, and in the process developed a set of guiding principles that shaped the architecture of the factory that went into production.

Build one agent per task

Once our classification agent reached a high level of accuracy, we focused on automating bug reproduction, fixes, and review of those fixes. We explored building a single agent equipped with skills for each step, but quickly realized that would come with a higher maintenance and troubleshooting burden over time.

Instead, we built a single agent for each specific task, making every new capability easier to reason about, test in isolation, and debug. Each one is scoped to a specific job, with its own prompts, context, and evals.

Today the factory has dedicated agents for every step in the flow:

  • Bug reproduction

  • Bug fixes

  • PR reviews

  • Backports

  • Documentation updates

  • Feature analysis

  • Feature implementation

Secure everything from the start

We implemented security with the second agent, because bug reproduction was the first step where the factory executed code based on content it didn't control.

A factory operating on a public repository has to assume attacker-controlled input: every issue, pull request, comment, and the links inside them are untrusted. Because successful open-source projects are high-value targets, threats range from malicious code changes and supply chain attacks to resource exhaustion, API key exfiltration, and prompt exfiltration.

Sandboxes are the foundation of our defense. Every agent in ai-sdk-factory runs inside an isolated Vercel Sandbox containing its code, its runtime, and only the secrets the agent's specific task needs. With those guardrails, untrusted content can shape what an agent proposes, but the damage any one task can do is contained to the sandbox.

We also built a shielding layer around the sandbox that controls what agents can reach over the network, blocking the paths an attacker would use to pull secrets out of the isolated environment.

The last line of defense is human review: nothing is merged without approval from a human on the AI SDK team.

Build value locally, then move to the cloud

The first several agents we built for the factory ran through a local CLI. That enabled our team to iterate quickly as we noticed inaccuracies, felt friction, and prototyped different ideas.

Once multiple steps were running reliably through the CLI, we were ready to move the system onto managed infrastructure. ai-sdk-factory uses:

  • Vercel Functions for the API, workers, and webhook ingress

  • Vercel Queues for task execution

  • Vercel Blob for logs

  • Vercel Sandbox for the agent workspaces

  • Neon Postgres for factory data

Today, GitHub webhooks feed the issue queue, and as soon as they arrive workers automatically pull them and kick off agent runs in sandboxes. We also built a monitoring UI that tracks every run in parallel, and visualizes the queue for the team of reviewers.

Shipping software through our factory

On July 24, a community member asked for blocked-domain support in OpenAI web search, and the request became issue #17898. The following section explains every step the software factory went through to process the issue, open a pull request with an implementation of the feature, and ultimately backport the merged feature to v5 and v6 of the SDK.

Classification

The first agent that runs in the factory classifies issues and pull requests. In this case, the ai-sdk-factory bot commented on the issue and applied a label, identifying the type as Feature with high confidence. The agent included its rationale for the classification in the comment.

Analysis

After classification, the analysis agent runs. Agents in the factory don't make any assumptions about the technical validity of a feature request or bug, so the analysis agent wrote a probe to confirm the absence of support for blocked domains. issue-17898-type-probe.ts was generated and run, and failed with an error when it looked for blocked-domains and didn't find it.

The failing probe proved the feature was missing on main, and the agent included it in the analysis as evidence.

The analysis agent then used the results of its investigation to build out a spec for the feature: add an optional blockedDomains filter to the existing web-search tool and map it to the provider's blocked_domains field.

The agent also confirmed the spec fit the SDK's provider-adapter architecture and was backward compatible, and even scoped documentation changes.

Implementation

Another agent then implemented the spec and opened a pull request. The implementation agent ran a live end-to-end test, executing an OpenAI web search with wikipedia.org blocked and confirming the domain wasn't reachable. The test was included as additional evidence on the pull request.

Automated review

Next, a review agent scored the change, and when it didn't find any concerns, approved it. The agent rated the feature as fully implemented, with:

  • Side-effect risk: low

  • Performance risk: none

  • Backwards-compatibility risk: low

Human review

Finally, Lars read the chain of evidence from the agents, reviewed the code changes, and merged PR #18033 into main.

Backporting

Once Lars merged the initial PR, ai-sdk-factory opened additional PRs for two backports, #18035 for v6 and #18036 for v5. The v5 backport did not apply cleanly, so the factory agent labeled and committed the conflicted state, identified and validated a fix, and pushed it seventeen minutes later. After review, Lars merged both backport PRs.

Results

We are just over four weeks into running the software factory in production. Here are the results:

PRs merged to main

Between 25-35% of the PRs we merge on a weekly basis are now authored by ai-sdk-factory agents.

Backports

Factory PRs are above 50% of weekly merges to the v6 release line, and v5 looks similar. Backports used to be work we skipped because dealing with merge conflicts wasn't worth the effort. v5 and v6 get far better support now.

Issues

In July, over 75% of closed issues were closed by the factory.

Open issues fell from a peak of 1,022 in late June to 844 by early August, and open bugs are down roughly 25%.

The ai-sdk-factory runs in public, so you can see every pull request it has authored on the repo.

Improving the factory becomes the job

The most interesting part of running the factory is what happens when it fails. Every run ends one of four ways: success, flawed, blocked, or manual. Only success ships, so the rest are signal that re-enters the system as feedback.

  • A flawed run means an agent produced the wrong thing, and the fix is better prompts, better context, or a new eval case so the same mistake gets caught automatically next time

  • A blocked run means the environment was missing something, like a credential, a service, or a dependency, and the fix is provisioning it

  • A manual run marks a boundary we drew on purpose, and forces us to ask whether improvements in the factory justify removing it

Each of those fixes expands the automation boundary, and every week the factory can handle work that it couldn't be trusted with before.

Running the factory is the same discipline teams already apply to their test suites and pipelines, but pointed at the system that does the work, instead of the system that checks it. In a world where agents define the SDLC, improving the factory will become the standard engineering job.

Implement a harness by passing that package to createACP and configure basic harness mapping.

title: Inside the Vercel intern experience
description:
The best way to learn is by shipping product to users in production, and that's why we don’t treat our interns as temporary guests. Every intern at Vercel is expected to operate like a core part of our engineering team from day one.

This past winter, we welcomed a small cohort of those interns to our headquarters in San Francisco. Over an intense four months, they contributed to some of our most important products: the CDN, v0, financial infrastructure, AI Gateway, and more. They shipped features used by millions, helped close the gap for enterprise deals, and in more than a few cases, left a mark that will outlast their time here.

Meet the Winter '26 intern cohort

Yash Kothari, CDN Team

University of Waterloo

What Yash shipped:

Yash's internship spanned the full CDN stack, from infrastructure to CLI to UI in the dashboard.

His first major project was Project-level routing, which is part of the new CDN tab in the Vercel dashboard. This feature lets customers update routing rules, including redirects, rewrites, and header transforms, from the dashboard, API, CLI, or SDK, without needing to redeploy their project or touch a single line of code. Yash built the underlying API endpoints (including a staging/publish workflow), the vercel routes CLI commands, and contributed AI-powered route generation. Right after launch, hundreds of teams immediately adopted it and created thousands of rules.

"One of my favorite things about my internship was that at Vercel you get a lot of autonomy and ownership," Yash said. "I hopped on calls with enterprise customers, saw my work featured on Vercel's changelog, and demoed my work in a live YouTube community session."

In the second half of his internship, Yash worked on Vercel's Firewall and Security products. He shipped the vercel firewall CLI command, enabling users and AI agents to configure custom rules, IP blocks, and firewall controls directly from the terminal. He also built an AI-powered Firewall Rule Builder that lets users describe a desired rule in natural language and generates a WAF custom rule automatically.

Kavin Valli, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kavin shipped:

Kavin worked across the full v0 platform over four months, taking on projects that ranged from user-facing features to cost efficiency for the system’s backend infrastructure.

He started by building Folders and v0 Projects end-to-end: core CRUD operations, a library page redesign, favoriting, visibility controls (private/team/public), and folder sharing. He also closed a critical gap in v0's version history by shipping the manual commit button, which ensured that manual edits in the VM editor properly created commits and blocks, which closed the loop between manual edits and v0's iteration model.

His highest-leverage work came later in the term, when he focused on VM and sandbox infrastructure. By splitting VMs into tiered pools and routing smaller projects to a cost-efficient default pool, Kavin significantly reduced memory usage and infrastructure cost for roughly 80% of sandboxes.

"I worked on v0 and got thrown into the deep end pretty quickly, especially around the v1 launch," remembered Kavin. "It was a bit chaotic at times, but that's something I actually enjoyed."

His final and most involved project was taking ownership of the v0 Slack agent. He shipped Slack preview deployments for safe testing, rebuilt the router agent with improved thread history and SAML re-auth resume, redesigned project context tracking, and built out the full PR flow including v0 labels, Slack thread links, and merged/closed state tracking. The result was an agent that went from rough around the edges to something teams can genuinely rely on.

Mingchung Xia, Financial Infrastructure Team

University of Waterloo

What Mingchung shipped:

Mingchung pushed over 250 PRs in four months and became one of the top contributors on Vercel's central control systems monorepo.

His most externally visible project was the v1/billing/charges API endpoint and the vercel usage CLI command, which let users view their usage and costs in the standardized FOCUS v1.3 FinOps format. Originally scoped as a full-internship project, Mingchung completed it early and expanded its scope into a joint launch with Vantage. The work was subsequently adopted by Meta, Notion, Porsche, and other prominent companies to analyze their Vercel spend in a modern, compliant format.

His most technically complex project was designing and building Vercel's core entitlements system, which is the infrastructure that enables granting, revoking, and provisioning entitlements across project-based monetization, add-ons, enterprise, and marketplace work streams. The system architecture incorporated strong and eventual consistency guarantees, async and synchronous derivations, transactional outboxing, write-ahead logs, plan change manifests, stale-validation sentinels, and materializations. It was rolled out to production and backfilled across all active subscriptions.

"Most companies don't give interns or even existing engineers the opportunity to touch payment systems or billing infrastructure, let alone own it end to end," explained Mingchung. "Correctness is imperative when you're working with money, and I got to experience that firsthand at Vercel."

He finished his internship by shipping Vercel Buy, a new billing service supporting frictionless purchasing for agent credits, gateway credits, v0 credits, and pro subscriptions, complete with a CLI surface.

Mingchung will be joining Vercel full-time on the Financial Infrastructure team after completing his degree.

Kevin Thomas, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kevin shipped:

Kevin's work spanned ML infrastructure, enterprise features, reliability engineering, and incident response, often simultaneously.

His most ambitious self-directed project was v0's auto model routing system: a full pipeline that automatically routes user prompts to the right model tier based on complexity. Kevin proposed the system, built the labeling pipeline, experimented with multiple classifier architectures (embedding-based MLP classifiers, TF-IDF baselines, fine-tuned TinyBERT), and integrated everything into TypeScript-only functions for production deployment. By launch, the system had processed over 1.4 million v0 messages and became the default for all non-enterprise users, reducing decision fatigue and latency for a very large share of v0's user base.

"From working on on-call incidents and vulnerabilities in month one to working directly with enterprise customers in April, I've gotten to work on an unusually wide range of meaningful problems," Kevin said at the end of his internship.

In the latter half of his internship, Kevin focused on enterprise work, most notably the v0 × Snowflake integration. He built enterprise admin controls for model access, RBAC for team skill management, resolved issues in SAML and isolated tenant environments, and shipped the integration itself. This work directly unblocked enterprise customers, supported renewals, and addressed live customer issues.

Kevin also served as a primary investigator for several incidents around signup, billing, auth, and account access, staying at the center of v0's reliability work throughout his term.

Sylvie Zhang, AI Gateway Team

University of Pennsylvania

What Sylvie shipped:

Sylvie worked across the AI Gateway service, contributing to everything from database and backend logic to observability, the frontend, and documentation.

Her first project was Price Strikethrough, surfacing provider MSRP as a strikethrough price alongside Gateway pricing, making provider discounts visible to end users. It touched the full stack and gave her a complete view of the AI Gateway product from the start.

"All that sounded daunting to a student like me with little experience," Sylvie said, "but it was the best learning experience I could have asked for."

Her most impactful and technically demanding project was the AI SDK v5 → v6 endpoint migration for AI Gateway's OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible endpoints. As the AI provider landscape had grown significantly more complex since v5 was designed, maintaining the legacy version had become a bottleneck, especially for handling token usage granularity differences across providers. Sylvie led the migration with a disciplined approach: deep cross-provider knowledge to catch incorrect AI-generated assumptions, systematic multi-turn and cross-provider testing scripts, concurrency testing to surface race conditions, proactive customer communication, and a deliberate fallback strategy that left legacy code in place until the migration proved stable.

The result was a cleaner, more maintainable Gateway service better equipped to handle the continued evolution of AI providers and models.

Advice for future interns

We asked these interns to share their top advice for future cohorts.

Take ownership from day one

Vercel gives interns real autonomy, but that means it's on you to use it well. Don't wait to be assigned work. Take initiative, identify what needs to be done, and start shipping.

Ask questions

Every intern said the same thing: no one at Vercel makes you feel like a burden for asking. The team genuinely wants you to succeed, so use that to your advantage and ask.

Work in public

Share your PRs in team channels. Post updates. Present at Demo Days. The feedback loop is fast, and the visibility helps you iterate and build trust faster.

Talk to people outside your team

Some of the best conversations happen across team lines with engineers, designers, finance, and people in roles you've never considered. Go to the office. Grab lunch with someone new.

Give yourself time to ramp up

The codebase, the culture, and the pace can be a lot at once. Don't rush. The first few weeks are for absorbing, not sprinting. Take time to ramp well, and you will be able to run fast.

Apply to become a Vercel intern

There are additional internship opportunities coming soon. If you want to join our next cohort, check our career site in September to apply.

title: Sign JWTs from your Functions without managing private keys
description:
Vercel KMS lets you sign JWTs and arbitrary messages from your Vercel Functions using managed asymmetric signing keys, so private keys never live in your code or environment variables. Your function authenticates with its Vercel OIDC token, and the private key stays inside Vercel's key management service while verifiers use only the public key.

With Vercel KMS you can:

  • Create and rotate issuers and signing keys (RSA and ECDSA) from the CLI and dashboard.

  • Sign JWTs with custom claims and a configurable TTL, or sign raw bytes, using the @vercel/kms package.

  • Grant a project signing access per environment, including production, preview, development, and custom environments.

  • Constrain the claims a project can request per grant, and validate token claims against a JSON Schema.

  • Verify signed tokens anywhere. Each issuer publishes a public OpenID Connect Discovery document at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/.well-known/openid-configuration and a JWK set at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/jwks.json, so any standard OIDC or JOSE library can validate tokens without Vercel-specific code.

Sign a token inside a function:

Verify a token anywhere with a standard JOSE library, using the issuer's public JWKS:

Set up an issuer and grant a project access from the CLI:

As a best practice, create a separate issuer per project and environment. Isolating issuers keeps each token audience distinct, scopes signing access to exactly one project and environment, and lets you rotate or revoke keys for one without affecting the others.

To get started, read the docs or open Key Management in your team's dashboard.

title: Type a pipe() That Checks Every Step: Variadic Tuples, infer and One Recursive Type
description:
• Book: The TypeScript Type System
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Open Effect's Function.ts and count the signatures of pipe. There are 20: one for a bare value, then one more for every extra function, up to 19. RxJS 7's standalone pipe types nine functions and then falls back to a catch-all signature that returns UnaryFunction<T, unknown>. Hand it a tenth function and the output type is gone.

Those libraries know exactly what they are doing. When TypeScript 4.0 shipped variadic tuple types, the release notes called this pattern "death by a thousand overloads", and overloads are still how the big libraries type pipe. The reason is that a single generic signature that checks every step is harder to write than it looks, and it gives some things up.

You're going to write that single signature anyway: about 40 lines of types, checked by tsc --noEmit, and then the four places it breaks so you know when overloads win.

Step 1: read the ends with infer

Start with four small helpers. In and Out pull the parameter and return type out of a one-argument function. First and Last pull the first and last element out of a tuple.

// pipe.ts
export type Fn = (arg: any) => any;

type In<F> = F extends (arg: infer A) => any ? A : never;
type Out<F> = F extends (arg: any) => infer R ? R : never;

type First<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [infer F, ...unknown[]] ? F : never;
type Last<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [...unknown[], infer L] ? L : never;

Last matches with a leading rest element, [...unknown[], infer L], which TypeScript has accepted since 4.2. With these you can write the obvious pipe type: the input of the first function, the output of the last.

type NaivePipe<Fns extends Fn[]> =
  (input: In<First<Fns>>) => Out<Last<Fns>>;

It reads the ends and never looks at the middle. Give it trim (string to string), len (string to number) and shout (string to string) and it reports (input: string) => string, even though shout would receive a number at runtime. A pipe type that only reads the ends is an as cast with better marketing.


Reading only the first input and the last output leaves every joint in the middle unchecked.

Step 2: walk the list with one recursive type

The real check has to visit every adjacent pair. Recursive conditional types (TypeScript 4.1) let a type refer to itself in its own branches, so you peel one function off the front, compare its input with the value flowing in, and recurse on the rest.

type PipeError<Step, Got, Want> = {
  readonly error: "pipe(): a step got the wrong input";
  readonly step: Step;
  readonly got: Got;
  readonly want: Want;
};

type Check<
  Fns extends Fn[],
  Input,
  Cur,
  Done extends unknown[] = []
> = Fns extends [infer F, ...infer Rest extends Fn[]]
  ? [Cur] extends [In<F>]
    ? Check<Rest, Input, Out<F>, [...Done, F]>
    : PipeError<[...Done, F]["length"], Cur, In<F>>
  : (input: Input) => Cur;

export type Pipe<Fns extends [Fn, ...Fn[]]> = Check<
  Fns,
  In<First<Fns>>,
  In<First<Fns>>
>;

Four details carry the weight here.

infer Rest extends Fn[] puts a constraint on the inferred rest, a feature from TypeScript 4.7. Without it, Rest can't be passed back into Check, whose first parameter demands Fn[].

[Cur] extends [In<F>] wraps both sides in brackets on purpose. A bare Cur extends ... on a type parameter is distributive: if a step returns string | number, the check would split into one branch per member and hand you a union of a function and an error. The brackets compare the whole union at once.

Done collects the functions already visited. Its only job is to number the failing step: [...Done, F]["length"] is the 1-based position of F as a number literal type.

The recursive call is the entire branch result. Nothing wraps it, and that makes Check tail-recursive, which matters when chains get long.

The runtime part is short:

export function pipe<Fns extends [Fn, ...Fn[]]>(
  ...fns: Fns
): Pipe<Fns> {
  const run = (input: unknown) =>
    fns.reduce((acc: unknown, fn) => fn(acc), input);
  return run as unknown as Pipe<Fns>;
}

Fns extends [Fn, ...Fn[]] on a rest parameter makes TypeScript infer the arguments as a tuple, one element per function, which is what Check walks. The double cast is the honest part: the body can't prove a deferred conditional type, so you assert once at the boundary and callers get the checked type. The overloaded libraries pay the same toll in their own way; Effect's implementation signature is pipe(a: unknown, ...args: Array<any>): unknown.

Step 3: prove it with @ts-expect-error

A type you can't test is a type you will break by accident. // @ts-expect-error (TypeScript 3.9) suppresses the error on the next line, and if that line has no error, tsc reports Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive. That turns every expected failure into an assertion.

// pipe.types.ts
import { pipe } from "./pipe";

type Equal<A, B> =
  (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends
  (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2)
    ? true
    : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const trim = (s: string) => s.trim();
const len = (s: string) => s.length;
const isLong = (n: number) => n > 10;
const shout = (s: string) => s.toUpperCase();

const ok = pipe(trim, len, isLong);
export type OkIsTyped = Expect<
  Equal<typeof ok, (input: string) => boolean>
>;

// @ts-expect-error the input must be a string
ok(42);

const broken = pipe(trim, len, shout);

// @ts-expect-error step 3 wants a string, gets a number
broken("  hello  ");

// @ts-expect-error a broken pipe is not a function
const f: (s: string) => string = broken;

// @ts-expect-error pipe() needs at least one step
pipe();

Equal compares two types strictly, so a result that drifts to any or to a wider type fails it; Expect fails to compile when handed false. A minimal tsconfig.json next to the two files:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler"
  },
  "include": ["pipe.ts", "pipe.types.ts"]
}

Install the compiler with npm i -D typescript, then run npx tsc. The config needs TypeScript 5.0 or newer for "moduleResolution": "bundler"; the types themselves need 4.7. If any expectation stops holding, either an Expect line or an unused directive fails the build, locally or in CI.

Where the recursive version breaks

Look again at the broken test. The pipe(trim, len, shout) line compiles. The type of broken is PipeError<3, number, string>, and the error only appears where you call it or assign it to a function type. Hovering broken tells you the step, what it got and what it wanted, which beats a silent unknown, but the red squiggle sits on the wrong line. Overloads don't have this problem: each step is its own parameter, so a mismatch is an argument error on the exact function that's wrong. There is a variant that rewrites the rest parameter to the expected tuple so the error moves onto the bad argument; ecyrbe's write-up shows one. I haven't run it, and a commenter there reports a gap in its first-to-second step check, so test it the same way before you trust it.

Generic steps lose their type parameter. Take const wrap = <T>(x: T): T[] => [x]. When In and Out match a generic signature against infer, the type parameter doesn't survive; TypeScript issue #38964 shows ReturnType of <T = string>() => T coming out as unknown. So pipe(trim, wrap, join), with join taking string[], fails with got: unknown[]. The fix is an instantiation expression (4.7): pass wrap<string> as the step and the chain checks. Overloads get this for free, because each step is matched against (a: A) => B with A already known, and since TypeScript 3.4 a composer can even propagate a generic step's type parameters into the result.

Inline lambdas aren't typed from the previous step. In Effect, pipe(" hi ", (s) => s.trim(), (s) => s.length) types each s from the step before it, because every overload names the intermediate types as separate type parameters. In ...fns: Fns, nothing ties the second slot's parameter to the first slot's return, so an unannotated (s) => s.length has no way to learn that s is a string. The best it gets is the any from the Fn constraint, and an any step checks nothing. Annotate every inline step, or write the steps as named functions.

Long chains hit the depth limit, depending on how you wrote the recursion. The TypeScript PR that added tail-recursion elimination lets tail-recursive conditional types loop 1,000 times before giving up, and lowered the general limit for the rest to 100. Check is tail-recursive, so a 30-step pipe is nowhere near the ceiling. Rewrite it so the recursive call sits inside something else, a tuple spread or a union, and you are back under the general limit, where the failure is the familiar Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite from the 4.5 release notes. Even well under the limit, the 4.1 notes warn that recursive types can increase type-checking time, so keep the step types themselves simple.

When overloads are still the better choice


Overloads write one signature per chain length. The recursive type writes one signature that walks the list.

The rule that falls out of the four breaks: choose by who writes the steps.

If callers write steps inline, as lambdas, or pass generic helpers like map and filter, use overloads. That is the RxJS and Effect situation, where most steps are operators with type parameters and most callbacks are unannotated. Contextual typing per step and per-argument errors are worth more than an unlimited chain length, and very few real pipelines need more than the 19 functions Effect covers.

If callers pass named, already-typed, non-generic functions, use the recursive type. Validation chains, middleware lists and data transforms assembled from a registry all fit: the steps already carry their own types, chains can be longer than any overload stack, and the PipeError type names the failing step. Ship it with the @ts-expect-error file so the next refactor can't quietly break the check.

If this was useful

The recursive Check type is a small version of a pattern that keeps coming back: walk a tuple with infer, carry state in an accumulator, keep the recursion in tail position. The TypeScript Type System goes deep on that toolkit: generics, mapped and conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types. If you already write TypeScript daily, that's the one to read next; if you're still getting comfortable with narrowing and modules, start with TypeScript Essentials.

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Coming from Kotlin, Java or PHP? The two bridge books replace the first two for you. Shipping TypeScript at work, with build tooling and published packages? TypeScript in Production covers that layer.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

title: Agent Skills Go to the Lab
description:
Agent Skills Go to the Lab

Three signals landed in the same 24-hour window on October 16, 2026. On GitHub Trending, K-Dense-AI/scientific-agent-skills was pulling 1,158 stars per day, sitting at 51,288 total — making it the third-fastest mover on the board. On X, Sakana AI's David Ha (@hardmaru) shipped AI Scientist v3, branded "The Agentic Scientist," alongside the MASS paper on recursive self-improvement via multi-agent self-supervision. And in Karlsruhe, the Energy Materials Acceleration Platform (E-MAP) at KIT continued demonstrating that autonomous robotic labs are no longer a grant proposal — they are running experiments in glovebox-sealed environments, mixing semiconductor inks, depositing thin films, and measuring the results without a human touching a pipette.

📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on AgentConn →

The convergence is not a coincidence. It is the same pattern we have been tracking on AgentConn since the skills-go-vertical wave in May: the agent-skills ecosystem that developer tooling popularized — obra/superpowers at 300K stars, affaan-m/ECC at 281K, the entire Claude Code skills directory — is being ported into science. And the port is stress-testing the pattern in ways that coding never did.

Our thesis: Science is the first vertical that demands the skills ecosystem grow trust infrastructure. Coding skills can fail gracefully — a bad refactoring skill wastes tokens but doesn't endanger anyone. A bad molecular-synthesis skill could order hazardous reagents, contaminate a cell culture, or produce irreproducible results that waste months of downstream work. The scientific-skills-library pattern is where "just ship a SKILL.md" meets "who validated this protocol?"

The K-Dense Library: Anatomy of a Scientific Skill

View repository on GitHub →

K-Dense-AI's scientific-agent-skills is not a prompt collection. It is a curated library of 177 validated skills spanning biology, chemistry, cheminformatics, proteomics, clinical research, materials science, and lab automation. Each skill follows the same SKILL.md format that Claude Code and Cursor expect, but the contents are fundamentally different from what a coding skill contains.

A typical coding skill says: "When the user asks to refactor, follow the red-green-refactor cycle." A typical K-Dense scientific skill says: "When the user needs to analyze protein-ligand binding affinity, use AutoDock Vina with these parameters, validate the docking score against the PDBBind v2020 benchmark, and flag any binding energy below -7.0 kcal/mol as a potential hit requiring MD simulation follow-up."

The difference is not just domain vocabulary. It is a shift in the consequences of getting it wrong. The skill carries:

  • Validated parameters — not guessed defaults but values vetted against established benchmarks
  • Dependency chains — most skills require uv for Python environment management, and many need specific bioinformatics toolchains (BLAST, HMMER, RDKit)
  • Output validation — the skill specifies what a correct result looks like, so the agent can self-check before reporting to the researcher
  • Safety constraints — some skills explicitly refuse to generate synthesis routes for controlled substances or to recommend dosages

The project started as "Claude Scientific Skills," a Claude-Code-specific collection. Its rename to "Scientific Agent Skills" in 2026 was deliberate: the skills now work with any agent supporting the open Agent Skills standard — Cursor, Codex, Google Antigravity, and others. The MIT license means anyone can fork and adapt. K-Dense also ships a companion app, K-Dense BYOK, that lets researchers run the skills locally with their own API keys — a free, open-source AI co-scientist that runs on your desktop.

💡 For agent builders: The K-Dense library is a case study in what "vertical skills" look like when they mature past the "awesome-list" stage. If your harness can install npx skills add K-Dense-AI/scientific-agent-skills, your users can turn their coding agent into a research agent. That is the value proposition. The risk: each skill can run code, install packages, make network requests, and modify files. Review each SKILL.md before installing. The project's own README says the same thing.

The 250,000+ researchers number is self-reported and unverifiable from outside the project. But the GitHub trajectory is real: from roughly 44K stars in September to 51K in mid-October, with a star velocity that puts it ahead of most developer-tooling repos. The demand signal is genuine even if the adoption count is marketing.

Sakana's AI Scientist v3: From Paper-Writer to Agentic Scientist

View original post on X →

On the same day K-Dense was trending, Sakana AI's @hardmaru announced AI Scientist v3, subtitled "The Agentic Scientist." The original AI Scientist (August 2024) was a breakthrough for end-to-end research automation — it could generate hypotheses, write code to test them, analyze results, and draft a paper. The v1 methodology paper was published in Nature in March 2026, a first for a fully automated AI research system, with collaborators from UBC, the Vector Institute, and Oxford.

v2 dropped the dependency on human-written templates, introduced agentic tree search, and generalized across ML domains — though at the cost of lower per-run success rates. A workshop manuscript from v2 scored 6.33 at the ICLR 2025 ICBINB workshop, but Sakana acknowledged none of the three generated papers met the bar for a main-conference publication.

v3 ships alongside the MASS paper (Recursive Self-Improvement via Multi-Agent Self-Supervision, 1.8K likes on X), which describes a framework where multiple agent instances collaborate and critique each other's work before converging on a research direction. The branding shift from "AI Scientist" to "The Agentic Scientist" signals what has changed: v3 does not treat the agent as a single researcher executing a linear pipeline. It treats the agent as a team — a principal investigator that decomposes problems, delegate-agents that explore sub-problems, and a review-agent that evaluates quality before anything gets written up.

The timing drew commentary from Jurgen Schmidhuber (@SchmidhuberAI), who reprised his 1987 recursive self-improvement priority claims while also disclosing that he has joined Sakana AI as Chief Scientific Advisor. The symbolism is thick: the godfather of the idea that machines should improve themselves is now advising the team shipping the most visible implementation.

E-MAP and the Self-Driving Lab Convergence

The third signal in the cluster is physical rather than digital. KIT's Energy Materials Acceleration Platform (E-MAP) represents the closed-loop version of what K-Dense's skills do in the open-loop digital world. Inside a glovebox-sealed environment, robotic systems handle material preparation, sample transport, thin-film deposition, and characterization — all without human hands. A microfluidic module mixes semiconductor inks autonomously. Construction began in 2023; the platform now operates as a self-driving lab for thin-film photovoltaics and optoelectronic materials.

E-MAP is part of a larger wave. PNNL's AutoLabs, published in Scientific Reports in June 2026, built a translation agent that converts experimental goals into instructions for the Big Kahuna robotic platform — researchers can run 5 to 10 times more experiments than would be practical manually. A Nature Machine Intelligence paper from July 2026 described an AI agent that autonomously sets up and runs X-ray experiments at SLAC, adjusting parameters mid-run. And the Helmholtz Association is planning an Acceleration Alliance that would link autonomous labs across multiple research centers in Germany.

The convergence point is clear: skills libraries provide the what (protocols, parameters, validation rules), and self-driving labs provide the where (robotic execution, closed-loop measurement). Neither half works alone. A K-Dense skill that specifies "deposit a perovskite thin film at 150C for 30 minutes" is useless without a robot that can execute that instruction. A robot waiting for instructions is useless without a curated protocol telling it what to deposit, at what temperature, and how to evaluate the result.

What the Community Is Saying

The scientific-agent-skills trend drew reactions across multiple platforms, and the commentary reveals the tension between enthusiasm and skepticism that defines this moment.

View original post on X →

NVIDIA's Jim Fan (@DrJimFan) open-sourced ASPIRE v1.0, an agentic robotics framework with real-robot skill discovery and self-improvement. The framing is significant: NVIDIA is positioning agent skills as the software layer for physical robots, not just coding assistants. ASPIRE lets robots discover and refine their own skills through real-world interaction — a loop that mirrors what K-Dense does for digital research agents but in physical space.

View original post on X →

Meanwhile, @arankomatsuzaki flagged a sobering benchmark: 9 frontier agents were tested on 15 open scientific follow-up problems, producing 135 research papers. Most failed. The benchmark reveals the gap between "an agent can use scientific tools" and "an agent can do science" — tool access is necessary but nowhere near sufficient.

View original post on X →

And @iScienceLuvr posed the meta-question that many researchers are quietly asking: "How did NLP researchers deal with their entire field being solved by LLMs?" (1.3K likes). The subtext: if agent skills can reliably execute standard research protocols, what happens to the graduate students and technicians who currently execute those protocols manually? The question is not hypothetical — K-Dense's researcher user base suggests the automation has already begun for routine computational work.

The Trust Gap: What Science Demands That Coding Doesn't

This is where the scientific-skills-library pattern diverges from everything the agent-skills ecosystem has built so far, and it is the reason this story matters beyond the star counts.

When you install a coding skill from obra/superpowers, the worst case is that the agent writes bad code that fails tests. The feedback loop is fast: run the tests, see the failure, fix the skill. The blast radius is your local branch.

When you install a scientific skill, the failure modes are fundamentally different:

  1. Irreproducibility — if the skill specifies wrong parameters for a protein docking calculation, the results look plausible but cannot be reproduced. The researcher publishes, others try to replicate, and the failure surfaces months later. The feedback loop is measured in publication cycles, not CI runs.

  2. Safety — a skill that generates synthesis routes for molecules needs guardrails that coding skills never need. K-Dense addresses this partially (some skills refuse controlled-substance queries), but the problem is combinatorial. A benign skill A combined with a benign skill B can produce a dangerous workflow C.

  3. Validation provenance — who vetted the 177 skills? Against what benchmarks? When were they last updated? In coding, the test suite is the validator. In science, validation requires domain expertise that the skill consumer may not have.

  4. Regulatory compliance — a pharmaceutical skill that helps design clinical trials needs to respect FDA guidelines. A materials science skill that suggests chemical compositions needs to be aware of REACH regulations. These constraints do not exist in the coding world.

The agent-config-skills-supply-chain-attack-surface we covered in August was about malicious skills injecting code. The scientific version is more subtle: it is about well-intentioned skills producing wrong results that no one catches because the consumer trusted the "validated" label.

⚠️ The Contrarian Corner: Here is the uncomfortable argument: skills libraries are prompt collections with better marketing. 177 SKILL.md files do not make an AI scientist any more than 177 recipe cards make a chef. Without closed-loop lab execution, without real-time instrument feedback, without the tacit knowledge that comes from years of bench work, these skills are theater — they make the agent sound like a scientist while doing the computational equivalent of reading a textbook aloud. The 51K stars measure hope, not capability. The benchmark that tested 9 frontier agents on 15 real scientific problems and found most failing is the honest signal. The star count is the marketing signal. Do not confuse the two.

What This Means for Agent Builders

If you build agent harnesses, the scientific-skills-library pattern introduces requirements your platform needs to handle — or it will be outcompeted by platforms that do:

1. Skill validation metadata. Coding skills self-validate via tests. Scientific skills need explicit metadata: who validated this skill, against which benchmarks, when, and under what conditions. Your skill registry needs a validation block alongside the SKILL.md.

2. Composition safety. When a user installs 20 skills from K-Dense, some of those skills may chain together in ways nobody tested. Your harness needs composition-aware safety checking — at minimum, flagging when Skill A's output feeds into Skill B's input in ways neither skill was tested for.

3. Audit trails. Reproducibility requires that every step an agent takes — which skill it invoked, with what parameters, producing what output — is logged in a format that a reviewer or regulator can audit. The agent-skills-marketplace conversation needs to include provenance tracking, not just discovery and install.

4. Domain-specific guardrails. A generic "don't do dangerous things" instruction is not sufficient. Scientific skills need domain-specific guardrails: do not synthesize controlled substances, do not recommend off-label dosages, do not generate clinical trial designs without IRB-level disclosures. These guardrails need to be part of the skill standard, not bolted on by each individual harness.

💡 For practitioners: If you are a researcher evaluating K-Dense or similar scientific skill libraries, start with computational skills where you can verify outputs against known benchmarks (molecular docking, sequence alignment, structure prediction). Do not start with workflow-automation skills that chain multiple tools — the composition risks are not yet well-understood. Treat every skill the way you would treat a new lab protocol from a colleague: trust but verify, and document your verification.

The Road Ahead

We are watching the agent skills ecosystem bifurcate. One branch — developer tooling — will continue to move fast, accumulate stars, and optimize for developer experience. The other branch — scientific and industrial verticals — will move slower, accumulate citations instead of stars, and optimize for trust.

K-Dense's scientific-agent-skills library is the bridge between the two branches. It ships like a developer tool (MIT license, npx install, works with Claude Code) but it serves a scientific audience that measures success in reproducibility, not deployment speed. Sakana's AI Scientist v3 pushes the frontier on what autonomous research agents can do. E-MAP and the self-driving lab wave prove that the physical infrastructure to close the loop between agent decisions and real-world experiments is being built right now.

The prediction: within 12 months, the top 10 agent-skills repositories by star count will include at least three scientific or industrial verticals. The skills-directory race was Act One — general-purpose skills for general-purpose developers. Act Two is vertical skills for domain experts. The lab is where Act Two begins.

Originally published at AgentConn

title: Turn a Job Role Into an Agent Task Spec: Scope, Limits and Escalation in Code
description:
When a team says "we want an AI employee", the first job is not picking a model. It is cutting a role into tasks you can specify, limit and check. Here is one way to write that down as code.

This is an illustrative role (sales operations analyst), not a customer story. I have no performance numbers to share.

Step 1: List tasks, not the role 

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Literal

@dataclass
class TaskSpec:
    name: str
    inputs: list[str]
    allowed_tools: list[str]
    output: str
    owner: str                      # a named human
    escalate_when: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    mode: Literal["workflow", "agent"] = "workflow"

TASKS = [
    TaskSpec("clean_lead_list", ["crm.leads"], ["crm.read", "crm.update_field"],
             "list of fixes with reasons", owner="ops_lead",
             escalate_when=["merge two records"]),
    TaskSpec("draft_followup", ["lead", "last_call_notes"], ["crm.read", "email.draft"],
             "draft only, never sent", owner="sales_rep",
             escalate_when=["price mentioned", "refund mentioned"]),
]

Notice mode. Anthropic's guide separates workflows (fixed code paths) from agents (the model picks the steps) and says agents bring higher cost and compounding errors, so test them in a sandbox with guardrails. Start every task as a workflow. Move one to agent only when the steps truly cannot be fixed.

Step 2: Enforce the limits outside the model 

def run(task: TaskSpec, call_tool, request):
    for step in plan(task, request):
        if step.tool not in task.allowed_tools:
            return escalate(task, f"tool not allowed: {step.tool}")
        if any(w in step.text.lower() for w in task.escalate_when):
            return escalate(task, f"rule hit: {step.text[:60]}")
        result = call_tool(step)
        audit_log(task.name, step, result)
    return finish(task)

The allowed list and the stop words live in your code, not in a prompt. A prompt can be argued with. A check in code cannot.

Step 3: Make a person own each task

owner is a required field. If a task has no owner, it does not ship. The owner reviews a weekly sample from the audit log and can switch the task off.

Step 4: Keep the claims small

  • Draft, do not send, until the owner trusts a task.
  • Log every tool call with inputs and outputs.
  • Write the stop rules from real incidents, not guesses.

What I would not claim

An agent here is a bundle of tasks with limits. It is not an employee in any legal sense, and this spec does not replace a role. Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index describes agents as "digital colleagues" taking tasks at human direction, and calls the person who manages them an "agent boss". That matches the owner field above.

The next step is a review loop: sample the log, tighten the rules, then widen the task.

Tej Pandya, founder of GrowEasy.ai.

title: How to Build Ultra-Fast WordPress Sites in 2026: The Essential Developer Stack
description:

A fast website starts with clean theme architecture. Unlike heavy legacy themes packed with thousands of unused stylesheets, a lightweight theme like Astra Pro loads in less than 0.5 seconds with vanilla JavaScript. It gives you deep styling controls, sticky headers, and mega menus without adding DOM bloat.
