title: Meta ships Muse Wonder, with six reasoning levels
description:
Meta AI has released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, which it describes as its new "most capable models". The details come from a post by Simon Willison, who also announced the 0.2 release of his llm-meta-ai plugin, which adds support for the new model to his LLM tool. Meta's own announcement is on its research blog.

What is in the release

Muse Wonder comes with six reasoning levels: minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh and max. The source does not say what each level changes or how they differ in cost or speed, and it gives no pricing or availability details beyond the plugin update for the Meta AI API.

How it is rated

Artificial Analysis scores Muse Wonder at the Max level as equivalent to GPT-6.1 Sol. Willison suggests these may be Meta's first models in what he calls the "Fable class". That classification is his reading, not something Meta has confirmed in the source.

The pace

Willison notes that Muse 1.3 came out on September 2nd and Muse 1.2 on August 5th. In his words, Meta is putting out a new model a month. He adds that the improvement between releases is material, judging by his informal test of asking each model to draw a pelican riding a bicycle. That test is a quick visual check, not a formal benchmark, and the source offers no other measure of the gains between versions.

What is not in the source

There are no prices, rate limits, context window sizes or rollout dates in the source, so none are given here. Anyone planning to use the model for production work will need Meta's documentation for those details.

title: “This app might stop working soon”: Atlassian Connect apps
description:
On 9 October an admin wrote on Figma's forum that they had "received a notification indicating that your app may stop working after January 2027", and asked what it meant for their site. Connect end of support begins on 31 January 2027, 106 days from the day I'm writing this. On our own test site the admin screen gave two different dates for it.

Figma answered the next day. They assumed the admin meant Figma for Jira and said they plan to move it to Forge "by the end of the year". I liked that answer, because for most apps only the vendor can give it.

If you've seen "This app might stop working soon", or one of its cousins, on a Jira or Confluence app, Atlassian is telling you the app still has Connect parts. On our test site the Connected apps page tagged 4 of its 57 entries Legacy. Its banner said January 2027, and the tooltip on the Legacy tag said December 2026. Same page. Weird, I know.

Finding the affected apps takes a few clicks per site, and most of what's left after that is emails to vendors. If you want the background on why Atlassian is retiring Connect, Mihai covered it in Atlassian Connect end of support: 31 January 2027. This one is the admin's to-do list.

Our Connected apps page: 4 Legacy tags, two dates, no Connect column

We opened Connected apps on our wolfaenpak test site on 16 October 2026 and clicked through its three pages and the details screens. We read Atlassian's documentation the same day.

  1. No column, tag or filter says Connect or Forge. The list has the columns App, Edition, Installed by, Connections and Actions. The end-of-support signal is a yellow "Legacy" tag, on 4 of 57 entries. The word Connect only shows up inside a Legacy app's details, as a link to Atlassian's post.
  2. One page, two dates. The banner says "unsupported after January 2027". The tooltip on the Legacy tag says "This app may stop working after December 2026". The tooltip is a month earlier.
  3. The colour of the panel tells you the vendor's plan. Blue means the vendor has told Atlassian it will migrate before end of support. Yellow means the vendor said no, is undecided or said nothing, or that a newer version of the app is waiting for you.
  4. Atlassian's own Connect integrations aren't tagged. 12 of them are on our site, all with versions ending in -AC, and we found nothing that says whether end of support applies to them.
  5. Two shortcuts for spotting Connect didn't help. The details URL looked the same for the Legacy apps and our Forge app, and the old app-management API doesn't list Forge apps at all.

What “This app might stop working soon” means, and why a Forge app can still show it

The wording you see depends on when and where you saw it. "This app might stop working soon" is the title of a developer-community thread from 20 May 2026 that's had 2,382 views, about a banner that appeared inside apps. Atlassian staff said in that thread the message was meant only for non-Marketplace apps, rolled it back the same day, and later said it had been "scoped to canary tenants only". yasoon titled a support page after it, and that page still gives December 2026.

What admins see now is quieter. Atlassian documents the current copy on What admins see on the Connected Apps page, last updated 10 September 2026: "This app is running on a platform that will be unsupported after January 2027." Exalate quoted a third version in its support post, "This app may stop working after January 2027", and admins on Lucid's and Figma's forums repeat the same words. All three are the same warning about the same thing.

A Forge app can still get it, too. That one surprises people. Atlassian set the rule in its March 2025 timeline post. In its words, "an app that has a Forge manifest and a mix of Connect and Forge modules will be considered a Connect app until all Connect modules are removed." Exalate said exactly that about its own app in September: its package "still includes a Connect component alongside its Forge implementation", so the warning shows. A vendor telling you "we're on Forge already" and the warning are both true at the same time, until the last Connect piece is gone.

Connect end of support: December 2026 or 31 January 2027?

It's 31 January 2027. Atlassian moved it on 3 August 2026, in Getting Ready for Connect End of Support: "we're extending the end of support date from December 2026 to January 31, 2027." The developer changelog repeats it on 7 August. The pages updated after that use the new date too. They include the private-apps page and the migration-module page (both 10 August), what admins see (10 September) and the app migration page (23 September). The last one even says the date "was extended from December 2026".

December survives in older pages nobody went back to edit (the March 2025 timeline post says "Q4 CY2026", the August 2025 post on custom apps "the end of 2026"), on some vendor pages, and in our tooltip.

So plan for 31 January 2027. If someone in your company has December in a slide, they're probably reading the tooltip or a 2025 post, and it's an easy mistake when the product says it too.

How to identify if an app is Forge or Connect: four checks

Atlassian's own knowledge-base article for this question tells you to open each app's Marketplace listing and look for a descriptor link. It was last updated in September 2025, before the admin labels existed, and it's slow with more than a handful of apps. These are the checks I'd run instead, in this order.

Check 1: open Connected apps and look for the Legacy tag

Go to Atlassian Administration, select Apps, then Sites, pick your site, and select Connected apps in the left navigation (Atlassian's Manage an installed app page has the same path). From the organization's Atlassian apps page there's also a link, "Looking for your Marketplace and third-party apps?", which opens a site picker and lands you in the same place. You need to be an organization admin or a site admin.

Inside a product, the old Manage apps screen is gone. On our site both Jira and Confluence now say "App management has moved to Administration", with a "Take me there" button. The Jira sidebar item is still called "Manage apps", while the message says "Apps > Manage your apps". A bit confusing, but both take you to the same page.

Then page through the list. All of it. Our test site needed three pages for 57 entries, and 16 of those were Rovo MCP connectors that the system installed. The four Legacy tags were all third-party Marketplace apps:

App on our test site Vendor Tag Details panel
ScriptRunner for Jira The Adaptavist Group Legacy blue, links the vendor's Forge plan
Navigation Menus for Confluence (quick & easy orientation) Seibert Legacy blue
STAGIL Navigation Menus and Themes for Confluence STAGIL by catworkx Legacy not opened
User Management for Confluence (bulk & timed inactive users) TechTime Initiative Group Legacy not opened

Keep in mind the tag is a pointer. It tells you nothing about how far along the vendor is. An Atlassian staff member called the "at risk" signal "complicated and conservative" in a September thread and said to expect "false positives", many with simple fixes. So a Legacy tag means "look at this one": the app has Connect parts, and the vendor may already be most of the way off them.

Check 2: open View app details and read the panel colour

A Legacy app's details page has a panel at the top. Atlassian's banner table says the wording is the same whatever the vendor declared, and the colour carries the meaning: blue when the vendor declared willMigrateToForgeBeforeEOS: YES, yellow when it declared no or undecided, and yellow by default when it declared nothing. A vendor whose app has no Forge manifest yet can't declare anything, so it always gets the generic yellow message. Both Legacy apps we opened, ScriptRunner and Seibert's Navigation Menus, were blue. We didn't see a yellow one on our site.

If the panel is blue, click "Learn more", because it goes to the vendor's own migration page (for ScriptRunner that's Adaptavist's "moving to Atlassian Forge" page). If it's yellow and has a Learn more link, that's the vendor's plan, and the plan may well be "no". If it only points you to the Marketplace listing, the vendor hasn't declared anything, so contact them there.

There's also a yellow "Update your app now" variant. It appears when your version is older than one with a Forge manifest. Updating removes that message, and if the new version still has Connect parts you'll get the regular panel instead.

Check 3: look at the Authorization tab

This one's for when you want to see the difference with your own eyes. On our site, ScriptRunner's Authorization tab mixes plain-English permissions with old Connect-style ones in capitals: ACT_AS_USER, ADMIN, DELETE, PROJECT_ADMIN and READ. Our own Forge app, Sentinel Vault, lists only plain permissions such as "Read Confluence detailed content" and "App Storage scope".

I wouldn't use this as a test by itself. It's a hint. I find it most useful when you're talking to a vendor and want to ask which of those permissions will change after the move.

Check 4: find Atlassian's own Connect apps

The Legacy tag skips Atlassian's own apps. I didn't expect that. On our list, six entries have a details link containing /user-connected-apps/connect/jira/ and an app key: Atlassian Assist, Atlassian Home for Jira Cloud, Automation for Jira, Jira Service Management Widget, Opsgenie and Statuspage for Jira. Opsgenie's details page shows version 2.0.3-AC and a "Descriptor URL" link. Connect apps have a descriptor; Forge apps have a manifest.

Six more are easy to miss. Confluence Cloud for Microsoft Teams, Confluence Cloud for Slack, and Jira Cloud for Microsoft Teams, Outlook, Slack and Spreadsheets sit at the top of our list with no details link at all, so the URL trick can't see them, but the Marketplace lists all six as Connect. So for Atlassian's own integrations, I'd simply note down every row that says "by Atlassian".

I couldn't find an Atlassian statement on whether these are in scope for end of support, are exempt, or are being migrated. A developer asked "Why hasn't Atlassian migrated its own apps?" on 21 August, and nobody from Atlassian answered in the thread. I'm not going to guess. If your teams depend on one of them, Automation for Jira especially, ask your Atlassian account team or open a support ticket and get the answer in writing.

Two shortcuts that didn't help on our site

Atlassian's August 2025 post on custom apps said you could tell Connect from Forge by the details URL: Connect apps had /connect/<product>/<app-key>/ in it and Forge apps an opaque ID. On our site only Atlassian's own Connect apps had /connect/ in the URL. All four Legacy apps had the same opaque ID format as our Forge app, Sentinel Vault. (The two we opened had blue panels, which need a Forge manifest, so they're probably Connect apps partway to Forge. The test may still work for a pure Connect app. We didn't have one to try.)

The other shortcut is the old app-management REST API (/rest/plugins/1.0/), which older inventory scripts call. We called it on our site: Jira returned 206 entries, 10 of them flagged as Connect, all of them Atlassian integrations with an -AC version. Confluence returned 211 entries with 2 Connect ones. None of our own four Forge apps appeared, and neither did the other third-party apps, Legacy ones included. It looks like an inventory and it isn't one, so I'd stick to the Connected apps page and page through it by hand.

What admins see on the Connected apps page: end-of-support warnings and LEGACY apps since July 2026

Atlassian rolled the admin messages out in stages from mid-July 2026: apps with no declaration, a "no" or "undecided" in late July, and apps whose vendor declared "yes" in September. Some apps are blocked on a missing Forge feature that Atlassian accepted as a blocker. Those are left out of the messages for now, and get them a month after the blocker is resolved.

One Atlassian page still reads as if none of this has happened. The overview page for adopting Forge, last updated in March 2025, says the migration-intent feature is "only available to a canary cohort of developers" and that "the messaging will not be visible to all users yet". The page about what admins see is newer (10 September) and says the messages rolled out to all customers, which matches what we saw on our site.

For private apps, the ones your company built itself or had built and installed by link, Atlassian's guidance uses the same "LEGACY" status and the same Connected apps page. Atlassian's March 2025 timeline said installing new private Connect apps would stop from March 2026, so most private Connect apps you find will be older than that.

What to ask each vendor about its Connect to Forge migration

For Marketplace Connect apps, Atlassian's FAQ says "No action is required at this stage from you as an admin". It tells you to contact the vendor through the app's listing. I'd do that now rather than in January, because a vendor's support queue in the last weeks before a deadline is not a fun place to be. These are the questions that get you a usable answer:

  1. When will a version with no Connect modules be out? Ask for a month, and ask whether it's "Forge" or "Forge with remaining Connect modules", since Atlassian still counts the second as Connect.
  2. Will the move need my approval? A Forge update that changes permissions, adds outside connections or changes remote backends is usually a major version, and major versions wait for an admin to consent. Atlassian's Limitations and differences page for apps adopting Forge says the first Forge version may or may not need approval. If it does, find the "Update" tag on Connected apps, open View app details, review the new permissions and select Update. Mihai wrote up the 11 changes that force a Forge major version from the vendor's side, if you want to know what to expect.
  3. Will my data and configuration come across? Atlassian staff confirmed in September that data migration only works within the same Marketplace listing. If you're thinking of swapping to a different vendor's Forge app, there's no built-in way to bring your data along.
  4. Where will my data live afterwards, and does the app send anything outside Atlassian? Atlassian's data residency glossary says Connect app data "may be stored outside of the Atlassian cloud environment by a third-party app vendor". An app can also qualify for the Runs on Atlassian badge, which needs Atlassian-hosted compute and storage, matching data residency and admin control over data egress. Others keep their own servers. Either can be fine, as long as you know which one you're getting.
  5. Will the Runs on Atlassian badge change? Atlassian's Manage an installed app page warns that an update can gain or lose eligibility. Its absence doesn't prove an app is still on Connect, because the badge has extra requirements on top of Forge. We went through what the badge does and doesn't promise in our post about Sentinel Vault's AI review.

A good vendor answer looks like K15t's Forge transition page, which lists each app with a dated status ("Migration done (July 2026)", "Migration in progress. Target: end of October 2026"). A worrying one is no answer, or a date that still says "late 2026" without saying what happens in January.

Here's the email I'd send, adjusted for the app:

Hi, we run <app name> on <site>.atlassian.net. Our Connected apps page tags it
Legacy ahead of Connect end of support on 31 January 2027.
1. In which month will you release a version with no Connect modules left?
2. Will that update need admin approval, and which permissions change?
3. Will our data and configuration carry over automatically?
4. Where will our data be stored afterwards, and does the app send data outside Atlassian?
Thanks, <name>

If the vendor says no, or never answers

Give it two weeks, then ask once more through the support link on the Marketplace listing. If the answer is "no plan" or silence, treat the app like one of your own private apps (that section is below): find out who uses it, look for a native feature or another app that does the job, and plan the switch before January. Keep in mind Atlassian's data migration only works within the same Marketplace listing, so with a different vendor's app your data comes across only if that vendor offers an import, and otherwise you start fresh. A blue panel needs less of this. I'd still send the email, mostly to get the approval and data questions answered.

What stops working after 31 January 2027, and what keeps running

Nothing in Atlassian's pages says your Connect apps switch off on 31 January. The March 2025 post says customers "won't lose access to the app". The August 2026 post says Atlassian will "share more detail on timelines and next steps for Connect beyond end of support". There's no shutdown, block or uninstall date published anywhere I looked.

What does change, from the August 2026 post: "Atlassian will only address critical security patches. Support SLAs will be relaxed, and Connect will no longer evolve alongside the Atlassian platform." Connect capabilities can be removed "with significantly less notice". And the sentence I'd put in front of anyone who wants to wait it out: some platform changes "will cause apps to stop functioning without advance notice". The 2025 post put it more bluntly, that end of support means "use at your own risk".

Is that a reason to panic about each Legacy tag? I don't think so. Atlassian says "over 95% of paid app seats have been migrated to Forge", counted in paid seats rather than apps. It doesn't say whether apps that still have Connect parts count as migrated, and ScriptRunner, one of the biggest paid apps, still carries the Legacy tag on our site. So I'd expect the gaps to sit mostly with small apps, free apps and private ones, but check the big ones too.

There's also an audit angle. An Atlassian staff member wrote in June that for enterprise customers with SOC 2 and ISO 27001 obligations, an unsupported framework is "a material risk". Those customers were already asking how to find their Connect apps. If your auditors ask, the Connected apps page and the vendor answers are your evidence.

Private Connect apps you built yourselves: rebuild, replace or uninstall

I think private apps are where admins have most of the work. There's no vendor to email. Atlassian says it "won't directly update or rewrite installed apps" and won't support apps left on Connect after 31 January 2027. Its private-apps guidance boils down to a short audit for each LEGACY private app. Work out what business problem it solves and who uses it. Check whether a native Jira or Confluence feature, or a simpler workflow, could replace it. Then rebuild it on Forge, replace it, or uninstall it.

Atlassian's August 2025 post lists the signs of a private app. It was installed by link or in developer mode and isn't in Marketplace search. You hold its source code, and it has no licensing information. On the Connected apps page, a Marketplace app has a related-links sidebar and a private one doesn't.

If nobody knows who built it, Atlassian's advice is to bring in a Solution Partner. Any team with Forge experience and access to the code can do the rebuild. It's work we do too, and our Forge app development page is the place to start, but please check the uninstall option first. A private app nobody can name an owner for is often an app nobody uses.

An admin checklist for the 106 days before 31 January 2027

This is the order I'd work in, starting this week:

  1. Open Connected apps for each site you own and write down the apps with a Legacy tag or an Update tag, plus every row that says "by Atlassian".
  2. Open View app details for each Legacy app and note whether the panel is blue or yellow, and the "Learn more" link if there is one.
  3. Apply pending updates on apps that show the "Update your app now" message, after reading the new permissions.
  4. Email the vendor of each Legacy app with the questions above, yellow ones first. Keep their answers with your audit evidence.
  5. Ask your Atlassian account team about the "by Atlassian" rows from step 1 that your teams rely on.
  6. Decide on each private app: rebuild, replace or uninstall, with an owner and a date before January.
  7. Check again in December. The tags and panels change as vendors declare and ship, and Atlassian said it will eventually show migration notices inside the apps themselves, with advance notice and a testing period first. I couldn't confirm whether those in-app notices are live yet.

Planning a migration around the same January date? Mihai's post on why Cloud Fortified keeps probing an old Connect URL shows what a vendor's half-finished move can look like from the inside.

Where we stand, and where I could be wrong

We're a vendor too, so you should know where we sit: our four apps (CogniRunner, Sentinel Vault, LeanZero Management and Cost Slasher) have no Connect modules, and the Marketplace marks their current versions as not Connect.

This is one test site on one morning. Keep that in mind. Our list is full of development installs and test apps, so the 4-of-57 figure says nothing about a normal company's site, where I'd expect more Marketplace apps and more tags. I didn't open the details panels for STAGIL or TechTime. I didn't see an end-user banner inside an app either. And the wording has varied a lot this year, so yours might read differently. If you see a version I haven't quoted here, send a screenshot to office@leanzero.net and I'll add it.

My recommendation: do steps 1 to 4 of the checklist before the end of October, so the vendors have had three months to answer before January. Then spend whatever time is left on your private apps, because nobody else is going to fix those for you.

Originally published on leanzero.net. More Atlassian, Forge and local-AI write-ups at leanzero.net/blog, and if you're planning a migration or a Forge app, that's what we do: leanzero.net/services.

title: When Your AI Assistant Gets Frontier Brains: The Work You Can Newly Hand Over (and What to Verify)
description:
Every few months, the model inside a consumer AI assistant gets quietly replaced with a smarter one. Most coverage treats this as a leaderboard event — who's on top, who got embarrassed. For a small business owner, it's something more practical: a moving line. Capability jumps move the line between work you have to do yourself and work you can hand over.

Meta just moved the line. The Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full models are the company's first genuine frontier models, and they were built specifically for agentic tasks — the release examples are navigating an insurance claim, making sense of a lease, and working through someone's finances. Two details matter beyond the benchmarks: Active Memory, which carries what matters to you across conversations, and Active Focus, which keeps a task moving when it gets hard — trying other approaches, recovering from errors, and checking in before following through on anything important.

One honesty note before the hype: Wonder is rolling out to subscribers first, not the entire free tier today. So the shift is arriving in tiers, not all at once. But the direction is set — the assistant you already use is getting a brain that doesn't just summarize work, it does work. Here's how to think about what newly crosses the line, and where you still have to be the checkpoint.

What a capability jump actually changes

The question is never "which model is smartest." It's "which of my tasks just crossed from assistant-shaped to doer-shaped." Assistant-shaped work produces a summary of a job. Doer-shaped work produces the job. Every tier jump converts a category you used to babysit into a category you can delegate, and the conversion is worth real money — but only if you notice it.

The Wonder-class jump is specifically about long, multi-step work over messy real documents. That's the category that used to bounce. Three task families just crossed the line:

  1. Document wrangling. Hand over a lease, a supplier contract, an insurance policy, or a franchise agreement and ask for the obligations extracted: what you owe, when, what triggers penalties, what's unusual compared to a standard agreement. A weaker model gives you a generic summary. A frontier-class one reads the actual text in front of it and works the problem — and with memory, it remembers what it found when you ask a follow-up next week.

  2. Disputes and claims. Assembling the timeline from a messy email thread, drafting the escalation chain for an unpaid invoice or a rejected insurance claim, and keeping it moving across multiple touchpoints over days. This is exactly the multi-step, follow-through-shaped work agentic models are now built for — the claim-navigation example in Meta's release is not a hypothetical use case; it's the design target.

  3. Financial sense-making. "Here's my last three months of statements — what changed, what should I worry about?" Not bookkeeping; a first-pass read that tells you where to look. You verify before acting, but the hours of gathering and initial pattern-spotting move off your desk.

Notice what's not on the list: anything where the output goes straight to a customer without review, anything requiring knowledge of facts you can't verify, and anything that's your actual judgment. Capability jumps convert tasks, not responsibility.

The boundary that didn't move

Here's the part the benchmark charts won't tell you: Wonder Full scores 30 on AA-Omniscience — a factual-recall test — versus 46 for Claude Opus 5.5. Knowledge is the model's thin side. Its relatively low hallucination rate means it's less likely to invent missing facts, which is a real mitigation. It is not a license to skip verification.

So draw the verify line explicitly. Before anything derived from Wonder-class work touches reality, check:

  • Dates and deadlines. Renewal windows, notice periods, claim filing limits. A missed deadline is where a summarized document becomes a lawsuit.
  • Dollar amounts. Every figure extracted from a contract, policy, or statement gets checked against the source. Transposition errors are cheap to catch and expensive to miss.
  • Legal and policy references. If the output cites a statute, a clause, or a coverage term — open the source and confirm it says what the assistant says it says.
  • Anything with regulatory or financial force. The pattern is simple: the stronger the consequence of being wrong, the less delegable the verification.

The useful feature here is Active Focus's check-in behavior — the model is built to pause and confirm before following through on anything important. That's a natural checkpoint, if you use it. Set the expectation up front: "Show me the draft and the extracted facts before anything gets sent or filed." A frontier brain with a checkpoint habit is an employee. Without one, it's a liability with good prose.

Run the conversion test this month

Don't take a benchmark's word for it — run your own. Pick two real tasks from the doer-shaped categories above, one document wrangle and one dispute or claim that's actually rotting on your list. Give the full messy inputs, not a cleaned-up version. Then score it the only way that matters: did the job get done — obligations extracted, timeline assembled, escalation drafted — or did you get a nice summary of a job that still needs doing? Verify the facts on the short list above, and time-box the whole thing to a week.

If it finishes, you've just converted hours of skilled reading and drafting into review work. If it doesn't, you've learned the line hasn't moved for your use case yet — and it will, probably within a quarter, because the direction of frontier capability arriving inside consumer assistants is now the least uncertain thing in technology.

The models will keep improving. The owner's job doesn't change: decide what crosses the line, keep the verify list short and non-negotiable, and let the checkpoint — not the benchmark — be the thing you trust.

If you want the full delegation framework — the permission ladder that matches tasks to trust levels, the first-month inspection habit, and the escalation contract format that tells an agent exactly when to come back to you — it's written down in The AI Agent Owner's Playbook. $49 CAD, instant download.

title: Shared neural renderer cuts agent learning rounds
description:
Shared visual engines are the missing lever for scaling code‑defined simulation, and AgentGarten proves that a single neural renderer can slash the number of learning rounds required for agents to master new games. Instead of millions of reinforcement‑learning episodes, agents converge after just four rounds when fed rendered observations.

Before this work, most visual RL pipelines relied on handcrafted graphics pipelines or heavyweight game engines that demanded per‑world rendering code and massive interaction budgets. Techniques such as domain randomization and pixel‑based policies typically required millions of steps to acquire even rudimentary tactics, and the community accepted long training horizons as inevitable for visually rich environments.

Agents learn from just 4 rounds compared with millions for a conventional reinforcement learning counterpart. “Our empirical study demonstrates a substantial gain in learning efficiency, with agents learning from just 4 rounds compared with millions for a conventional reinforcement learning counterpart.”[1] The shared neural renderer supplies real‑time visual observations across many worlds, letting each round of experience be distilled into playbooks that subsequent agents inherit and refine.

In hide‑and‑seek, shelters appeared by round 4 and ramp crossings by round 10, and the same procedure improved outcomes in four further worlds. “In hide-and-seek, seen only through rendered observations, shelters appeared by round 4 and ramp crossings by round 10, and the same procedure improved outcomes in four further worlds.”[1] Complex spatial strategies—hiders building panel shelters by round 4 and seekers constructing ramps to cross walls by round 10—emerge within ten interaction cycles, a dramatic acceleration over prior pixel‑based baselines.

The results are limited to code‑defined worlds whose dynamics are expressed through structured conditions exported to the renderer; visual fidelity remains lower than that of photorealistic engines, and the Adversarial Forcing distillation step may not generalize to unseen physics or textures. Moreover, the “millions versus 4 rounds” comparison hinges on conventional RL baselines rather than the strongest pixel‑based models, leaving open how the approach scales when paired with more sophisticated agents.

Benchmark suites for visual reinforcement learning should add a shared‑renderer track that measures episode efficiency under a common neural rendering service. If agents can acquire complex behaviors in single‑digit rounds, development cycles across dozens of simulated games will contract dramatically, reshaping how research teams allocate compute and time.

References

  1. AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents

title: A cancer drug is a classifier. My body is the dataset.
description:
I'm a data scientist with stage IV cancer. I build an AI tool that matches patients to clinical trials — but the model I can't stop thinking about isn't in my code. It's the drug in my arm.

A cancer treatment is a classifier. Not as a metaphor — literally. Every dose of chemo, every round of radiation, every targeted drug makes the same binary call, billions of times over: this cell — kill it, or spare it? The ground truth is malignant or healthy. The whole fight is a classification problem, and my body is the dataset it runs on.

Once you see it that way, the confusion matrix stops being a diagram and becomes a diagnosis.

I'm not the first to see it. In 2014 a group of researchers formalized exactly this — cancer drugs as classifiers — into a framework for designing more selective drugs, treating a therapy as a (suboptimal) classifier that tells malignant cells from healthy ones by their molecular profiles (Lawlor et al., PLOS ONE 2014). They modeled the classifier from the outside, to build better ones. I've spent two years living inside its test set — and the view from in here is different.

The four cells — and they're literal cells

True positive — a cancer cell killed. The therapeutic effect. The tumor shrinks. This is the only cell anyone is rooting for.

False positive — a healthy cell killed. This is toxicity. Every false positive has a name: the hair, the crashed blood counts, the mouth sores, the neuropathy in my feet. Side effects aren't a separate thing from the treatment — they are its false-positive rate, made flesh. Not all of it is a cell struck dead; some is healthy tissue damaged, a nerve misfiring, an immune system thrown off balance. But it's the same error at root — the drug acting where it shouldn't, and the body paying for it.

False negative — a cancer cell that survived. The ones that got away. And here is what makes this the most unforgiving classifier I know: it can take just one false negative — a single surviving cell with the capacity to seed new growth — to rebuild the entire tumor. Miss that one positive and, months later, it quietly undoes all the true positives you were so proud of. And the cell that survives needn't be one that was always going to: under the drug's pressure, cells can acquire resistance they didn't start with — so what grows back is often a harder problem to classify than the one you began with.

True negative — a healthy cell, correctly left alone. The silent majority — most of me, on a good day. Nobody celebrates a true negative, but they're the reason I can walk around between infusions.

The metrics are the whole history of oncology

Oncologists don't say precision and recall. But that's what a century of cancer drugs has been chasing.

When the goal is a cure, recall has to be almost perfect. Of all the cancer cells, what fraction did you kill? In most machine-learning problems you can live with 0.9. Here, 0.9999 can still lose — because the 0.0001 that survived is alive and dividing. Cancer is the classification problem where a handful of missed positives regrow into the whole thing. That's why treatment is so brutal: you're not trying to be mostly right, you're trying not to miss a single one.

And no single systemic drug gets there. A drug in the bloodstream reaches everywhere and kills imperfectly — broad coverage, mediocre recall. So a cure, when it's possible, is an ensemble: induction chemo shrinks the tumor to cut the burden, then surgery or radiation takes the bulk with near-perfect recall inside its field, and systemic therapy mops up whatever slipped the net. Each classifier covers another's blind spot. You stack them because not one of them, alone, clears the last cell.

Precision is the part your body pays for — a different question from recall. Not what fraction of the cancer you killed, but: of all the cells you killed, what fraction were actually cancer? Chemotherapy is a catastrophically low-precision classifier. Its decision rule is barely a rule at all — "kill whatever's dividing fast" — so its false positives are precisely your fast-dividing healthy tissues: the gut lining (nausea), the hair follicles (baldness), the bone marrow (the blood counts that crash). The side-effect profile is just a readout of a crude decision boundary.

And the two trade off — that tradeoff is cancer treatment. Push the dose higher to raise recall — kill more cancer, at least until the dose-response flattens — and precision falls: more healthy cells die, more toxicity, until the false positives start threatening to kill the patient themselves. The maximum tolerated dose an oncologist reaches for is, exactly, how far you can trade precision for recall before the false positives turn lethal. Chemo asks you to poison your whole body a little to be more sure you got the cancer.

So the entire arc of better cancer drugs is a campaign to raise precision without surrendering recall — to sharpen the boundary so it catches cancer and spares the healthy. Targeted therapies pick a mutation only the cancer carries. Antibody-drug conjugates — the class of the drug in my arm — bolt a targeting antibody onto a chemotherapy warhead: a feature engineered to lower the false-positive rate by carrying the poison closer to the cancer. Closer, not exclusively — the payload still leaks in transit, the target still sits on some healthy cells, and the neuropathy in my feet is proof the false positives never hit zero. A sharper boundary, not a perfect one. A tumor-specific target is nothing but a feature with real area under the ROC curve — one that separates malignant from healthy cleanly. Most targets don't, quite; they're shared with some normal tissue, and that leftover overlap has a clinical name too: on-target, off-tumor toxicity. False positives from an imperfect feature.

Immunotherapy retrains the classifier itself. Cancer survives partly by looking like self — fooling the immune system's own classifier into labeling it "healthy." Checkpoint inhibitors take the brakes off that classifier. And when the retrained immune system starts over-calling — attacking healthy tissue it now flags as foreign — you get colitis, pneumonitis, thyroiditis: autoimmune side effects that are, exactly, the immune classifier's false positives.

And all of it runs on the worst class balance imaginable — which is exactly what makes precision so merciless. Cancer cells are a vanishing fraction of the cells in a body. So a drug can be highly specific — spare the overwhelming majority of healthy cells, hold its false-positive rate low — and still kill more healthy cells than cancer ones in sheer count, simply because the healthy cells so enormously outnumber the targets. High specificity, low precision: that's the signature of a rare positive class, and it's why even a fairly selective drug can feel like it's poisoning your whole body. Put that beside a false-negative cost that's existential and a false-positive cost paid in your own tissue, and I don't know a harder classification problem.

A worked example: the drug in my arm

Put the drug I'm actually on through this lens. Becotatug vedotin is an antibody-drug conjugate: an antibody that recognizes EGFR — a protein my cancer, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, carries at high levels — welded to a cytotoxic warhead called MMAE. MMAE (monomethyl auristatin E) is a microtubule poison: it jams the scaffolding a cell has to build in order to divide, and it's so potent that it would be far too toxic to put into a vein on its own. That toxicity is the point: the antibody is what makes an otherwise-unusable warhead usable, by carrying it only where it's wanted.

And "where it's wanted" isn't a single feature. For the drug to kill a cell, several things all have to be true at once: EGFR on the surface for the antibody to grab, the whole conjugate pulled inside and digested to free the MMAE, the cell dividing when the poison lands, and no pump spitting the drug back out. The real feature is that conjunction — EGFR and internalizing and dividing and not-effluxing, all ANDed together — and that's exactly why it's selective: almost no healthy cell checks every box, so the false positives fall. It's also where resistance hides, because a cell escapes by failing any single clause — shed the antigen, go dormant, or learn to efflux the drug.

Its Phase 3 trial pitted it against the conventional alternative: standard chemotherapy, the doctor's choice of capecitabine or docetaxel — drugs whose decision rule is essentially "attack whatever divides fast." Docetaxel, in fact, goes after the very machinery MMAE does — the microtubules a cell needs to divide — just in mirror image. The warhead wasn't exotic; what changed was the aim: a sharp feature against a crude one.

In classifier terms, the result is exactly what the sharper feature should buy. Against chemotherapy, becotatug vedotin produced about two and a half times the response rate (30.2% vs 11.5%), roughly doubled the time before the cancer regrew (median progression-free survival 5.8 vs 2.8 months; hazard ratio 0.63), and trended toward longer survival at the interim look (17.1 vs 12.0 months; hazard ratio 0.73, not yet conclusive) — all in patients whose disease had already slipped past two or more prior lines of treatment (ASCO 2025, abstract LBA6005). It didn't win with a more violent poison — its warhead is a cytotoxic like the others. It won with a better boundary: a feature, EGFR, that tells my kind of cancer cell from my healthy ones more cleanly than "divides fast" ever could.

That's the whole thesis in a single trial — and worth stating precisely. Those numbers describe a population, not a prophecy. A median is a fact about a few hundred strangers; what the drug is doing inside me I read off scans and side effects, not off a survival curve. But the reason it's the drug in my arm at all is that, across that population, a sharper feature beat the doctor's best crude one.

The objective function changes when it spreads

Everything above assumes you're playing for a cure — driving recall toward one, because a single survivor regrows the tumor. That's curative intent: early-stage disease, the adjuvant setting, the places where gone is still on the table.

I'm not in that setting. My cancer is metastatic — it spread. For some people even that leaves a narrow path to cure: oligometastatic disease, a few deposits you can still ablate one by one. But mine is widespread, and there the arithmetic changes — not because the drugs got weaker but because the ensemble lost its best member. Surgery and radiation reach near-perfect recall inside a field; they can't touch disease seeded microscopically through the whole body. Take the local step away and only the broad, imperfect systemic classifiers are left — and alone, they don't reach one. Recall of 1.0 isn't a target I keep missing; for disease spread like mine, it's no longer the one I'm realistically playing for. Durable control is.

So the objective function changed. I'm not trying to classify every cell correctly, once. I'm running a control problem — hold the tumor burden down, keep the false positives (the toxicity I'll carry for as long as this lasts) livable, and keep the classifier running as long as the math allows. The false negatives I've stopped trying to zero out. I've conceded them; the fight now is over what they're allowed to do, and how much of me it costs to hold them there.

A curative patient is solving a one-shot classification: miss nothing. I'm solving something closer to control — keep a system in a tolerable state, over time. A different loss function entirely. And in mine, a false positive I'll carry for years can weigh more than a false negative I've already made my peace with.

Every new line of treatment is the next split in the tree

A classifier doesn't have to be a single decision. String them together and you get a decision tree: a sequence of splits, each one working only on the data that survived the split before it. That's what lines of treatment are. First-line therapy makes its cut; the cancer that comes back is, by definition, the subset of cells that landed in that drug's false-negative region — the ones it couldn't separate out. So when I choose a next line, I'm choosing the next split in the tree, and it only ever operates on the survivors.

Which quietly dictates a rule every oncologist already follows: don't reach for a drug whose boundary looks like the last one's. A split highly correlated with one you've already made buys almost no information — the cells it could have carved off are already gone, and what's left is precisely the part that kind of feature can't touch. That's cross-resistance, stated in the language of trees: near-zero conditional gain. It's why the next line usually changes mechanism rather than reloading a cousin of the drug that just failed, and why we stack combinations — several splits at once, each covering the cells the others miss — always weighed against what each new cut costs in healthy tissue.

But two things break the tidy picture, and both are why this is the hardest version of the problem. The first: the data isn't fixed. Every split I make changes the distribution. It kills the sensitive cells and leaves behind — enriches — the resistant ones. I'm not fitting one tree to a frozen dataset; I'm splitting a population that reshapes itself, adversarially, in answer to every cut. Each line selects for the clone that beats it. Changing mechanism is the counter-move — a fresh feature the survivors haven't been selected against, which buys back some of the lost ground. How much depends on how independent the new mechanism is: swap one cytotoxic for a close cousin and the survivors' general hardiness — drug efflux, dormancy, a defused self-destruct — carries straight over; hand the killing to something that works on entirely different rules, like the immune system, and the reset can be far deeper. What moves that floor is the overlap between the new mechanism and the ones the tumor has already beaten — not the number of lines you've been through. Overlap keeps it high; a mechanism independent enough can push it back down. It's never guaranteed to be one-way: the right switch can leave the tumor more vulnerable, not less.

The second is that I'm choosing these splits almost blind. In a real decision tree you know every feature value and every label, so you can compute which split gains the most. I can't. I don't fully know which features my tumor is even carrying — the molecular readout is partial, and a snapshot ages. The response odds are borrowed from trial populations that aren't me. So I'm not maximizing information gain; I'm maximizing expected information gain under deep uncertainty — and sometimes choosing a line not because it's the likeliest to work, but because it will tell me something about what I'm fighting. Explore versus exploit, played for the highest stakes there are.

Where it breaks: I can't see the matrix

Here's the part that keeps me up.

You never get to see this confusion matrix. You can't count the cells.

The whole four-box reality is inferred from two blurry shadows. Recall, I read off a scan — a tumor that shrank means a lot of true positives, roughly, in aggregate. Precision, I read off myself — how sick I feel is the false-positive rate, translated into symptoms. And the cell I most need to know is the one I can't see at all: the false negative. The single cancer cell that survived the last infusion and is, as I write this, quietly dividing. Minimal-residual-disease tests are a smudged attempt to glimpse that false-negative rate — did any escape? — and even they can't see one cell.

So the classifier runs across billions of cells in my body; I'm told its approximate recall months later, in a radiology report, and its precision continuously, in how I feel. The confusion matrix that decides how long I live is computed in the dark, and I only ever see its shadows on the wall.

The best classifier may not exist yet

Here's what makes control worth it. The set of classifiers I get to choose from isn't fixed. Every year, oncology ships better ones — drugs with sharper features, mechanisms that didn't exist when I was diagnosed. The drug in my arm now wasn't on the table for me when I started. The frontier — the best boundary anyone can yet draw between my cancer and me — keeps moving outward, slowly and unevenly, but it moves.

So for a metastatic patient, control isn't only holding a tolerable state for its own sake. It's buying time against that moving frontier — staying in the game long enough for a better classifier to arrive. The loss function isn't just "keep the tumor down"; it's "keep the tumor down until the tooling improves." Every month held is a month closer to a feature sharp enough to change the math. It's a bet, not a promise — the better drug may not come in time — but it's the bet the whole strategy rests on.

And you don't wait for it passively. The better classifier might already exist — in a trial that hasn't reached my clinic, in a drug class my oncologist hasn't reached for, in a study running in another country. So part of the job, the part I can actually control, is searching: scanning that frontier, continuously, for a boundary sharper than the ones I've already been offered. It's a discipline of its own — most of what you find won't fit, and a trial is a candidate, not a cure — but when the classifiers you've got are failing, looking is the move with the most upside left. It's not a coincidence that searching for a better one is the thing I decided to build.

The name of the thing

I find it steadying anyway — the way it's steadying to know the name of the thing trying to kill you. My treatment isn't a mystery or a punishment. It's a classifier working the worst class imbalance there is, paying for its false positives in my own healthy cells. Side effects are its precision problem. Recurrence is its recall problem. And with cure no longer the realistic goal for disease spread like mine, mine isn't trying to win the classification outright — only to keep it running, tolerably, for as long as the math allows. "Precision oncology" is the long campaign to sharpen the boundary enough to buy more of that.

Every cancer drug is a classifier. My body is the dataset. And the one cell that matters most — the one that got away — is the one neither of us can see.

title: Comment les réseaux DePIN gèrent-ils la vérification physique du matériel déployé (Proof of Physical Work) ?
description:
Rédigé avec l’aide de l’IA

Guide pédagogique crypto

Comprendre « Comment les réseaux DePIN gèrent-ils la vérification physique du matériel déployé (Proof of Physical Work) ? » avec des explications précises, des exemples et des sources vérifiables.

Mis à jour le 17/10/2026

Définition : de quoi parle-t-on ?

Les réseaux DePIN (Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Networks) sont conçus pour décentraliser la gestion d’infrastructures physiques telles que les stations météo, les relais IoT ou les serveurs edge. Contrairement aux chaînes de blocs traditionnelles qui vérifient uniquement des transactions numériques, ces réseaux intègrent un mécanisme appelé preuve de travail physique. Celui‑ci associe un jeton numérique à un appareil réel, garantissant que le matériel exploité est bien présent, opérationnel et respectueux des règles établies.

À quoi cela sert-il ?

La preuve de travail physique vise à sécuriser la confiance dans les réseaux DePIN. Elle permet aux participants de confirmer que le matériel déployé est réellement en place et fonctionne comme annoncé, ce qui est essentiel pour les services qui dépendent de la disponibilité géographique et de la performance des équipements. En imposant des vérifications physiques, les réseaux réduisent les risques de fraude, améliorent la qualité du service et facilitent la rémunération équitable des opérateurs.

Comment cela fonctionne, étape par étape

  • Déploiement du matériel et inscription Dans un premier temps, le propriétaire du dispositif scanne un code QR unique, qui localise l’équipement et l’enregistre dans le registre distribué. Cette action crée un identifiant numérique lié à l’adresse physique du matériel.

  • Collecte de données de performance Une fois l’appareil activé, des capteurs mesurent en continu la température, la vitesse d’horloge et la consommation énergétique. Ces mesures sont transmises à la blockchain sous forme de paquets cryptés, assurant l’intégrité des données.

  • Vérification indépendante et audit Des vérificateurs tiers, souvent des réseaux de drones ou des caméras autonomes, comparent les données transmises avec des lectures physiques sur place. Si les valeurs concordent, un nonce est ajouté au registre, attestant de la présence réelle du matériel.

  • Rémunération basée sur la preuve Une fois la preuve validée, le protocole distribue des jetons proportionnellement aux heures de fonctionnement et à la qualité mesurée. Ce système incite les opérateurs à maintenir le matériel en bon état et à répondre aux exigences de service.

Exemple concret (scénario fictif)

Imaginons un réseau DePIN de stations météo décentralisées. Un contributeur, Alice, installe une station dans une zone rurale. Pour valider son matériel, elle soumet des données GPS, des photos et des relevés météorologiques. Le réseau utilise un mécanisme de vérification multi-étapes : d'abord, un traitement groupé des données vérifie la cohérence des informations. Ensuite, des nœuds vérificateurs valident la géolocalisation via des satellites. Enfin, un consensus est atteint par vote des participants. Si la station est approuvée, Alice reçoit des jetons en récompense. Un jour, une anomalie est détectée : les données de température divergent des stations voisines. Le réseau déclenche une vérification physique aléatoire. Alice doit fournir une nouvelle preuve, sinon ses jetons sont gelés. Cette approche garantit l'intégrité du réseau tout en incitant les contributeurs à maintenir leur matériel.

Différences et cas d’utilisation

Preuve de travail physique vs. Preuve d'enjeuLa preuve de travail physique exige une vérification matérielle concrète, comme des données GPS ou des capteurs, tandis que la preuve d'enjeu repose sur la possession de jetons pour valider des transactions. La première est adaptée aux réseaux DePIN car elle lie la récompense à une présence physique, alors que la seconde privilégie l'investissement financier.Vérification centralisée vs. DécentraliséeUne vérification centralisée dépend d'une autorité unique pour valider le matériel, ce qui crée un point de défaillance. En revanche, une vérification décentralisée utilise un réseau de participants pour confirmer les données, réduisant les risques de fraude et augmentant la résilience du système.Preuve statique vs. DynamiqueUne preuve statique, comme une photo, peut être falsifiée ou réutilisée. Une preuve dynamique, telle que des données en temps réel ou des capteurs, garantit une vérification continue. Les réseaux DePIN privilégient cette approche pour s'assurer que le matériel reste opérationnel et bien localisé.

Avantages et intérêts possibles

  • Les réseaux DePIN qui utilisent une preuve de travail physique permettent de lier directement la récompense à la présence réelle d’un dispositif, ce qui décourage les acteurs malveillants qui ne pourraient simuler leur participation sans déployer effectivement le matériel requis.

  • En outre, la vérification périodique du fonctionnement du matériel via des capteurs ou des attestations cryptographiques crée un incitatif économique à maintenir les équipements en bon état, améliorant ainsi la fiabilité globale du service rendu aux utilisateurs du réseau.

Inconvénients et limites

  • La mise en œuvre d’une preuve de travail physique exige souvent l’installation de capteurs supplémentaires ou de modules de télémétrie, ce qui augmente le coût initial et la complexité de déploiement pour les petits opérateurs qui pourraient être écartés du réseau.

  • De plus, la dépendance à des mesures physiques externes introduit des points de failure liés à l’environnement (intempéries, vandalisme ou pannes de connectivité) qui peuvent entraîner des pénalités injustes ou des périodes d’indisponibilité non imputables à la mauvaise foi du participant.

Risques réels à connaître

  • La fraude matérielle est un risque majeur : des participants malveillants peuvent simuler la présence d'appareils ou falsifier des données pour obtenir des récompenses indues, compromettant l'intégrité du réseau.

  • Les pannes ou la dégradation du matériel peuvent entraîner une perte de revenus pour les contributeurs, surtout si le réseau ne prévoit pas de mécanismes de compensation ou de maintenance proactive.

  • La centralisation des fournisseurs de matériel peut créer des goulots d'étranglement, augmentant les coûts et limitant l'accès, ce qui va à l'encontre des principes décentralisés des réseaux DePIN.

  • Les attaques de sybil, où un acteur contrôle de multiples identités pour manipuler le réseau, sont plus faciles à exécuter si la vérification physique n'est pas suffisamment robuste.

Comment vérifier concrètement

  • Vérifier l'authenticité des appareils via des signatures matérielles ou des certificats uniques peut aider à prévenir la fraude, mais cela nécessite une infrastructure de suivi fiable.

  • Des audits périodiques par des tiers indépendants peuvent confirmer la présence et le bon fonctionnement des appareils, bien que cela ajoute des coûts et des complexités logistiques.

  • L'utilisation de capteurs intégrés pour surveiller l'état du matériel en temps réel permet une détection rapide des anomalies, mais elle dépend de la qualité et de la sécurité des capteurs.

  • Les mécanismes de réputation ou de pénalités pour les participants malhonnêtes peuvent dissuader les comportements frauduleux, mais ils doivent être équitables et transparents pour éviter les abus.

  • La décentralisation de la vérification via des nœuds multiples réduit les risques de manipulation, mais elle exige une coordination et une synchronisation complexes entre les participants.

Pour aller plus loin

Ces références officielles permettent de recouper les règles et les mises en garde ; elles ne valident pas un projet particulier.

  • AMF — informations et prévention pour les épargnants

  • Définition : Double vérification

  • Débuter en crypto

  • Checklist avant transfert

  • Assistant anti-arnaque

FAQ

Comment la preuve de travail physique diffère-t-elle de la preuve d'enjeu ?La preuve de travail physique vérifie l'existence et le fonctionnement d'un matériel réel, contrairement à la preuve d'enjeu qui se base sur la possession de jetons. Elle exige une validation tangible, souvent via des capteurs ou des signatures numériques, assurant que l'appareil est actif et conforme aux règles du réseau DePIN.

Quels défis pose la vérification décentralisée du matériel ?La vérification décentralisée nécessite un consensus entre les participants, ce qui peut ralentir le processus. De plus, la fiabilité des données dépend de la qualité des capteurs et de la sincérité des contributeurs. Une fraude ou une défaillance technique peut compromettre l'intégrité du réseau.

Pourquoi la preuve dynamique est-elle essentielle dans les réseaux DePIN ?Une preuve dynamique permet une vérification continue de l'état du matériel, contrairement à une preuve statique qui ne garantit qu'un état ponctuel. Cela assure que les appareils restent opérationnels et conformes, même en cas de changements ou de dégradations, renforçant ainsi la confiance dans le réseau.
