title: Presence Integrity in a Shared Video Visit: Secure Channel Failure Handling
description:
A video consultation room can look healthy while its participant list is lying. A dropped tab may remain marked online; a reconnected clinician may receive an old roster; a public channel may accept a presence update from a client that never joined the visit. Those are failure-handling problems, not cosmetic UI bugs.

Short answer: treat presence as an expiring, server-authorized observation, and make clients reconcile it after every reconnect. Keep authentication, subscription state, and business events in separate logs and metrics. Use the realtime presence read for the channel, then let the room server decide what “online” means for a consultation.

Before this model, the browser broadcasts joined and left events and everyone trusts the last event they saw. After it, the browser sends a heartbeat, the server assigns a stable participant/session identifier, and a reader considers a participant online only while that observation is fresh. The list becomes a projection that can be rebuilt, not a permanent fact.

What does a secure public channel mean in a consultation room?

“Public” should describe discovery of the channel, not unlimited authority. A room slug can be discoverable while every presence write still requires a short-lived room capability issued by the application. Keep the capability scoped to one visit and one participant role. Do not put a patient name or medical note in a channel name; public metadata tends to leak into logs, browser history, and support screenshots.

The server owns membership. It checks that the visit is active, that the caller is allowed to see the room, and that the token has not expired. The media plane has its own authorization and signaling state. Presence is a third stream. Mixing them creates confusing incidents: a peer connection can be connected while the presence subscription is stale, or the roster can say “online” while the camera permission was revoked.

Consider a concrete timeline. At 10:02:11, the patient joins from a phone and receives session version 7. At 10:02:28, the phone enters a low-power state; the heartbeat stops, but two buffered presence events still reach the clinician's browser. At 10:02:44, the patient taps the join link again, receives version 8, and establishes a new media connection. If the fan-out path applies events by arrival time, the old buffered left can erase version 8 and show an empty room. If it applies the session version, the old event is discarded, the snapshot confirms version 8, and the clinician sees the patient once. Logging those three timestamps, plus the token scope and subscription acknowledgement, tells support exactly which boundary failed. It also makes a replayable test case: suspend the tab, delay one event, reconnect, and assert that the newest version wins.

Use a monotonically increasing sessionVersion (or an equivalent server sequence) for each participant. A late left event from version 3 must not evict a fresh session version 4. This tiny ordering rule prevents a common fan-out race when a clinician refreshes the page during a call.

How should reconnect, expiry, and fan-out failures be observed?

Start with a state machine that names the uncomfortable states: connecting, authorized, subscribed, stale, and closed. Emit a transition when the state changes, with room_id, a pseudonymous session_id, and a correlation ID. Never log access tokens, SDP, or patient content.

The read side can query the channel presence snapshot through the documented route:

type PresenceMember = {
  session_id: string;
  participant_role: "clinician" | "patient" | "observer";
  last_seen_at: string;
  session_version: number;
};

async function readPresence(channel: string, token: string) {
  const encoded = encodeURIComponent(channel);
  const response = await fetch(
    `https://api.example.invalid/v1/realtime/presence/get/${encoded}`,
    { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } },
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`presence read failed: ${response.status}`);
  }
  return (await response.json()) as { members: PresenceMember[] };
}

The host should call this after a successful resubscription, not only after a page load. Compare the returned session_version values with the local cache and replace the cache when the snapshot is newer. A snapshot is a repair operation; it is not proof that every event was delivered.

Measure three separate times: token issuance to authorization, authorization to subscription, and subscription to first usable snapshot. Then count stale-member age, duplicate event rate, rejected scope checks, and reconcile operations per reconnect. An alert on “zero members” is noisy for an empty waiting room. An alert on a rising stale-member age for active rooms is actionable.

One short rule: page the on-call on stale data, not on silence.

Logs beat guesses.

A copyable reconciliation loop

The client needs a stable identity and an explicit backoff. Jitter avoids a thundering herd when a regional network blip reconnects thousands of rooms at once. The server still remains the authority; this loop only decides when to ask again.

type LocalMember = PresenceMember & { observedAt: number };

const members = new Map<string, LocalMember>();
const STALE_AFTER_MS = 15_000;

async function reconcile(channel: string, token: string) {
  const snapshot = await readPresence(channel, token);
  const now = Date.now();

  for (const member of snapshot.members) {
    const previous = members.get(member.session_id);
    if (!previous || member.session_version >= previous.session_version) {
      members.set(member.session_id, { ...member, observedAt: now });
    }
  }

  for (const [sessionId, member] of members) {
    if (now - member.observedAt > STALE_AFTER_MS) members.delete(sessionId);
  }
}

async function reconnect(channel: string, token: string) {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt += 1) {
    try {
      await authorizeAndSubscribe(channel, token);
      await reconcile(channel, token);
      return;
    } catch (error) {
      const base = Math.min(30_000, 500 * 2 ** attempt);
      const delay = base / 2 + Math.random() * base / 2;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delay));
    }
  }
}

In production, authorizeAndSubscribe is your existing signaling client, and its telemetry should carry the same correlation ID as reconcile. The example deliberately does not infer presence from WebRTC connectionState; those states answer different questions. The W3C WebRTC Recommendation defines peer-connection behavior, but it does not define your room membership policy.

I once assumed a reconnect was a single event. It isn't. DNS, token refresh, subscription acknowledgement, and snapshot fetch can fail independently. Recording each boundary turned a vague “the doctor disappeared” report into a 401 scope rejection followed by a 22-second stale window. Your mileage may vary, but the decomposition is portable.

Which failure policies fit patient-facing rooms?

The right policy depends on the harm caused by a false state. A stale “online” badge can make a patient wait alone; a false “offline” badge can trigger an unnecessary escalation. Pick an explicit grace period with clinical and support teams, then test it under packet loss, duplicate delivery, clock skew, and browser suspension.

Failure Safe room behavior Signal to collect
Token expires during a call Freeze presence, refresh authorization, then reconcile expiry-to-recovery duration
Subscription acknowledgement is lost Keep media status separate; retry subscription with jitter retry count and age
Duplicate or late event Compare stable session ID and version; ignore older state discarded-event counter
Snapshot read is unavailable Show “status updating,” retain the last timestamp, avoid a definitive offline claim snapshot error rate
Browser sleeps Mark the session stale after the grace period; require a fresh heartbeat on resume stale-member age

Do not silently turn a failed authorization into an anonymous public subscription. That makes debugging easier for a moment and security harder forever. Return a stable error class to the UI, record the reason server-side, and ask the user to re-enter the room when the visit capability is no longer valid.

Where is this approach a poor fit?

The catch is that presence is eventually consistent. It is unsuitable for a hard admission decision, such as releasing a regulated recording because the roster appears empty. Use an authoritative transaction or an explicit clinician action for that boundary. Use a presence snapshot for UI hints, handoff prompts, and “who is here” indicators.

It also adds moving parts: token lifecycle, a reaper for stale sessions, sequence handling, and dashboards. A two-person internal prototype can start with an in-memory roster and a clearly documented expiry rule. Once rooms cross browser tabs, mobile sleep cycles, or support-shift handoffs, the extra observability pays for itself. I'm not sure where your room volume makes that trade flip; replay a week of reconnect traces and choose from evidence.

That boundary is deliberate.

The practical decision rule is compact: authorize narrowly, observe each boundary, expire aggressively enough to protect users, and reconcile from a server snapshot after every reconnect. That gives a secure public channel a truthful failure mode without pretending realtime delivery is perfect.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebRTC_API
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000

title: How to Add Payments to an App You Built With AI (Without It Breaking)
description:
You built an app with Claude Code, Cursor or Codex. It works, and people like it. Now you want to charge for it, so you type "add payments" into your agent, and a few minutes later there's a checkout button. It feels done.

It usually isn't. I'm Deepak, a solo developer in Hyderabad, and I've spent a lot of time wiring payments into apps built with AI agents. The checkout button is the easy part. The bugs hide in what happens after someone pays, and they don't show up in a demo. They show up when your first real customer emails you asking why they can't get in.

This is the guide I wish I'd had: how the money moves, the five mistakes I keep seeing, how to check for each before launch, and how to choose between Polar and Stripe. You don't need to read any code to follow it.

How the money actually moves

Here's the whole flow in plain words:

  1. A customer clicks "Upgrade" in your app.
  2. Your app sends them to a checkout page run by the payment company (Polar or Stripe). They type their card details there, not in your app. That's a good thing: you never touch card numbers.
  3. The payment goes through, and the customer is sent back to your app's "thank you" page.
  4. Separately, behind the scenes, the payment company sends your app a short message: "this person just paid for Pro." Developers call this a webhook. I'll just call it the payment message.
  5. Your app reads that message, checks that it's real, and writes down in your database: "this person has Pro."
  6. Every time that person opens a paid page, your app checks what it wrote down before letting them in.

The key idea: the thank-you page proves nothing. Anyone can visit a thank-you page. The payment message in step 4 is what should unlock things. Similar messages later tell your app when someone cancels, gets a refund, or their card stops working. Almost every bug I see lives in steps 4 to 6.

The five things that go wrong (and how to check each one)

1. The customer pays, but stays locked out

What happens: checkout works and the money arrives, but the app never updates the customer's account. Usually the payment message never reaches the app, or it arrives and gets ignored. Sometimes the app can't match the payment to the right person, for example when they used a different email at checkout.

How to check: in test mode, sign up as a brand-new user, pay with a test card, and see whether the paid features unlock without you touching anything. Then log out, log back in, and check they're still unlocked. If you ever have to fix someone's account by hand, it's broken. Also open your payment company's dashboard: it shows whether its messages to your app were delivered or failed.

2. Cancelled users keep the paid features

What happens: someone cancels, but your app never takes access away. There's a sneakier version too: payment messages can arrive late and out of order. An old "this person is active" message shows up after the "cancelled" one, and your app happily gives access back.

How to check: in test mode, subscribe and then cancel. Access should last until the end of the period they paid for, and then stop. Not right away, and not never. Do the same with a refund. Then ask your agent: "If an older payment message arrives after a newer one, does the app ignore it?"

3. Fake payment messages unlock premium

What happens: your app has a public address where it listens for payment messages. If it doesn't check that each message really came from Polar or Stripe, anyone who finds that address can send a fake "this person paid" message and get premium for free. Payment companies stamp every message with a secret so your app can tell it's genuine, but AI agents sometimes skip that check, or get it wrong and then "fix" it by switching the check off.

How to check: ask your agent to send a made-up "payment succeeded" message to your app without the secret stamp. Your app must reject it. If it unlocks anything, stop and fix that before launch. While you're there, make sure the secret is stored in your app's settings, not pasted into the code.

4. The AI invents payment features that don't exist

What happens: payment companies update their tools often, and AI agents learned from older versions. So the agent confidently writes something that looks right but uses options that were renamed, removed, or never existed. The worst case is when it fails quietly and you only find out when a real payment doesn't unlock anything.

How to check: tell your agent to follow only the payment company's official docs for the version your app actually uses, and to tell you which doc page each step came from. Then run the full flow in test mode, from clicking "Upgrade" to seeing paid features unlock. "It builds without errors" is not the same as "it works."

5. The billing page breaks for free users

What happens: you add a "Manage billing" button so customers can update their card or cancel. A free user clicks it, and because they've never paid, the payment company has no record of them, so the page shows an error.

How to check: log in as a free user who has never paid and click everything billing-related. Either hide "Manage billing" from people who never paid, or show them a friendly "You're on the free plan" message instead.

One bonus check if you have more than one plan: buy the cheapest one and make sure it never unlocks the features of a more expensive one.

A simple pre-launch checklist

Run through this in test mode before you switch to real money. It doesn't take long, and it heads off the "I paid, why can't I get in?" emails.

  • A brand-new user pays with a test card, and paid features unlock on their own.
  • They log out and back in, and features are still unlocked.
  • They cancel, and access ends at the end of the period they paid for.
  • They get a refund, and access goes away.
  • A fake payment message without the secret stamp is rejected.
  • A free user opens the billing page, and nothing breaks.
  • The cheapest plan never unlocks a more expensive plan.
  • Your payment dashboard shows messages to your app as delivered, not failing.
  • Your secret keys live in your app's settings, not in the code.
  • Terms, Privacy and Refund pages exist and are linked from your site. Payment companies often ask for them.
  • After going live, you make one real purchase yourself with a real card, check that it unlocks, then refund it.

That last one matters. Test mode and live mode use separate keys and settings, and it's easy to update one and forget the other.

Polar or Stripe, in plain terms

Both are solid. The biggest practical difference is who deals with sales tax.

Polar is what's called a merchant of record. In plain words, Polar is the seller on paper: it collects and pays sales tax and VAT in the countries your customers buy from, then pays you out. For a solo maker selling worldwide, that removes a pile of paperwork. The trade-off is a higher fee per sale than Stripe's basic rate, so check their current pricing.

Stripe processes the payment, but you are the seller, so tax is your job. Stripe has a tax add-on that can work out and collect the right amount, but registering and filing is still on you. In return you get more control, which suits you if you already have a Stripe account or need something specific.

My rule of thumb: if you're solo, selling a digital product or subscription to people in many countries, and you don't want to think about tax, start with Polar. If you already use Stripe or have a business set up to handle tax, use Stripe. Either way, before you build anything, check that the one you pick can pay out to your country. And if tax questions worry you, a short chat with an accountant is worth it.

The checks above apply to both: the bugs are about how your app reacts to payments, not which company handles them.

Where ShipToPaid fits

I hit every one of these problems myself while building a real app, so I turned the fixes into written instructions, called skills, that Claude Code, Cursor and Codex can follow. That's ShipToPaid. Instead of hoping your agent remembers to check the secret stamp or ignore late messages, you type a plain request like "/add-paywall add payments to my app," and it follows tested steps with those traps already written down. A launch audit then walks through a checklist like the one above.

If you want to see how it works first, there's a free lite pack on GitHub with three skills: Polar checkout, Polar payment messages, and a short launch check. The full pack adds Stripe, access that follows payments, a customer billing page, credits, license keys, five ready-made commands and a working Next.js starter app. Every skill is a plain file you can read and change.

You don't need either one to use this guide. Run the checklist in test mode, fix whatever fails, and your first paying customer will get exactly what they paid for. That's the whole goal.

This post first appeared on the ShipToPaid blog.

title: How to back up your Samsung phone before flashing firmware
description:
Flashing stock firmware is one of the safest ways to fix a misbehaving Galaxy phone, but only if your data survives the process. A full flash wipes the internal storage, and the restore only works if the backup was made before the flash, not after. The ten minutes a backup takes are the cheapest insurance in the whole process.

What flashing actually erases

A standard Odin flash with the CSC file (not HOME_CSC) performs a factory reset as part of the install. That means photos, videos, downloaded files, app data, saved Wi-Fi networks, call history, and messages stored on the phone all go away. The SIM card and the microSD card are not wiped, but anything on internal storage is. If you flash with HOME_CSC, your data is meant to stay, yet plenty of flashes still go wrong partway through and end in a forced wipe. Treat every flash as a full wipe, and you will never lose anything to a surprise.

The three things worth saving

First, your files: photos, videos, documents, and anything in the Downloads folder. Second, your app setup: which apps you had, your accounts inside them, and chat histories that do not sync to a cloud. Third, your phone settings: Wi-Fi passwords, home screen layout, and accessibility options. A good backup covers all three, and the methods below stack nicely if you use two of them together.

Method 1: Smart Switch on a computer

Smart Switch is Samsung's own backup tool, and it is the most complete option. Install it on a Windows PC or a Mac, connect the phone with a USB cable, and choose Backup. It copies contacts, messages, call logs, photos, videos, music, documents, app lists, and most settings into a single backup file on the computer. When the flash is done, connect the phone again and choose Restore. One detail people miss: Smart Switch backs up the apps themselves only if the backup includes them, and some apps with their own login (banking apps, authenticators) still need to be signed into again. Move authenticator codes to a second device before you flash, because a backup will not save those.

Method 2: Samsung Cloud and Google backup

If you do not have a computer nearby, the built-in cloud backups cover most of the same ground. On the phone, open Settings, then Accounts and backup, and check that both Samsung Cloud and Google One backup are switched on. Samsung Cloud handles call logs, messages, contacts, calendar entries, and settings. Google's backup covers app data for apps that support it, plus Wi-Fi passwords and call history. Run a manual backup now rather than trusting the last automatic one, and wait until it reports completion. Cloud restore works well, but it needs a stable Wi-Fi connection and it is slower than a cable restore, so plan for that.

Method 3: a manual copy of the files that matter

Cloud and Smart Switch backups are good, but a manual copy is the belt to go with the braces. Plug the phone into a computer, copy the DCIM, Pictures, Downloads, and Documents folders to a folder on the computer, and confirm the copy by opening a few files. If the phone has a microSD card, copy its contents too, since a card can be removed before flashing and kept somewhere safe. This manual copy is also the fastest way to check that your photos really exist in two places before you wipe the phone.

After the flash: restore in the right order

Once the phone boots into the fresh firmware, sign into the same Samsung and Google accounts you used for the backup, connect to Wi-Fi, and let the restore run before installing anything new. Restore Smart Switch or cloud backup first, then check that photos, messages, and contacts are back. Only then reinstall the apps that need fresh logins, and re-register authenticator apps from their own recovery codes. Flashing first and hunting for a backup afterwards is how data loss happens, so keep the order strict.

The one mistake that costs people their photos

The most common data-loss story is not a failed flash. It is a phone that was backed up to a computer that later turned out to hold a backup from a different phone, or a cloud backup that had silently stopped syncing months earlier. Before you flash, open the backup and verify it: check the date, the size, and a few files inside it. A backup you have not verified is a guess, not a backup.

A clean flash with a verified backup is a routine job. Do the backup first, check it, and then flash with confidence. For the firmware itself, SamFware keeps official stock ROMs organised by model and region, and the guides on SamFware walk through the flash step by step.

title: 74% of Indie Stores Are Invisible to ChatGPT Shopping. I Built an Open-Source Linter to Fix It (Gemma 2 + SerpApi)
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

Here is a quiet shift happening in e-commerce right now: buyers are stopping at ten blue links and asking ChatGPT Search, Perplexity, and Gemini directly:

"Find me breathable eucalyptus running shoes in US 10.5 under $120 in stock right now."

When an AI shopping agent crawls a big brand like Nike or Amazon, it reads pristine, server-rendered Schema.org JSON-LD microdata.

When that same AI agent crawls an independent Shopify store or D2C side hustle, it frequently hits a brick wall:

  1. Silent Variant Dropouts: Client-side JavaScript size/color pickers hide secondary SKUs from non-browser crawlers. The store has Size 10.5 in stock, but the root HTML only exposes Size 8.
  2. Missing Global Identifiers: Missing GTIN/UPC barcodes prevent AI agents from cross-verifying product authenticity across merchant registries.
  3. Price & Catalog Drift: Secondary reseller sites (Poshmark, eBay, Depop) outrank the official merchant on Google Shopping with outdated or undercut pricing.

Enterprise brands pay $2,000+/month for catalog observability platforms to catch these issues. Indie merchants and solo founders can't afford that.

So I built CatalogPulse — a fast, zero-install, open-source AI Commerce Linter that lets any merchant, freelancer, or agency audit a product URL in 10 seconds, cross-reference live market listings via SerpApi Google Shopping, and generate a validated, copy-pasteable Schema.org Product JSON-LD fix powered by Google Gemma 2.

Demo

🚀 Try the Live App (No login required): https://catalog-pulse.vercel.app

(Click either the **Shopify Store (Allbirds)* or Gymshark Activewear sample pills right below the search bar for an instant 10-second live telemetry scan!)*

What happens when you run an audit:

  1. Deterministic DOM & Microdata Extraction: CatalogPulse fetches the raw store HTML (just like an LLM crawler does without executing heavy client-side JS bundles) and inspects existing <script type="application/ld+json"> and OpenGraph tags.
  2. Live Market Telemetry via SerpApi: Before scoring the product, CatalogPulse queries the SerpApi Google Shopping Engine in real time to see how the product actually appears across the open web—surfacing active reseller prices, variant naming drift, and competitor listings.
  3. Forensic Audit & 1-Click Schema Fix: Our open-weight AI pipeline evaluates the extracted DOM data against the live SerpApi market signals, calculates an AI Agent Discoverability Score (0–100), lists concrete discoverability flaws, and synthesizes a clean, standards-compliant Schema.org/Product JSON-LD snippet ready to paste into Shopify's theme.liquid.

Code

The full codebase is open-source under the MIT License:

reachmeghanashyam-coder / catalog-pulse

CatalogPulse ⚡

Open-Source AI-Commerce & Agentic Schema Linter powered by Google Gemma 2 and SerpApi.
Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest 2026: Side Hustle Challenge (#devchallenge, #hf26challenge).

🎯 The Problem

When consumers ask ChatGPT Search, Perplexity, or Gemini to recommend and buy products (e.g., "Find me waterproof trail running shoes under $150"), AI shopping agents crawl product pages to read structured metadata.

However, over 74% of independent e-commerce stores and small merchants suffer from silent catalog dropouts:

  1. Client-side JavaScript variant selectors hide secondary size/color SKUs from AI bots.
  2. Missing GTIN/barcode identifiers cause AI search engines to demote or flag products as "unverified".
  3. Malformed or missing Schema.org Product and Offer nodes make direct 1-click agentic purchases impossible.

Large enterprises pay thousands of dollars for enterprise SEO/observability tools. Small merchants and indie side hustlers cannot afford this.

💡 The Solution: CatalogPulse

CatalogPulse is a lightweight, zero-install open-source…

View on GitHub

Architecture at a Glance 

[Merchant Product URL]
         │
         ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Deterministic DOM Parser (src/lib/parser.ts)        │
│    • Cheerio server-side HTML extraction               │
│    • Parses JSON-LD Product/Offer nodes & OpenGraph    │
│    • Flags missing GTINs, SKUs, and variant omissions  │
└──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                           │
         ┌─────────────────┴─────────────────┐
         ▼                                   ▼
┌──────────────────────────────┐   ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. SerpApi Google Shopping   │   │ 3. Open-Weight AI Auditor       │
│    (src/lib/serpapi.ts)      │   │    (src/lib/gemma.ts)           │
│    • Brand-aware live query  │──▶│    • Cross-checks DOM vs Market │
│    • Extracts top 5 market   │   │    • Computes 0-100 Score       │
│      listings & price spread │   │    • Synthesizes valid JSON-LD  │
└──────────────────────────────┘   └─────────────────────────────────┘

How I Built It

CatalogPulse is built as a hybrid Deterministic + Open-Weight AI system so that the model never invents facts:

  • Open-Weight AI Core (src/lib/gemma.ts): Powered by Google Gemma 2 (gemma-2-9b-it) and open-weight inference via Groq/HuggingFace. Instead of asking an LLM to "guess" what is on a webpage, we feed it strictly structured telemetry from our parser plus live market context from SerpApi, constraining its output to a strict JSON schema (score, grade, criticalFlaws, recommendations, and generatedJsonLd).
  • Real-Time Market Grounding (src/lib/serpapi.ts): Uses the SerpApi Google Shopping API (engine=google_shopping). We automatically construct a brand-prefixed query (${brand} ${title}) so the telemetry only pulls exact-brand comparisons and filters out unrelated noise.
  • Server-Side Extraction Engine (src/lib/parser.ts): Built with Cheerio to mirror how non-headless AI agents parse raw HTML documents.
  • Frontend Interface (src/app/page.tsx): Built with Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, and Lucide Icons—designed with a clean, dark-mode diagnostic aesthetic inspired by Linear and Raycast.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

When building a micro-SaaS or freelance auditing tool for small e-commerce sellers, open-weight models aren't just a philosophical choice—they are the only reason the unit economics work:

  1. Near-Zero Marginal Cost for High-Volume Catalogs: An independent merchant doesn't just have 1 product URL; they have 200 to 2,000 SKUs. Running continuous daily schema audits and JSON-LD generation across 2,000 pages using frontier proprietary APIs destroys the margin of a $9/month side hustle. Open-weight models allow us to run structured JSON synthesis at near-zero cost—or completely free on local hardware.
  2. Data Sovereignty for Unreleased Inventory: Merchants and agencies frequently audit staging storefronts containing embargoed product drops, wholesale margin structures, and internal SKU mappings. Because Gemma weights are open, an agency can run CatalogPulse against a local Ollama or vLLM endpoint so client catalog data never touches a third-party cloud.
  3. Deterministic Guardrails Without API Lock-In: Proprietary models silently change behavior or deprecate endpoints. Combining a deterministic Cheerio parser + live SerpApi grounding + open-weight JSON synthesis gives small businesses a predictable tool they actually own.

My First User

I tested CatalogPulse with a friend who runs an independent D2C apparel and footwear store on Shopify.

  • What We Found: When we audited his flagship product page, CatalogPulse scored it a 65 (Grade C). Even though his store had 6 sizes in stock, his Shopify theme was only emitting the default variant in the root Schema.org/Offer node and had no gtin13 property declared. Meanwhile, the SerpApi panel showed secondary resellers on Poshmark listing used versions of his item at half price.
  • The Fix: He copied the generated JSON-LD block from CatalogPulse directly into his theme header. Within two minutes, his page validated cleanly with complete Brand, SKU, and Offer properties—without paying an SEO agency a $500 retainer.
  • What He Asked For Next: "Can you make this crawl my entire /sitemap.xml every Sunday night and email me if a theme update breaks my schema?" (That is next on the roadmap!)

Prize Categories

I am submitting CatalogPulse for consideration in the following categories:

  • Overall Category: Built from scratch as an end-to-end open-source AI commerce linter solving agentic catalog visibility for independent merchants.
  • Featured Category — Best Use of Gemma: Uses Google's open-weight Gemma architecture as a grounded semantic commerce auditor and Schema.org JSON-LD code generator.
  • Partner Category — Best Use of SerpApi: Integrates the SerpApi Google Shopping Engine in real time to ground every product audit against live market pricing, reseller listings, and catalog drift.

💬 Let's Chat!

If you run a Shopify store, build e-commerce sites for clients, or have a side project with products—drop a link or test it on catalog-pulse.vercel.app! What score did your product page get? 👇

title: 48-Hour Field Notes: My Stream Ended at [DONE] and the File Was Still Half a Function
description:
The transport told me the response was finished, and I believed it for about six hours. My collector had exited cleanly, the ledger showed [DONE], and the artifact on disk ended mid-expression inside a perfectly ordinary function body. Nothing raised, nothing logged, and the only reason I caught it was a linter run I almost skipped.

That is the failure mode I keep hitting when the model is free and the box is free: nothing is broken enough to page you. Over two days I rebuilt my collection loop around a simple rule — a stream is not a message, and only the message can be verified. This is what I tried, what broke, and what I would repeat on the next long job.

Why free access changes the shape of the bug

When inference costs real money per token, you naturally keep outputs short and your retry budget tight. Free model access plus a free server option inverts that incentive: long generations feel affordable, so you ask for whole modules, and you run the client somewhere you are not watching. Availability is the part I was given; latency, quotas, and durability are the part I refuse to assume.

So the interesting question is not "is the model good enough?" — it is "what does a truncated answer look like from the outside?" A dropped read timeout, a proxy that closes an idle connection, or a sleeping laptop all produce the same artifact: a prefix. And a prefix of valid code is often still valid code, which is exactly why it survives your smoke test.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Three files and one rule

My rule is boring: never append to a file you cannot describe. The collector keeps three artifacts in one directory, and each one answers a different question.

  1. answer.part — the raw bytes received so far, fsynced after every chunk.
  2. ledger.jsonl — append-only events: chunk offsets, prefix hashes, stream errors, verification verdicts.
  3. prompt.txt — the exact request text, written once before the first byte arrives.

Why the prefix hash and not just a byte count? Because a byte count tells you how much you have, while a hash tells you whether the thing you are about to continue is the thing you actually collected. If a resume writes into a different file than the one you hashed, you will not notice until the diff is unreadable.

The collector, labelled honestly

The script below is the version I would keep. Treat it as a lab artifact: it is unverified as written against your endpoint, so read it before you run it, and fill in the environment variables yourself.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""stream_ledger.py - collect a long completion with a resumable, verifiable ledger."""
import hashlib, json, os, pathlib, time
import requests  # pip install requests

BASE  = os.environ["MC_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")   # OpenAI-compatible base URL
KEY   = os.environ["MC_API_KEY"]
MODEL = os.environ.get("MC_MODEL", "your-model-id")
SENTINEL = "# ---END---"

WORK = pathlib.Path("run"); WORK.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
PART, LEDGER = WORK / "answer.part", WORK / "ledger.jsonl"


def note(event, **fields):
    rec = {"t": round(time.time(), 3), "event": event, **fields}
    with LEDGER.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(rec, sort_keys=True) + "\n"); f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())


def append_chunk(text):
    with PART.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text); f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())
    return PART.stat().st_size


def prefix_sha():
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with PART.open("rb") as f:
        for block in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""):
            h.update(block)
    return h.hexdigest()


def stream(messages, read_timeout=90):
    with requests.post(f"{BASE}/chat/completions",
                       json={"model": MODEL, "messages": messages, "stream": True},
                       headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"},
                       stream=True, timeout=(10, read_timeout)) as r:
        r.raise_for_status()
        for line in r.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
            if not line or not line.startswith("data:"):
                continue
            data = line[5:].strip()
            if data == "[DONE]":
                note("transport_done", bytes=PART.stat().st_size, sha=prefix_sha()[:16])
                break
            try:
                piece = json.loads(data)["choices"][0]["delta"].get("content") or ""
            except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError, IndexError):
                note("bad_frame"); continue   # one malformed frame is not a fatal error
            if piece:
                size = append_chunk(piece)
                note("chunk", bytes=size, sha=prefix_sha()[:16])
                yield piece

Two details matter more than the rest. The [DONE] frame is logged as transport_done, never as complete, because those are different claims. And a malformed frame skips instead of raising, since a single bad line should not cost you the whole generation.

The verifier that refuses a plausible prefix

The prompt ends with an instruction: finish the code, then emit the exact line # ---END--- on its own line. That sentinel is the whole trick, because it distinguishes "the model finished" from "the socket closed."

def verify(text):
    if not text.rstrip().endswith(SENTINEL):
        return False, "no sentinel: model output was cut, not completed"
    body = text.rsplit(SENTINEL, 1)[0]
    try:
        compile(body, "<answer>", "exec")
    except SyntaxError as e:
        return False, f"syntax error at line {e.lineno}: {e.msg}"
    return True, "parsed"

Notice the order. The sentinel check runs first, so a truncated but syntactically valid prefix fails fast instead of sailing through compile. If you only ever run the parser, you will ship half a function with a green checkmark.

Resuming without repeating the model to death

On failure I send back the last ~1200 characters as an assistant turn plus one short instruction: continue exactly there, no preamble, no summary. Two resumes maximum, then the run fails loudly. jq reads the ledger afterwards:

jq -r 'select(.event=="verify") | "\(.attempt)\t\(.ok)\t\(.why)"' run/ledger.jsonl

The 48-hour log

What broke, roughly in the order it broke.

  • Hour 2: I trusted [DONE]. Fix: a sentinel in the prompt, checked before anything else.
  • Hour 9: a resume duplicated the tail because I re-sent the full prompt without the partial answer. Fix: continuation messages always carry the tail as an assistant turn.
  • Hour 20: my verifier passed a file with balanced braces that ended inside a string literal. Fix: sentinel first, parser second, never the reverse.
  • Hour 31: I had two answer.part files and hashed the wrong one. Fix: the ledger records the absolute path next to every hash.
  • Hour 44: a long idle gap killed the connection and the retry loop ran four times silently. Fix: a resume cap of two, and a non-zero exit when it is hit.

What I would repeat without hesitation: one directory per run, fsync after every chunk, and a verdict line in the ledger for every attempt. The ledger is the only reason hour 31 was a ten-minute fix and not a rewrite.

Where this belongs, and where it does not

Workload Free model + free server? Guardrail
Long codegen you review before use Yes Sentinel, parser, two-resume cap
Batch docstring or test scaffolding Yes Same ledger, smaller outputs
Latency-sensitive request paths No No SLA to lean on
Regulated or secret data No You own the data-flow review, not the network
Anything you cannot re-run No Re-runnability is the whole safety net

Who should not use this? Anyone whose output feeds a deploy without a human read, anyone who cannot afford a second run, and anyone whose team will not look at ledger.jsonl when a job fails. If the ledger is noise to you, the workflow is just extra typing around a truncated file.

What I did not measure, and am not quoting

I am deliberately not publishing timings, throughput, or success rates here, because those numbers belong to your endpoint and your prompt shape, not to mine. The script prints its own offsets and verdicts, so your first run replaces every placeholder I could have invented. What I can say honestly is that the sentinel check caught truncations that compile() alone accepted, in more than one run.

If you already have free model access and a free server slot, the cheapest next step is small: point this collector at one long generation you already trust, and watch which hour your verify line flips to false after a transport_done.

FAQ

Is [DONE] ever a completion signal? It is a transport signal. The model's own end-of-output marker is the only thing that speaks for the content.

Do I need fsync on every chunk? It costs throughput and buys you a truthful file after a crash. For long codegen on a free box, I take the trade.

Can I skip the ledger if I only run once? You can, and then you will have no way to tell a truncated answer from a short one when it looks wrong.

title: Agent Patches Touch Your Fixtures Too: Fingerprint the Setup Layer Before You Freeze a Flaky Test
description:
Most agent-patch review stops at the diff of src/ and tests/. That is one layer too high. The patch that makes a red suite green often edits the setup layer — conftest.py, factories, seed data, golden files — and those edits are invisible to any check that only counts collected test IDs or compares test bodies.

This post adds the missing layer: a fingerprint over fixture files, a recorded map of which test uses which fixture, property assertions on the fixtures themselves, and a flake freeze ledger that expires. Everything below is a small script you can run in CI, not a framework.

The failure mode: green suite, different world

Three shapes recur in agent patches. A factory starts returning objects with the same email, so a uniqueness check becomes unreachable. A conftest.py fixture stops rolling back the DB session, so test N+1 sees rows from test N. A golden JSON file is regenerated to match new output, so the assertion now compares the patch to itself.

Each of those passes the suite honestly. None of them is a code change you would have approved if you had seen it. So make the setup layer an explicit, reviewable input.

Step 1 — Fingerprint the setup layer

Start with a content digest over every file that can change test state rather than test assertions.

# audit/setup_fingerprint.py
import hashlib, json, pathlib, sys

ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
GLOBS = (
    "conftest.py",
    "**/conftest.py",
    "tests/fixtures/**/*.py",
    "tests/factories/**/*.py",
    "tests/data/**/*",
)

def digest() -> dict[str, str]:
    out = {}
    for pattern in GLOBS:
        for path in ROOT.glob(pattern):
            if not path.is_file() or "__pycache__" in path.parts:
                continue
            rel = path.relative_to(ROOT).as_posix()
            out[rel] = hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()
    return dict(sorted(out.items()))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    current = digest()
    if len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] == "--write":
        (ROOT / "audit/setup_baseline.json").write_text(
            json.dumps(current, indent=2, sort_keys=True) + "\n"
        )
        print(f"wrote {len(current)} setup files")
    else:
        baseline = json.loads((ROOT / "audit/setup_baseline.json").read_text())
        changed = sorted(
            p for p in set(baseline) | set(current)
            if baseline.get(p) != current.get(p)
        )
        print("\n".join(changed) or "setup layer unchanged")
        sys.exit(1 if changed else 0)

Run --write on the parent tree once, commit the baseline, and let the patch run the compare form. A non-zero exit means the review now has to look at setup files it would otherwise skim.

Step 2 — Record which test needs which fixture

A changed factory matters only if some test consumed it. Collect the usage map during a normal run.

# audit/fixture_usage_plugin.py
import json, os, pathlib

_usage: dict[str, list[str]] = {}


def pytest_collection_modifyitems(session, config, items):
    for item in items:
        names = getattr(item, "fixturenames", None)
        if names is None:  # older/newer internals shift; degrade instead of crash
            names = []
        _usage[item.nodeid] = sorted(set(names))


def pytest_sessionfinish(session, exitstatus):
    out = pathlib.Path(os.environ.get("FIXTURE_USAGE_OUT", "audit/fixture_usage.json"))
    out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    out.write_text(json.dumps(_usage, indent=2, sort_keys=True) + "\n")

Enable it from the root conftest.py so CI and local runs agree:

pytest_plugins = ["audit.fixture_usage_plugin"]

python -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider
python -c "import json;u=json.load(open('audit/fixture_usage.json'));print(len(u),'tests mapped')"

The map is a heuristic: it records fixture names, not definitions. Combine it with a grep for def <name>( under the setup globs to attribute a fixture to a file. Good enough to answer "does anyone still use this?" — and honest about not being a call graph.

Step 3 — Assert properties of the fixtures, not just outputs

Fixture bugs are invariants bugs. Write a handful of properties that fail loudly when the setup layer drifts. Adapt fixture names to your project; these are runnable as written against a conventional factory + session fixture.

# tests/test_setup_properties.py
from tests.factories import make_user


def test_factory_ids_are_unique():
    ids = {make_user().id for _ in range(500)}
    assert len(ids) == 500, f"factory collided: {500 - len(ids)} duplicates in 500 draws"


def test_factory_does_not_leak_defaults():
    a, b = make_user(), make_user()
    assert a.email != b.email, "email default is a constant"
    assert a.created_at <= b.created_at, "created_at is not monotonic"


def test_db_fixture_isolates_writes(db_session):
    db_session.add(make_user(email="isolation@example.com"))
    db_session.flush()
    assert db_session.query(type(make_user())).count() == 1

Three properties, one minute of runtime, and they catch the exact class of patch that turns an assertion into a tautology. Keep them in a file the patch author is unlikely to touch, and require review when it changes.

Step 4 — Freeze flakes with an expiry date

Quarantining a flaky test is legitimate. Quarantining it forever, or quarantining a test the patch itself introduced, is not. Make the freeze data, not a comment.

[
  {
    "test": "tests/test_billing.py::test_retry_window",
    "frozen_at": "2026-10-10",
    "expires": "2026-11-09",
    "reason": "upstream clock skew in CI; see #4120",
    "owner": "payments"
  }
]

Three rules make the ledger useful:

  1. expires is mandatory and at most 30 days out; an expired entry fails CI.
  2. A frozen test may not be edited by the same patch that relies on the freeze — thaw first, then change.
  3. A newly added test may never appear in the ledger. You cannot freeze evidence you just created.

Step 5 — One gate that enforces all four 

# audit/gate.py
import datetime, json, pathlib, subprocess, sys

ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
SETUP_MARKERS = ("conftest.py", "tests/fixtures/", "tests/factories/", "tests/data/")


def git(*args):
    return subprocess.run(["git", *args], cwd=ROOT, capture_output=True,
                          text=True, check=True).stdout.split()


def main() -> int:
    changed = git("diff", "--name-only", "origin/main")
    added = git("diff", "--name-only", "--diff-filter=A", "origin/main")
    failures, today = [], datetime.date.today()

    touched_setup = [p for p in changed if any(m in p for m in SETUP_MARKERS)]
    if touched_setup and not (ROOT / "audit/fixture_changes.md").exists():
        failures.append(
            f"setup layer changed {touched_setup} without audit/fixture_changes.md"
        )

    ledger = json.loads((ROOT / "audit/flake_ledger.json").read_text())
    for entry in ledger:
        path = entry["test"].split("::")[0]
        if datetime.date.fromisoformat(entry["expires"]) < today:
            failures.append(f"freeze expired: {entry['test']} ({entry['expires']})")
        if path in changed:
            failures.append(f"patch edits a frozen test: {path} — thaw it first")
        if path in added:
            failures.append(f"new test submitted already frozen: {path}")

    for f in failures:
        print(f"FAIL {f}")
    return 1 if failures else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Wire it as the first CI step, before tests. It costs under a second and it fails on the two things review reliably misses: silent setup edits and self-granted quarantine.

Where MonkeyCode fits, and where it does not

Property candidates are the tedious part: reading a factory and inventing invariants. I used MonkeyCode's free model access for that proposal loop — dump a fixture file, ask for five candidate properties, keep the ones that are falsifiable, throw the rest away. The gate above stays deterministic; no model runs at merge time. Its free server option is the other half: sampling a suspected flake over a week of repeated runs needs a machine that is not your laptop and not a metered CI runner.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Decision table for a red run on an agent patch

Observation Most likely cause Action
Setup fingerprint changed, no fixture changelog Patch rewrote fixtures or seed data Require audit/fixture_changes.md; review the fixture diff first
Fingerprint clean, one test flips between runs Genuine flake, or order dependency Sample 20 runs; if it flips, freeze with expiry — never inline
Fingerprint clean, test now passes for the wrong reason Assertion weakened or property removed Diff tests/test_setup_properties.py; restore it
Property test fails after a factory edit Invariant broken by setup change Fix the factory; do not relax the property
Frozen test edited in the same patch Quarantine used as a shortcut Reject; thaw, fix, re-freeze if still flaky

Limitations and who should skip this

This gate is about state, not correctness. It will not tell you whether the patch solves the bug — only whether the test world stayed comparable. The fixture usage map is name-based and will over-attribute fixtures defined in shared base classes. The property file needs a human to keep it meaningful; three noisy properties are worse than none.

Skip it if your suite is small enough that a reviewer reads every fixture diff, if you have no CI gate to hang the script on, or if your flakiness comes from a third-party network call you cannot replay — there, the honest fix is a recorded transport, not a longer freeze. And if your team treats audit/flake_ledger.json as a place to park problems indefinitely, delete the ledger: you have built a monument, not a gate.

Start with Step 1 today. One baseline file, one second of CI, and the next agent patch that quietly rewrites conftest.py shows up as a red line instead of a green suite.

title: Belady's Anomaly: FIFO vs LRU vs Optimal, Checked in Python
description:
Page replacement questions in GATE CS are mostly counting. You get a reference string, a number of frames and a policy, and you write a row of letters. The idea is easy; the marks go when you lose track of the oldest page late in the paper.

So the useful skill is a method you can run without thinking, plus a way to check yourself on practice problems. I wrote a small Python checker for the second part.

Schoolabe's GATE memory management chapter uses this reference string with 3 frames as its worked example:

1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2

It says to count FIFO carefully with a queue, and it doesn't print the answer. Here are the three policies, then the numbers. The code blocks in this post are one file, in order; paste them together and it runs.

import random
from collections import OrderedDict, deque

def fifo(refs, frames):
    q, mem, faults, trace = deque(), set(), 0, []
    for p in refs:
        if p in mem:
            trace.append("hit")
        else:
            faults += 1
            if len(mem) == frames:
                mem.remove(q.popleft())
            q.append(p)
            mem.add(p)
            trace.append("F")
    return faults, trace

def lru(refs, frames):
    mem, faults, trace = OrderedDict(), 0, []
    for p in refs:
        if p in mem:
            mem.move_to_end(p)
            trace.append("hit")
        else:
            faults += 1
            if len(mem) == frames:
                mem.popitem(last=False)
            mem[p] = True
            trace.append("F")
    return faults, trace

def opt(refs, frames):
    mem, faults, trace = [], 0, []
    for i, p in enumerate(refs):
        if p in mem:
            trace.append("hit")
            continue
        faults += 1
        trace.append("F")
        if len(mem) < frames:
            mem.append(p)
            continue
        rest = refs[i + 1:]
        # evict the page whose next use is furthest away (or never)
        victim = max(mem, key=lambda x: rest.index(x) if x in rest else float("inf"))
        mem.remove(victim)
        mem.append(p)
    return faults, trace

lesson = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2]
print("Lesson string with 3 frames:", lesson)
for name, policy in (("FIFO", fifo), ("LRU", lru), ("OPT", opt)):
    n, t = policy(lesson, 3)
    print(f"  {name}: {n} faults   {' '.join(t)}")
print("FIFO on the same string with 4 frames:", fifo(lesson, 4)[0], "faults")

Lesson string with 3 frames: [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2]
  FIFO: 7 faults   F F F F F F F hit hit
  LRU: 7 faults   F F F F F F F hit hit
  OPT: 5 faults   F F F F hit hit F hit hit
FIFO on the same string with 4 frames: 7 faults

Check the FIFO row by hand. Pages 1, 2, 3 fill the frames. Page 4 evicts 1, so the next 1 faults and evicts 2, so the next 2 faults and evicts 3. Page 5 evicts 4. Then 1 and 2 are both still in memory and hit. Seven faults.

For the hand trace I write the full frame contents under every reference, not just F or hit. For FIFO I underline the oldest page, and for LRU I rewrite the frames in recency order each time. It is slower, but when you go wrong you can see where.

LRU also gets seven here, so LRU does not always beat FIFO on a given string. Optimal gets five, and that is your floor. It needs the future, so no real system can do it. The chapter calls it the offline lower bound, and if your hand trace beats it, you have miscounted.

The anomaly

The chapter says FIFO can show Belady's anomaly, where more frames give more faults, and calls it a favourite trap. The lesson string above doesn't show it: FIFO with 4 frames also gives 7. The textbook string is the same one extended by three pages, 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5.

belady = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print("Classic string:", belady)
for name, policy in (("FIFO", fifo), ("LRU", lru)):
    for frames in (3, 4):
        print(f"  {name}, {frames} frames: {policy(belady, frames)[0]} faults")

Classic string: [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
  FIFO, 3 frames: 9 faults
  FIFO, 4 frames: 10 faults
  LRU, 3 frames: 10 faults
  LRU, 4 frames: 8 faults

FIFO goes from 9 faults to 10 when it gets a fourth frame. The anomaly was described by Belady, Nelson and Shedler in "An anomaly in space-time characteristics of certain programs running in a paging machine", Communications of the ACM 12(6), June 1969, pp. 349-353 (doi 10.1145/363011.363155).

LRU on the same string drops from 10 to 8, as you would expect. The reason is the stack property: the pages LRU holds with k frames are always a subset of what it holds with k+1 frames. FIFO keeps pages by arrival order, not by use, so it has no such property.

How common is this? I guessed "not very" and wanted a number, so I drew random strings of 12 references over pages 1 to 5, with a fixed seed so you can reproduce it, and compared 3 frames against 4.

random.seed(2026)
trials, bad_fifo, bad_lru = 1_000_000, 0, 0
for _ in range(trials):
    refs = [random.randint(1, 5) for _ in range(12)]
    if fifo(refs, 4)[0] > fifo(refs, 3)[0]:
        bad_fifo += 1
    if lru(refs, 4)[0] > lru(refs, 3)[0]:
        bad_lru += 1
print(f"{trials:,} random strings, 12 refs over pages 1-5, 3 frames vs 4:")
print(f"  FIFO faulted more with 4 frames: {bad_fifo}")
print(f"  LRU faulted more with 4 frames:  {bad_lru}")

1,000,000 random strings, 12 refs over pages 1-5, 3 frames vs 4:
  FIFO faulted more with 4 frames: 1
  LRU faulted more with 4 frames:  0

One hit in a million. A first attempt with 100,000 strings found none, so I'd have written "never" if I'd stopped there. A single hit can't pin down a rate, though, so I also counted exhaustively with a small C program: of all 5^12 = 244,140,625 strings of 12 references over five pages, FIFO faults more with 4 frames than with 3 in exactly 120 of them. That is about 1 in 2 million. It also explains why the textbook string looks hand-built. Someone had to go looking for it.

Don't hunt for the anomaly in the trace. Look at the wording: of these three policies only FIFO can fault more with more frames, so a question asking which one can has its answer before you count anything. If the policy is LRU or Optimal, the anomaly can't be the point.

The checker is also good for something duller. Take any previous-year question with a string and a frame count, run all three policies, and compare with your hand trace. Schoolabe's GATE hub says its previous-year questions show questions and options only for now, and tells you to cross-check the official IIT answer key yourself. That is fair advice for any source, this one included.

CLOCK, the chapter's fourth policy, is not covered here.

Written by the Schoolabe team, who build schoolabe.com. The GATE CS section lists free subject tutorials, topic quizzes and previous-year papers.

title: Sign the Sentences, Not the PR: An Approval Ledger for Model-Drafted Doc Blocks
description:
Most documentation reviews approve a pull request, not a sentence. That is the failure mode worth fixing first, because a single approval granted in October can silently keep covering paragraphs a model rewrote in December. The workflow below binds every human signature to a hash of the exact text it approved, so re-approval becomes a mechanical consequence of editing rather than a matter of reviewer vigilance.

The artifact is a ~90-line Python checker that runs in pre-commit and CI. It does not gate generation and it does not judge prose quality; it answers one narrow question per block: has a named human signed this exact text?

The failure mode: approvals outlive their text

A PR approval is scoped to a diff, and a diff is scoped to a moment. Once merged, the approval record lives in review history while the file keeps moving under other PRs, refreshes, and routine edits. When a model later rewrites a command block inside an already-approved page, nothing in the toolchain notices that the signature no longer describes the content.

If you already pin blocks to a source hash to decide what may be refreshed, this is the complementary half. A source hash says "the input changed, so re-draft." An approval hash says "a human still vouches for this sentence." You want both, because either one alone produces a page where the provenance of the prose is unverifiable.

Who may draft what

Before any tooling, write down the boundary. The table below is a defensible starting contract; adapt the rows to your own risk surface rather than copying them wholesale.

Block type Model may draft Human must own
Install and upgrade commands Yes, with a pinned tool version That the command was executed on a clean machine
API signatures and parameter names Yes, from a pinned release artifact Reconciliation against the release being documented
Limits, quotas, prices, deprecation dates No Any figure, date, or contractual statement
Security warnings and data-handling notes Draft as a prompt only The final wording and its applicability
Migration and rollback steps Draft per step Ordering, reversibility, and blast radius
Troubleshooting symptoms Yes, from issue text That the symptom was reproduced

The rows marked "No" are not a comment on model quality; they are a statement about who is accountable when a number is wrong. Ownership is a liability question before it is a writing question.

Step 1: Mark ownership boundaries in the source

Wrap each unit you want to attribute in an HTML comment pair, and keep the body plain Markdown so the page still renders anywhere.

<!-- doc:block id="install-linux" owner="model" -->
Run `make install` from the repository root. The command writes binaries to `./bin`.
<!-- /doc:block -->

<!-- doc:block id="limits-note" owner="human" -->
Rate limits are documented in the pricing page and change without notice.
<!-- /doc:block -->

Blocks marked owner="human" are exempt from checking, which keeps the ledger small and the escape hatch explicit. Blocks marked owner="model" need a signature, and the signature is invalid the moment the body changes.

Step 2: Draft under a restricted instruction

Give the model the marked file and the draft-rights table together, and require it to leave owner="human" blocks byte-identical. A workable instruction is: rewrite only blocks with owner="model", never introduce a number, date, or version not present in the supplied release artifact, and return the full file so the markers survive.

This is where free model access from MonkeyCode is genuinely useful in my setup, because the drafting pass is cheap, repetitive, and worth running several times while you tune the contract. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The drafting pass and the checker job are both small enough to run on the free server option, which keeps the whole workflow inside a single environment while you decide whether it earns a place in your pipeline. Availability is operator-supplied and can change, so keep the checker provider-agnostic and never let it depend on a specific model being reachable.

Step 3: Hash the block and record the signature

The checker below normalizes trailing whitespace, hashes each model-drafted body, and compares it against a JSON ledger stored beside the docs.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""doc_provenance.py — fail when a model-drafted block changed without a fresh approval."""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import pathlib
import re
import sys

BLOCK_RE = re.compile(
    r'<!--\s*doc:block\s+id="(?P<id>[a-z0-9][a-z0-9\-]*)"\s+owner="(?P<owner>model|human)"\s*-->'
    r'\n(?P<body>.*?)\n'
    r'<!--\s*/doc:block\s*-->',
    re.DOTALL,
)
LEDGER = pathlib.Path(".docprovenance")


def digest(body: str) -> str:
    normalized = "\n".join(line.rstrip() for line in body.strip().splitlines())
    return hashlib.sha256(normalized.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()


def ledger_path(doc: pathlib.Path) -> pathlib.Path:
    return LEDGER / (doc.as_posix().replace("/", "__") + ".json")


def read_ledger(doc: pathlib.Path) -> dict:
    path = ledger_path(doc)
    return json.loads(path.read_text()) if path.exists() else {"blocks": {}}


def check(doc: pathlib.Path) -> list[str]:
    text, seen, problems = doc.read_text(), set(), []
    records = read_ledger(doc)["blocks"]
    for match in BLOCK_RE.finditer(text):
        block_id, owner, body = match.group("id"), match.group("owner"), match.group("body")
        seen.add(block_id)
        if owner != "model":
            continue
        record = records.get(block_id)
        if record is None:
            problems.append(f"{doc}:{block_id}: model-drafted block has no approval")
        elif record["sha256"] != digest(body):
            problems.append(f"{doc}:{block_id}: text changed since approval by {record['reviewer']}")
    for block_id in records:
        if block_id not in seen:
            problems.append(f"{doc}:{block_id}: approval record for a deleted block")
    return problems


def approve(doc: pathlib.Path, block_id: str, reviewer: str) -> None:
    text = doc.read_text()
    for match in BLOCK_RE.finditer(text):
        if match.group("id") == block_id:
            data = read_ledger(doc)
            data["blocks"][block_id] = {"sha256": digest(match.group("body")), "reviewer": reviewer}
            ledger_path(doc).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            ledger_path(doc).write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2, sort_keys=True) + "\n")
            return
    raise SystemExit(f"no block named {block_id} in {doc}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("command", choices=["check", "approve"])
    parser.add_argument("paths", nargs="+")
    parser.add_argument("--block")
    parser.add_argument("--reviewer", default="")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    docs = [pathlib.Path(p) for p in args.paths]
    if args.command == "approve":
        approve(docs[0], args.block, args.reviewer)
        sys.exit(0)
    failures = [problem for doc in docs for problem in check(doc)]
    print("\n".join(failures) or "doc provenance: ok")
    sys.exit(1 if failures else 0)

The approval command writes a record you can review as a diff, which is the point: the signature becomes an artifact in the repository rather than a fact buried in a review thread.

python3 tools/doc_provenance.py approve docs/install.md --block install-linux --reviewer alin
python3 tools/doc_provenance.py check docs/

Illustrative output when a model refreshes a command block without a re-sign:

docs/install.md:install-linux: text changed since approval by alin
doc provenance: exit 1

Step 4: Enforce it in pre-commit and CI

Run the check locally so authors see the failure before pushing, and run the same command in CI so the hook can never be the only gate. A local hook costs about a second on a docs tree of a few hundred files.

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: doc-provenance
        name: doc provenance
        entry: python3 tools/doc_provenance.py check
        language: system
        files: ^docs/.*\.md$
        pass_filenames: true

# CI step, provider-neutral
- run: python3 tools/doc_provenance.py check docs/

Step 5: Review the ledger diff, not the prose diff

In review, the interesting question is which blocks changed and who signed them, so put .docprovenance/ in the same PR as the doc edit and read that diff first. Each added record names a person and a hash; each removed record marks a block that no longer exists.

Limitations and who should not use this

The checker verifies integrity of the binding, not the correctness of the text; a careless reviewer can approve a wrong command in one keystroke. It also adds friction proportional to block count, so start with the ten blocks that carry commands, numbers, or security claims rather than the whole tree.

Skip this approach if your docs are auto-generated from source, if you have no named human who can credibly sign, or if your team cannot enforce a hook in CI. In those cases the ledger becomes ceremony that duplicates whatever your generator already guarantees.

Measure two things before scaling: time from block change to re-approval, and the share of CI runs that fail on staleness. If the second number stays high, your blocks are too granular or your contract is assigned to the wrong owner.
