  generated_at: string;
  capabilities: Array<{
    id: string;
    method: string;
    path: string;
    available: boolean;
  }>;
};

async function readInfraiManifest(attempt = 0): Promise<DiscoveryManifest> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return readInfraiManifest(attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }

  return (await response.json()) as DiscoveryManifest;
}

function toSafeEvent(
  error: unknown,
  surface: ErrorSurface,
  correlationId?: string,
): SafeErrorEvent {
  const value = error instanceof Error ? error : new Error("Unknown failure");

  return {
    surface,
    name: value.name,
    message: value.message.slice(0, 500),
    occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    correlationId,
  };
}

@Catch()
export class GlobalErrorFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  constructor(private readonly capture: Capture) {}

  async catch(error: unknown, host: ArgumentsHost): Promise<void> {
    const http = host.switchToHttp();
    const request = http.getRequest<{ headers: Record<string, string | undefined> }>();
    const response = http.getResponse<{
      status: (code: number) => { json: (body: unknown) => void };
    }>();
    const status = error instanceof HttpException ? error.getStatus() : 500;

    await this.capture(
      toSafeEvent(error, "http", request.headers["x-request-id"]),
    );
    response.status(status).json({ statusCode: status });
  }
}

export async function runWorkerJob(capture: Capture): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await Promise.reject(new Error("Worker task failed"));
  } catch (error) {
    await capture(toSafeEvent(error, "worker"));
    throw error;
  }
}

export async function runCronJob(capture: Capture): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await Promise.reject(new Error("Scheduled task failed"));
  } catch (error) {
    await capture(toSafeEvent(error, "cron"));
    throw error;
  }
}

export function installProcessHandlers(capture: Capture): void {
  process.on("uncaughtException", (error: Error) => {
    void capture(toSafeEvent(error, "process"));
  });
  process.on("unhandledRejection", (reason: unknown) => {
    void capture(toSafeEvent(reason, "process"));
  });
}

export async function verifyCaptureContract(): Promise<void> {
  const manifest = await readInfraiManifest();
  const capture = manifest.capabilities.find(
    (capability) =>
      capability.method === "POST" &&
      capability.path === "/v1/errors/capture" &&
      capability.available,
  );
  if (!capture) throw new Error("Error capture capability is unavailable");
}

Call verifyCaptureContract during an integration check, then use the capability-specific schema and TypeScript example returned by discovery to implement the concrete Capture; this avoids fabricating request fields or pinning an undocumented payload. Register the filter globally and wrap each worker and scheduled entry point. A production process handler also needs an explicit shutdown policy after capture; continuing after an uncaught exception can leave state uncertain. Keep that lifecycle decision separate from the reporting adapter. This sequence is deliberately less convenient than pasting a guessed POST body. It is also the point of a self-describing API: the executable integration follows the current machine-readable contract.

One subtle trap remains. A try/catch can report a job that throws, but it cannot report a job that never starts. That gap is structural, not an exception-filter bug.

Silence has no stack trace.

The trust-boundary checklist changes the vendor decision

Before sending even the narrow event above, draw the processor chain. Record the application region, ingestion region, downstream processors, retention duration, deletion mechanism, and which party can access stored payloads. Require evidence for each cell. An unspecified value is not a promise.

Infrai's observability surface does not provide a per-user log deletion interface, while retention and cold-storage configuration are not exposed. Do not route personal data there on the assumption that it can later be erased by user identifier. Keep direct identifiers out of the event, use an internal correlation ID, and retain the identifying join only inside the system whose deletion controls you own. A specialist provider is the better choice when configurable residency, contractual retention, per-user deletion, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Session Replay, or a distributed span tree is mandatory.

The boundary also extends beyond storage. Notification delivery is a separate processor relationship, as are paging, SMS, and webhooks. Infrai has no native notification routing, so an app can poll recent unresolved groups and feed its own alert path. That is workable for a small queue and explicit polling budget. It is a poor fit when mature escalation policies are the requirement.

How do the real alternatives compare?

Do not collapse error trackers and uptime monitors into one category. They answer different failure questions, and the data they receive differs.

Option Evaluate it for Boundary or limitation to verify
Sentry Specialist application error tracking Verify region, retention, deletion, replay, and source-map settings against the exact plan and deployment choice.
Datadog A broader observability stack where errors must correlate with other telemetry The wider telemetry footprint can increase both processor scope and noise; define which payloads and tags are allowed.
Bugsnag Specialist error monitoring with an application-focused workflow Confirm data-location and deletion terms, and test how grouping behaves on the app's real exception mix.
Infrai A small REST ingestion boundary with public schema discovery and no required vendor SDK Bring separate alert routing; it has no heartbeat, span-tree query, replay, or source-map symbolication.
Healthchecks Detecting scheduled work that did not run It complements exception capture; it is not the store for HTTP and worker exception detail.

This is not a universal ranking. Sentry or Bugsnag deserves the first trial when deep error-investigation features drive the decision. Datadog makes more sense when one established platform already owns telemetry correlation and its data boundary is approved. Healthchecks closes the negative-space problem: a missed ping reveals silence that no exception pipeline can observe.

For Infrai, the unusual advantage is inspectability. Public discovery returns the contract and runnable examples before a key is used. Still, discovery of an API schema does not establish residency, retention, deletion, or processor commitments. Those require separate, current evidence.

Measure this before copying the design

Start with signal quality, not event volume. Over a representative release, inspect the ratio of actionable groups to noisy duplicates, the fraction of HTTP, worker, cron, and process failures carrying a correlation ID, capture-path latency, dropped reports, and the time from a new unresolved group to an operator seeing it. For an agent loop, measure token cost and model latency separately, then verify that the correlation ID joins those records without copying prompts into error payloads.

Also run two blunt tests: stop a scheduled job without throwing, and request deletion for a test user. The first proves whether heartbeat coverage exists. The second proves whether the full processor chain can satisfy the deletion path instead of merely documenting one.

No magic here.

The chosen design is useful because its boundary is small enough to reason about. Centralize capture, minimize the payload, preserve correlation, and let specialist systems handle the guarantees they actually provide. If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai discovery documentation and inspect the live capability contract before wiring the adapter.

Sources

  • https://docs.nestjs.com/exception-filters
  • https://docs.nestjs.com/techniques/task-scheduling
  • https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#event-uncaughtexception
  • https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#event-unhandledrejection
  • https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/
  • https://docs.sentry.io/
  • https://docs.datadoghq.com/
  • https://docs.bugsnag.com/
  • https://healthchecks.io/docs/
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery

title: A Trading Bot Is Easy. A Trading Engine Is Not
description:
Building a trading bot is surprisingly straightforward.

Get some market data. Calculate a few indicators. Generate a BUY or SELL signal.

Maybe connect it to an exchange.

Congratulations. You have a trading bot.

But here's the question that changed how I approached NERV Trade, my Java-based trading engine:

What happens after the signal?

What if the broker accepts your order but never responds?

What if an order is partially filled?

What if the same execution arrives twice?

What if the application crashes while updating a position?

And what happens when the application restarts while orders are still active?

These aren't hypothetical edge cases you can safely ignore when building an automated trading system.

They're architectural problems.

And solving them is what separates a simple trading bot from a reliable trading engine.

1. The Trading Bot Everyone Starts With

Most trading projects begin with an architecture similar to this:

Market Data
     |
     v
Technical Indicators
     |
     v
Trading Strategy
     |
     v
BUY / SELL / HOLD

For example, imagine a simple Java strategy:

public enum Signal {
    BUY,
    SELL,
    HOLD
}

public Signal evaluate(
        BigDecimal fastMovingAverage,
        BigDecimal slowMovingAverage) {

    int comparison =
            fastMovingAverage.compareTo(slowMovingAverage);

    if (comparison > 0) {
        return Signal.BUY;
    }

    if (comparison < 0) {
        return Signal.SELL;
    }

    return Signal.HOLD;
}

This is a simplified illustration, not NERV Trade's actual strategy implementation.

It demonstrates the basic idea.

Given market observations, produce a trading signal.

You can improve the strategy by introducing:

  • Multiple indicators
  • Multi-timeframe confirmation
  • Volatility analysis
  • Market regime detection
  • Risk-adjusted signals

But regardless of how sophisticated the analysis becomes, the output is still fundamentally a decision.

BUY
SELL
HOLD

And a decision isn't an execution.

That's where the interesting engineering begins.

2. A BUY Signal Is Not an Order

Suppose our strategy produces:

BUY BTCUSDT

What does that mean?

Does the strategy want to buy Bitcoin?

Has an order been created?

Has the exchange accepted the order?

Has the order been filled?

These are different states.

A more realistic architecture separates them:

Market Data
     |
     v
Analysis
     |
     v
Strategy
     |
     v
Risk Evaluation
     |
     v
Trade Intent
     |
     v
Local Order
     |
     v
Broker Submission
     |
     v
Execution Reports

Each component has a specific responsibility.

Component Responsibility
Analysis Interpret market conditions
Strategy Decide what action to propose
Risk Determine whether the action is permitted
Trade Intent Own the trading lifecycle
Local Order Represent the requested broker action
Broker Adapter Communicate with the external venue
Execution Processor Accept and account for actual fills

This separation is important because a trading decision can lead to multiple orders.

And one order can produce multiple executions.

A strategy should not need to understand those execution details.

Its responsibility is to express an intention.

The execution engine is responsible for determining what actually happened.

3. An Accepted Order Is Not an Executed Order

Consider an order to buy 10 units.

The simplest implementation assumes:

BUY 10
   |
   v
FILLED 10

But a broker might produce:

BUY 10
   |
   v
ACKNOWLEDGED
   |
   v
PARTIALLY FILLED: 3
   |
   v
PARTIALLY FILLED: 7
   |
   v
FILLED: 10

The order has a lifecycle.

Its state changes over time.

A simplified representation might look like:

public enum OrderStatus {
    CREATED,
    SUBMITTED,
    ACKNOWLEDGED,
    PARTIALLY_FILLED,
    FILLED,
    CANCELLED,
    REJECTED
}

Again, this is an illustrative model rather than NERV Trade's exact domain API.

The important distinction is that an order's status is not the same thing as its economic effect.

An order might be acknowledged without any execution.

It might be partially filled and later cancelled.

It might be fully filled through several independent executions.

The engine must track both:

What the broker says about the order

and

What executions have actually occurred.

Those are related but different responsibilities.

4. Partial Fills Introduce Accounting

Let's take the previous example.

Order: BUY 10

Execution 1: BUY 3 @ 100
Execution 2: BUY 4 @ 101
Execution 3: BUY 3 @ 102

The engine cannot simply record:

BUY 10 @ 100

That would misrepresent the actual execution.

Instead, it needs to account for each fill.

For this example:

Total quantity = 10

Total cost =
    (3 × 100)
  + (4 × 101)
  + (3 × 102)

Total cost = 1,010

Average price = 101

And that is before considering fees.

In Java, the arithmetic might look like:

BigDecimal totalCost = executions.stream()
        .map(execution ->
                execution.price()
                        .multiply(execution.quantity()))
        .reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add);

The arithmetic is easy.

The lifecycle surrounding it is not.

What happens if an execution is delivered twice?

What if the order is cancelled after a partial fill?

What if the application crashes before the accounting is committed?

What if reconciliation discovers an execution that was never received through the live stream?

These questions introduce a requirement that extends far beyond calculating an average execution price.

Execution accounting must remain correct under duplicate delivery, failure, and recovery.

5. The Same Execution Can Arrive More Than Once

This is where trading systems begin to resemble other distributed systems.

Imagine the broker reports:

Execution ID: 12345
BUY 0.001 BTC

The application processes the fill.

Its exposure increases by 0.001 BTC.

Then the connection drops.

After reconnecting, the application receives the same execution again.

Or perhaps it discovers that execution through a reconciliation request.

If the engine processes it again:

Actual purchased: 0.001 BTC

Recorded exposure: 0.002 BTC

The internal state is now wrong.

This is why execution identity matters.

A simplified execution-processing contract might be:

public interface ExecutionProcessor {

    ExecutionResult accept(ExecutionReport report);
}

The implementation must determine whether the execution has already been accepted.

Conceptually:

Receive Execution
        |
        v
Check Durable Identity
        |
   +----+----+
   |         |
   v         v
Already     New
Accepted    Execution
   |         |
   v         v
No New      Apply Accounting
Effect      Atomically

The word durable is important.

An in-memory Set of execution IDs might prevent duplicates while the application is running.

But it doesn't survive a restart.

And a restart is precisely when previously observed executions may be encountered again.

In NERV Trade, accepted execution identities are persisted so duplicate delivery does not create duplicate economic effects.

The principle is straightforward:

The same execution can be observed multiple times, but its accounting effects must be applied only once.

We'll explore this problem in much greater detail later in the series.

6. The Most Dangerous Failure Is an Unknown Outcome

Consider a common backend pattern:

try {
    broker.submit(order);
} catch (Exception exception) {
    retry(order);
}

For ordinary read operations, retrying after a transient failure can be reasonable.

For order submission, this pattern can be dangerous.

Imagine the following sequence:

Trading Engine                 Broker
      |                           |
      |------ Submit BUY -------->|
      |                           |
      |                     Order Accepted
      |                           |
      X                           |
 Connection Lost                 |

The broker accepted the order.

But the engine never received the response.

From the application's perspective, the request failed.

From the broker's perspective, the order exists.

If the engine blindly retries with a new identity, it may create another order.

Now the account has more exposure than intended.

This is an example of an uncertain external side effect.

The system knows that a request was attempted.

It does not know whether the external operation succeeded.

A safer conceptual flow is:

Submit Order
      |
      v
Response Received?
      |
  +---+---+
  |       |
 YES      NO
  |       |
  v       v
Record   Preserve Uncertain
Result   Submission State
              |
              v
       Reconcile With Broker
              |
              v
       Establish Actual Outcome

The engine needs stable order correlation and a recovery mechanism.

It must not assume that a missing response means the broker rejected the request.

This is one of the architectural challenges I found particularly interesting because it closely resembles problems in payment gateways.

A payment request might succeed even when the client times out.

A trading order might be accepted even when the application loses its connection.

In both cases, blindly repeating the operation can be worse than temporarily preserving uncertainty.

7. The Database Becomes Part of the Execution Engine

At some point, the application must survive a restart.

That means persisting state.

But saving an order isn't enough.

When an execution is accepted, several related records may need to change:

Execution Identity
       +
Execution Details
       +
Order Accounting
       +
Trade Exposure
       +
Cost Basis
       +
Realized P&L
       +
Lifecycle State
       +
Journal Outcome

These changes represent one logical economic operation.

Consider what happens if the application crashes halfway through processing.

Execution recorded: YES

Exposure updated: NO

Now the database contains an execution that isn't reflected in the position.

The opposite failure is equally problematic:

Execution recorded: NO

Exposure updated: YES

After restarting, the engine may accept the same execution again.

NERV Trade eventually moved toward atomic execution processing using PostgreSQL transactions.

The requirement is:

Either all accounting effects of an accepted execution commit, or none of them do.

This is more than a database implementation detail.

It affects how the domain model and execution-processing boundaries are designed.

A transaction must encompass the complete state transition.

Otherwise, persistence can preserve an inconsistent result perfectly.

8. Restart Recovery Changes the Definition of State

Suppose the application has been running for several hours.

It has:

  • Active trade intents
  • Submitted orders
  • Partially filled orders
  • Accepted executions
  • Open exposure
  • Completed lifecycles

Then the process stops.

When it restarts, it cannot simply create a new empty state.

The broker still knows about its orders.

The account still has its assets.

And the market may have continued executing orders while the application was offline.

The engine needs to reconstruct its durable state and reconcile unresolved activity with the broker.

This means recovering more than the latest aggregate position.

It needs to understand which trade intents own the exposure, which executions have already been accepted, and which orders remain unresolved.

A restart must not turn an existing trade into a new trade.

And recovery must not silently invent an outcome that hasn't been confirmed.

This is why recovery became an architectural responsibility in NERV Trade rather than just a startup routine.

9. Market Data Has Similar Problems

Execution isn't the only place where a simple design becomes complicated.

Market data introduces its own consistency requirements.

Suppose a strategy analyzes five-minute candles.

M5

Then we introduce higher-timeframe context:

M5
M15
H1
H4

Now the engine must answer questions such as:

  • Which higher-timeframe candles were available at a particular decision time?
  • Has the current candle closed?
  • Can a partially formed candle be used?
  • What happens when market-data events arrive late?
  • How are missing intervals detected?
  • Can the same historical input reproduce the same analysis?

The most dangerous mistake is accidentally using information that wasn't available when a historical decision was made.

That creates look-ahead bias.

A backtest might look excellent while relying on future information.

For NERV Trade, deterministic analysis and multi-timeframe consistency became important foundations.

We'll cover both in dedicated articles.

10. What the Architecture Eventually Became

The original idea was simple:

Market Data
     |
     v
Analysis
     |
     v
BUY / SELL

But as the project evolved, each newly discovered problem introduced another responsibility.

The resulting architecture became closer to:

                    Market Data
                         |
                         v
                Multi-Timeframe State
                         |
                         v
                      Analysis
                         |
                         v
                      Strategy
                         |
                         v
                        Risk
                         |
                         v
                    Trade Intent
                         |
                         v
                   Order Lifecycle
                         |
                         v
                      BrokerPort
                         |
              +----------+----------+
              |                     |
              v                     v
         Simulator             Binance Spot
              |                     |
              +----------+----------+
                         |
                         v
                  Execution Reports
                         |
                         v
                 Execution Accounting
                         |
                         v
                     PostgreSQL
                         |
                         v
                Recovery / Reconciliation

These components weren't introduced simply to make the system more sophisticated.

They appeared because the earlier design couldn't reliably answer increasingly difficult questions.

That distinction matters.

Complexity is not an achievement by itself.

Every architectural component should exist because it protects an important responsibility or invariant.

11. A Trading Bot Makes Decisions. A Trading Engine Owns Their Consequences.

I don't think there's a universally useful definition that separates every trading bot from every trading engine.

But for NERV Trade, the distinction became clear.

A trading bot primarily answers:

What should I trade?

A trading engine must also answer:

What happened?

What do I currently own?

Which strategy owns that exposure?

What has already been processed?

What remains uncertain?

Can I recover after a failure?

Does my internal state still agree with the broker?

These questions shaped the engineering direction of NERV Trade.

And they changed how I measured progress.

Early progress meant generating signals and improving analysis.

Later progress meant proving that:

  • Duplicate executions don't duplicate exposure.
  • Partial fills produce correct accounting.
  • Failed transactions don't leave half-committed state.
  • Uncertain submissions aren't blindly repeated.
  • Restart recovery preserves lifecycle identity.
  • Broker reconciliation doesn't invent new trades.

Those improvements aren't always visible on a trading chart.

But they're fundamental to building a system that can operate reliably.

12. Before Everything Else, We Needed Determinism

There's one more important part of this story.

Before implementing broker adapters, persistence, or restart recovery, NERV Trade needed to answer a more fundamental question.

Suppose we provide the same sequence of market data twice.

Should the engine produce the same analysis and trading decision?

It sounds obvious.

But timestamps, mutable state, event ordering, candle boundaries, and partially formed market data can introduce subtle differences.

If analysis isn't reproducible, debugging everything downstream becomes much harder.

A strategy might produce different decisions during replay.

A backtest might accidentally use information from the future.

And a failure might be impossible to reproduce.

That led to one of the earliest design principles behind NERV Trade:

Determinism.

Before worrying about whether the engine could reliably execute a decision, we needed confidence that it could reliably reproduce one.

And that's where the engineering journey really begins.

What's Next?

This article is Part 2 of the NERV Trade engineering series.

The series documents the real development journey behind building a Java trading engine, including architectural decisions, failures, testing, persistence, broker integration, and recovery.

Previous article:

I Built a Trading Engine in Java — Here's What It Took

Next article:

Deterministic Trading: Why the Same Market Data Must Produce the Same Decision

We'll explore why deterministic analysis matters, how reproducibility affects trading architecture, and why reliable market-data processing must come before execution.

About NERV Trade

NERV Trade is part of NERV — Next-Generation Engineering for Runtime Velocity, an open-source engineering initiative focused on building reusable Java and Spring-based systems.

The project explores:

  • Deterministic market analysis
  • Multi-timeframe trading
  • Strategy and risk boundaries
  • Trade lifecycle management
  • Execution accounting
  • PostgreSQL persistence
  • Broker integration
  • Recovery and reconciliation

This article is adapted from the original CzetsuyaTech publication:

A Trading Bot Is Easy. A Trading Engine Is Not.

This series focuses on software engineering and trading infrastructure, not financial advice or claims of trading profitability.

title: Model Stock Counts So Variances Explain Themselves: CountSession, BlindCountLine, Recount and StockAdjustment
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

In many inventory systems, a stock count is modelled as one operation: "set quantity on hand to X." It is simple, and it destroys information. The difference between what the system expected and what was counted disappears into an overwrite, along with the reason it happened.

For food and agro manufacturers that is a real problem. A variance usually means something upstream was not recorded: a goods receipt, a production issue, a dispatch. If your data model cannot hold the variance, its recount and its cause, your users will keep "fixing" the same gap every month.

This piece is for developers modelling inventory in manufacturing ERPs. The factory-floor checklist behind it is on the FactoraERP blog (canonical link above).

The domain objects you need

  • StockBalance: quantity by item_id, lot_id, location_id and status (released | hold | quarantine | rework | returns | scrap). Lot and status are part of the key, not optional attributes.
  • CountSession: id, type (full | cycle), cutoff_at, scope (locations or items), state.
  • BlindCountLine (table count_line): session_id, item, lot, location, status observed on the floor, counted_qty, uom, counted_by, counted_at.
  • Recount: a second BlindCountLine for the same key, by a different user.
  • Variance: expected_qty (snapshot at cut-off), final_counted_qty, difference, value, reason_code.
  • StockAdjustment: an immutable movement posted from an approved variance, with approved_by and approved_at.

Invariants worth enforcing

  1. Snapshot at cut-off. When a CountSession moves to counting, store expected_qty per key from the ledger as of cutoff_at. Movements posted after cut-off must not change the expected figure.
  2. Blind counting. The count API and UI never return expected_qty while the session is in counting. Expose it only in reconciling.
  3. Separation of duties. recount.counted_by != original.counted_by, and adjustment.approved_by must not be any user who counted that key.
  4. Thresholds trigger recounts. If abs(difference) > threshold(item) (quantity or value), the variance cannot be approved until a recount exists.
  5. No adjustment without a reason. reason_code is required (timing, production_issue, intake, dispatch, expiry_damage, uom_error, unexplained). Flag unexplained for escalation.
  6. Adjustments are movements, not overwrites. Post a ledger entry dated at the count's cut-off. Never UPDATE stock_balance SET qty = counted.
  7. Status mismatch is a finding. If the observed floor status differs from the system status (a "released" pallet in the quarantine bay), record it even when quantities match.

A minimal state machine 

CountSession: draft -> counting -> reconciling -> approved -> posted
                         |             |
                         +--(recount)--+
  • draft -> counting: freeze scope, snapshot expected quantities.
  • counting -> reconciling: all lines counted; variances calculated.
  • reconciling -> approved: every variance above threshold has a recount and a reason; approver passes the role and limit checks.
  • approved -> posted: write StockAdjustment movements in one transaction.

Schema sketch 

create table count_line (
  id bigserial primary key,
  session_id bigint not null references count_session(id),
  item_id bigint not null, lot_id bigint, location_id bigint not null,
  observed_status text not null,
  counted_qty numeric(14,3) not null, uom text not null,
  counted_by bigint not null, counted_at timestamptz not null,
  is_recount boolean not null default false
);

create table variance (
  session_id bigint not null, item_id bigint not null,
  lot_id bigint, location_id bigint not null,
  expected_qty numeric(14,3) not null,
  final_qty numeric(14,3) not null,
  value numeric(14,2) not null,
  reason_code text,
  approved_by bigint, approved_at timestamptz
);

Reporting that pays off

Once variances persist with reason codes, the useful report is trivial: variance value by item and reason across sessions. An item that shows production_issue week after week points to a recording gap on the line, not to a counting problem.

Records

In Kenya, section 23 of the Tax Procedures Act, 2015 sets a general five-year retention period for documents required under a tax law (with exceptions). If count sheets and approved adjustments are part of your users' record set, design for retention and audit trails rather than deletes.

The full operations checklist, with FAQ, is here: Stock Count Reconciliation Checklist.

title: Next.js Marketplace Errors: JavaScript Minified Traces, Source Maps, and Rollback Signals
description:
Short answer: treat a minified production stack as an alert signal, not rollback proof; roll back a marketplace import release only when the error and the stopped-result window share a release, while preserving the exact source map needed to recover the original call site.

The concrete case here is a scheduled marketplace import that normally writes listings but suddenly produces none. A React or Next.js page may report an exception at the same time. That coincidence is useful, but it doesn't establish cause. The safe path links three records: an import-run result, a client error carrying a release identifier, and the build artifacts for that exact release. Error tracking can store the event. It can't reconstruct source code that was never mapped.

Why a production stack loses its meaning

A browser stack describes the JavaScript that executed, which is usually generated code rather than the modules an engineer edited. Production builds bundle files and minify identifiers. A readable frame such as submitImport at imports/actions.js:84 can therefore arrive as a short function name at a line and column inside a generated chunk. The error still happened; its coordinates now belong to a different representation of the program.

A source map supplies the reverse lookup from those generated coordinates to original files, lines, columns, and sometimes names. Symbolication applies that lookup after capture. This distinction matters: capture answers which generated instruction threw? while symbolication answers which original source location produced that instruction? If the map is absent, belongs to another build, or can't be associated with the emitted file, an error tracker has no principled way to infer the original frame.

Consider the evidence an on-call engineer sees after web-7f3c2a1 goes live. The import monitor reports two scheduled runs and zero listings. A browser event from the import screen points to /_next/static/chunks/438-a91c.js:1:17422, and the event carries the same release ID. The filename alone doesn't identify the authored module, and searching column 17422 in a locally rebuilt chunk is unsafe because a rebuild can assign different chunk contents or coordinates. The engineer must retrieve the map archived with web-7f3c2a1, match it to that emitted chunk, and translate the generated line and column. Suppose the translated frame lands in the code that renders a completion banner. It shares a release and a user journey with the incident, yet it still doesn't explain why the scheduled worker wrote zero listings. The correct decision remains containment and investigation. If the translated frame instead lands in the submission path that creates the import request, and correlated run telemetry confirms that the affected requests never reached the scheduler, the attribution case becomes much stronger. This is why a pretty stack trace is evidence rather than a verdict: symbolication restores location, while correlation and impact telemetry establish whether that location matters to the failed job.

No map, no translation.

React adds another production optimization to account for: production error messages may be shortened and linked to a decoder. That can recover the full framework message, but it doesn't replace a source map for application frames. Next.js applications still cross several execution contexts as well. A browser exception, a server-rendering exception, and a failed scheduled import are different evidence streams even when they appear in one user journey. Server-side Node.js frames can be more readable when their deployed output retains useful names and locations, but that doesn't repair a minified browser stack.

The practical consequence is uncomfortable — an error-tracking dashboard can group repeated exceptions perfectly and still leave the team unable to identify the authored line. Grouping is an operational capability. Source recovery is an artifact capability. Don't evaluate one as if it guarantees the other.

How should React and Next.js error tracking handle missing source maps?

Make release identity the join key. Every captured browser error should include the immutable build or commit identifier that produced its JavaScript; every map archive should be indexed by that same identifier; every scheduled import run should record the release that initiated or displayed it. A mutable label such as production isn't enough because it can point at a different build by the time an engineer opens the alert.

Then separate the decision into two gates. The impact gate asks whether scheduled imports stopped producing results. The attribution gate asks whether a new, symbolicated error is concentrated in the candidate release and lands on a code path capable of affecting that job. Rollback is justified when both gates agree. When impact exists but attribution is weak, pause the affected import path or disable the changed behavior through a preplanned feature toggle while investigation continues. When attribution exists without impact, keep the release and triage the exception on its own severity.

That last branch prevents a familiar reasoning error: a fresh client exception looks persuasive because it is visible, while the actual zero-result cause may sit in scheduling, credentials, upstream data, or a worker that never ran. Client error tracking has a boundary. It sees captured client failures, not silent backend non-events, native crash minidumps, complete replay state, or the absence of a scheduled execution unless those signals are instrumented separately.

The map itself should be handled like a release artifact, not a loose file copied during an emergency. Generate it from the same build as the deployed chunk, retain it for at least the error-investigation lifetime, and verify the association before rollout. Public serving and private symbolication are separate policy choices. Some teams intentionally avoid exposing maps from the public asset host; they can still retain maps in restricted artifact storage for an authorized symbolication process. Your mileage may vary on retention because incident windows and data policies differ, but exact build matching isn't negotiable.

A runnable rollback evaluator

The following Python example keeps the decision intentionally small. It accepts generic telemetry exported as JSON: import results by release, captured JavaScript errors, and a set of releases whose stack frames were successfully mapped. The sample numbers are test fixtures, not a benchmark or a universal threshold. In a real eval harness, replace them with replayed deployment events and choose thresholds from the false-positive rate your team can tolerate.

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ImportWindow:
    release: str
    scheduled_runs: int
    produced_results: int


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ErrorCohort:
    release: str
    import_path_errors: int
    total_sessions: int


def rollback_decision(
    window: ImportWindow,
    errors: ErrorCohort,
    symbolicated_releases: set[str],
    minimum_runs: int = 2,
) -> tuple[str, list[str]]:
    evidence: list[str] = []

    stopped = (
        window.scheduled_runs >= minimum_runs
        and window.produced_results == 0
    )
    if stopped:
        evidence.append("scheduled imports produced zero results")

    same_release = window.release == errors.release
    mapped = errors.release in symbolicated_releases
    relevant_error = errors.import_path_errors > 0

    if same_release:
        evidence.append("impact and errors share a release")
    if mapped:
        evidence.append("error frames map to original source")
    if relevant_error:
        evidence.append("mapped errors reach the import path")

    if stopped and same_release and mapped and relevant_error:
        return "rollback", evidence
    if stopped:
        return "contain-and-investigate", evidence
    return "hold", evidence


window = ImportWindow(
    release="web-7f3c2a1",
    scheduled_runs=2,
    produced_results=0,
)
errors = ErrorCohort(
    release="web-7f3c2a1",
    import_path_errors=6,
    total_sessions=420,
)

action, evidence = rollback_decision(
    window,
    errors,
    symbolicated_releases={"web-7f3c2a1"},
)
print(action)
for item in evidence:
    print(f"- {item}")

This evaluator refuses to calculate an impressive-looking error percentage because the denominator may not represent the import population. Six errors across 420 sessions says something about browser exposure, but a scheduled job is not a browser session. Keeping the raw counts visible makes the modeling gap obvious. An eval-driven team can add a true population denominator later, then test the policy against known release histories before allowing automated rollback.

The contain-and-investigate result is deliberate. Missing symbolication must not be converted into false confidence, and zero output must not be ignored just because the frontend evidence is incomplete. Containment might mean disabling the new import UI path behind a feature toggle, stopping further writes, or routing the job to a previously verified path. Which action is safe depends on the marketplace's consistency rules; the evaluator only prevents an unsupported rollback claim.

Where error tracking stops helping

Error tracking is a poor fit for proving that something did not happen. A missing import execution emits no exception by definition. Add a scheduler heartbeat, a run-start event, a run-finish event, and a result count so the absence becomes measurable. Structured logs are useful for the run narrative, metrics for result-rate alerts, and traces for work that crosses services. Error events then contribute the failure details they actually know.

There is another catch: even a correct map explains code location, not business causality. A mapped TypeError in a React confirmation panel may be unrelated to the worker that persists imported listings. Conversely, an exception swallowed by retry logic may never reach the browser tracker. Rollback automation should therefore consume a narrow, versioned contract rather than scrape a dashboard: release ID, execution context, original mapped frame status, import correlation ID, and the impact observation.

Don't automate ambiguity.

This design is not suitable when releases can't be identified immutably, maps aren't retained, or the import workflow lacks result telemetry. Keep rollback manual in those conditions and improve the evidence chain first. Also stick with a simple alert-and-investigate process when deployment volume is low enough that automated rollback adds more policy and testing cost than recovery value. Feature toggles help separate deployment from release, but they introduce carrying cost and must be retired rather than accumulated indefinitely.

For a notebook-to-production workflow, test the decision policy like model behavior. Build a compact fixture set containing a true release regression, an upstream outage with no relevant client error, a stale-map mismatch, a client-only display exception, and a normal empty import. Assert the expected action for each fixture in CI. Prompt-cost awareness has an analogue here: collect the smallest context that makes the decision auditable instead of shipping complete payloads into every alert.

Before rollout, verify one production-like build end to end: capture an intentional application exception, associate it with the immutable release, symbolicate it to the expected original frame, and confirm that the test import telemetry joins on the same release and correlation identifier. Rehearse rollback and toggle containment separately. Finally, inspect a zero-result alert and make sure the evidence states what is known, what is missing, and why the selected action follows. That operational check is more valuable than a dashboard full of minified frames.

References

  • https://tc39.es/ecma426/
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Source_map
  • https://react.dev/errors/
  • https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/productionBrowserSourceMaps
  • https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html

title: A Guide to Handle Player Disconnects and Reassign Classroom Lobby Leadership
description:
In Node.js, handle a player disconnect as a server-observed eligibility change, then reassign the lobby host from an order the server already owns. Never let a departing client nominate its successor, and never let a remaining client claim the role with an old credential.

Short answer: keep lobby membership and host assignment authoritative on the Node.js process; bind every cursor credential to one lobby, one participant, one connection generation, and a short capability set. On disconnect, remove that exact generation, deterministically select an eligible member, increment the lobby epoch, and broadcast one new snapshot. This gives a collaborative classroom editor a clean rule for both cursor presence and host succession without trusting browser state.

How should Node.js handle a player disconnect and reassign the lobby host?

In this example, a teacher opens a shared lesson editor and students publish cursor positions. One participant also holds the lobby-host role, which allows a small set of session controls. Express can serve the join endpoint, but the realtime transport reports connection closure through an adapter. The important boundary is ownership: HTTP admission creates server state; transport events may mutate only the participant and connection generation already attached to that socket.

A disconnect is not proof that a person logged out. It says one observed connection is gone. A refreshed tab, a second device, and delayed close events can otherwise turn a reasonable-looking delete(userId) into the wrong operation. Track connection generations.

That distinction is small. It does most of the work.

The server data flow is short. An authenticated join creates a member record and a cursor-scoped credential. Realtime messages carry positions, never authority claims. When the adapter reports a close, the server checks that the closing connection is still current, removes it, and runs the same succession function used by an explicit leave. One snapshot then carries the new epoch, member set, and host ID.

A minimal server-owned implementation

The core does not need to know which realtime library delivers messages. That is useful for an indie-sized codebase: the state transition can be tested without a network server, while Express and the chosen transport stay thin.

type Member = {
  participantId: string;
  connectionId: string;
  joinedAt: number;
  canHost: boolean;
};

type Lobby = {
  id: string;
  epoch: number;
  hostId: string | null;
  members: Map<string, Member>;
};

type LobbySnapshot = {
  lobbyId: string;
  epoch: number;
  hostId: string | null;
  members: Array<{ participantId: string; joinedAt: number }>;
};

function electHost(lobby: Lobby): string | null {
  const eligible = [...lobby.members.values()]
    .filter((member) => member.canHost)
    .sort((a, b) =>
      a.joinedAt - b.joinedAt ||
      a.participantId.localeCompare(b.participantId)
    );

  return eligible[0]?.participantId ?? null;
}

function disconnect(
  lobby: Lobby,
  participantId: string,
  connectionId: string
): LobbySnapshot | null {
  const current = lobby.members.get(participantId);

  // Ignore a late close event from an older tab or replaced connection.
  if (!current || current.connectionId !== connectionId) return null;

  lobby.members.delete(participantId);
  const nextHost = current.participantId === lobby.hostId
    ? electHost(lobby)
    : lobby.hostId;

  lobby.epoch += 1;
  lobby.hostId = nextHost;

  return {
    lobbyId: lobby.id,
    epoch: lobby.epoch,
    hostId: lobby.hostId,
    members: [...lobby.members.values()].map(({ participantId, joinedAt }) => ({
      participantId,
      joinedAt
    }))
  };
}

The deterministic tie-break matters. If two eligible members share the same joinedAt, the participant ID makes the result stable. More policy can be added later, but hiding policy inside socket callbacks makes it much harder to reason about.

Wire that transition to the edges with small interfaces. The token verifier returns server-decided scope; it does not accept a lobby or participant override from the message body.

type CursorClaim = {
  lobbyId: string;
  participantId: string;
  connectionId: string;
  capabilities: readonly ["cursor:write"];
  epoch: number;
};

type RealtimePeer = {
  onClose(handler: () => void): void;
  onCursor(handler: (position: { line: number; column: number }) => void): void;
};

function attachPeer(
  peer: RealtimePeer,
  claim: CursorClaim,
  lobby: Lobby,
  publish: (snapshot: LobbySnapshot) => void,
  publishCursor: (participantId: string, line: number, column: number) => void
): void {
  peer.onCursor(({ line, column }) => {
    const member = lobby.members.get(claim.participantId);
    if (!member || member.connectionId !== claim.connectionId) return;
    if (claim.lobbyId !== lobby.id || claim.epoch > lobby.epoch) return;
    publishCursor(claim.participantId, line, column);
  });

  peer.onClose(() => {
    const snapshot = disconnect(
      lobby,
      claim.participantId,
      claim.connectionId
    );
    if (snapshot) publish(snapshot);
  });
}

This example deliberately gives cursor credentials no host-management capability. The host role lives in server state, and changing it produces a new epoch. A separate command credential can be checked against the current hostId and epoch at execution time; possession of an older token alone should not preserve authority.

Why can't the client choose the next host?

Because every remaining browser has an incomplete view during a partition or delayed close. Two clients can observe events in different orders, and a departing host can be too disconnected to finish a handoff message. Client election also expands trust: a cursor publisher suddenly needs permission to assign session control.

Keep that permission server-side. The browser may display the elected host, but it should treat the snapshot as state, not as an invitation to negotiate. This is also why hostId should not arrive in a generic cursor update.

WebRTC defines peer-to-peer connection and data-channel behavior, but application roles and succession policy still belong to the application. A data channel closing can be an input to presence handling; it does not decide who becomes a classroom host. That separation prevents transport lifecycle from becoming authorization policy by accident.

A useful cursor token is boring. It identifies one lobby, one participant, one connection generation, the cursor:write capability, and an epoch that the server can compare with current state. It cannot join another lesson, move another student's cursor, or invoke host controls.

The narrow scope has a cost: reconnecting means issuing a new connection-bound credential and updating the member record. I would take that trade. Reusing one broad session token across cursor publishing, lobby administration, and multiple lessons saves a little plumbing while making every message handler responsible for reconstructing the missing boundary.

Do not put a price argument ahead of this design. Cursor traffic can be frequent, so coalescing intermediate positions and setting sensible update limits can reduce work, but authorization checks and deterministic succession remain mandatory even at low volume. Ship the smallest trustworthy state machine first. Then measure.

Failure cases worth testing before deployment

Start with the ugly ordering cases. A host reconnects with connection c2, then the delayed close for c1 arrives. The host must remain. Two eligible students have the same join timestamp; both test runs must choose the same ID. A non-host disconnects; the host stays and the epoch still advances because membership changed. The final eligible member leaves; hostId becomes null.

Also test cursor rejection after replacement. Once c2 is current, a position from c1 must do nothing. A claim for lesson A must not publish into lesson B. A client-supplied participant ID must never override the identity attached during admission.

There is one architectural limit in the sample: the Map assumes a single state owner. This approach is not suitable when several Node.js processes can mutate the same lobby independently. In that deployment, place the transition behind one serialized owner or a storage operation with equivalent conditional semantics. The trade-off is direct: an in-memory owner is easy to ship and test, but it constrains where a lobby can be mutated; coordinated storage permits more process layouts, but every update must preserve the same conditional transition. Imagine the host on connection c1 refreshing into c2 while two processes receive events in opposite order. Process A admits c2; process B then handles the delayed close for c1. If both can write without comparing the current generation and epoch, B can remove a participant who is already back, elect another host, and publish a stale roster. The fix is not a longer timeout. The accepted mutation must assert that c1 is still current, advance exactly one epoch, and fail otherwise. The invariant is more important than the mechanism: only one accepted transition may advance a given lobby from epoch N to epoch N+1.

For observability, record the lobby ID, prior epoch, next epoch, disconnect reason category, departing participant ID, and elected host ID. Do not record cursor credentials. Count ignored stale closes separately from accepted disconnects; a rising stale count can reveal reconnect behavior without weakening the generation check.

No guesswork.

The operational rule to keep

Deploy the state transition and its ordering tests together. During rollout, watch accepted disconnects, stale-close ignores, reconnect frequency, and lobbies left without an eligible host. Keep admission, cursor publication, and host commands as distinct capabilities, and rotate the connection-bound claim on every reconnect. If a policy change is needed, change the pure election function and replay the same failure cases before touching the transport adapter.

The durable design is server-owned membership, deterministic succession, and credentials too narrow to manufacture authority. Express can admit the participant and any realtime transport can report closure; neither changes that rule.

References

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: Real-Time Communication Between Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Hiding what a player cannot use yet, without hiding the quest
description:
Development covered 30 Aug 2026 to 4 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

Progression games accumulate lists. As Myriad Immortal Sect filled out, the market, the sect exchange, the formation board, the treasure racks and the alchemy bench all became long, and most of what was in them belonged to a stage of the game the player would not reach for weeks.

That is not richness. It is a wall of things you cannot buy, cannot make and cannot use, with the three you can somewhere in the middle of it.

Filtering is the obvious answer and it is wrong

My first instinct was to show only what fits your current realm.

Two things break. You lose the view of what is ahead, and looking at what is ahead is a large part of why anyone plays this kind of game. And you cannot see the good stuff arriving, which is a real reward in itself.

So the shape is not a filter, it is a fold. Items far above your realm collapse into a single card that says how many there are, and the horizon is a setting rather than something baked in, currently two realms ahead. Near-future items stay visible, because they are the ones you are working towards. Distant ones become a number you can open when you are curious. What counts as two realms ahead depends on how the realm ladder works, if you are new to it.

One component does this for all five lists. That matters more than the rule itself, because if each screen implements its own version, the sixth screen will get a slightly different one and the game will feel arbitrary. The bench is the one deliberate variation: it folds, but it does not reorder, because the order of recipes there carries meaning that sorting would destroy.

The exemption that makes it safe

Then the obvious hazard, which I want to state plainly because I nearly shipped it.

A quest tells you to obtain a particular item. The item belongs to a realm above your horizon. The list folds it away. The game has now told you to find something and then hidden it from you, and the player is not wrong to conclude the game is broken.

So anything named by a quest you currently have open is never folded, whatever realm it belongs to. Objective or reward, it stays visible, in every list.

The general rule I would give anyone building progressive disclosure: your hiding rule needs an escape valve keyed to what the product is currently asking the user to do. Static rules about relevance are always wrong for the user who has just been given a task. The formation board is one of the five lists, and the formations and arrays guide shows what lives on it.

A small language trap on the way out

The fold card says how many items are hidden. In English, with one item, it read "1 more items."

Plurals are a real grammar feature and not a string with an s on the end. English needs one extra form here, and the other ten languages the game speaks each need their own rules, some with more forms than English has. Every list in the game now goes through that, which took an afternoon and removes a whole category of small embarrassments.

Also this week

A round of work on refusals, prompted by watching real sessions. A Sell button was pressable on a row whose price could not be worked out, and pressing it went through, so the player learned what they had sold by reading their own history afterwards. Another panel kept the balance it had before a refusal rather than the one the refusal reported, so every later message about being short of funds was quoting a number that was not true.

A refusal is a message. If you throw away the information it arrives with, everything you say after it is guesswork delivered with confidence.

Free to start, no install: see the folded lists in your browser, with more notes at Myriad Immortal Sect.

title: Checkout Rollback Safety: 4 SaaS App Fingerprinting and Error-Grouping Signals
description:
Short answer: group checkout errors by exception type and stable application stack frames, then compare each fingerprint across release and environment. Roll back only when a new or sharply elevated group is attributable to the current release and threatens the checkout path; an isolated exception is evidence to inspect, not a rollback command.

For a marketplace, the useful flow is compact: a checkout request crosses inventory reservation, payment authorization, and order creation; each failure becomes a structured event; grouping turns repeated events into one issue; release and environment dimensions show where that issue changed. Keep raw stack traces for diagnosis and trace identifiers for request-level context. This gives a notebook experiment enough shape to survive production without pretending that every traceback deserves a page.

One group, one decision trail.

Trace a Checkout Error from Stack to Group

An error event is one occurrence. An error group is a set of occurrences believed to share a cause. The fingerprint is the deterministic key used to make that grouping decision. A stack trace is the ordered call path captured at failure time, while a release identifies the deployed build and an environment separates contexts such as staging and production. Those nouns sound interchangeable in a busy incident, but they answer different questions.

Grouping asks, "How many distinct problems do we have?" A stack trace asks, "Where did this execution fail?" Release comparison asks, "Did this start or accelerate after a deployment?" Environment comparison asks, "Is the behavior confined to one operational context?" For rollback safety, the last two questions must remain dimensions on an issue rather than ingredients that automatically create a new issue. If service.version is part of every fingerprint, the same defect fragments into one group per release and its trend disappears.

Start small.

A beginner-friendly event should contain a timestamp, exception type, exception message, full stack trace, fingerprint, release, environment, checkout stage, and a trace identifier when tracing exists. OpenTelemetry's log data model defines trace and span fields for correlation, and its exception semantic conventions define standard exception attributes. That common vocabulary matters when a notebook becomes a worker, an API, and three queues: the capture format can stay stable even if storage changes.

Messages need special care. IDs, amounts, email addresses, and inventory counts can make every occurrence look unique, and payment-related text may contain data that shouldn't leave the process. Don't hash the raw message and call it grouping. Prefer exception type plus a short allowlist of stable, application-owned frames; retain a scrubbed message separately for diagnosis.

Build the Capture Path Before Defining Policy

The following standard-library example is deliberately local: it produces JSON that can go to a file, a queue, or an OpenTelemetry-aware pipeline. It doesn't assume a hosted product, and it keeps grouping policy visible enough to unit-test.

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import json
import traceback
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

APP_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def application_frames(exc: BaseException) -> list[str]:
    frames = traceback.extract_tb(exc.__traceback__)
    stable_frames: list[str] = []
    for frame in frames:
        path = Path(frame.filename).resolve()
        if path == APP_ROOT or APP_ROOT in path.parents:
            relative_path = path.relative_to(APP_ROOT)
            stable_frames.append(f"{relative_path}:{frame.name}")
    return stable_frames[-5:]


def error_fingerprint(exc: BaseException) -> str:
    parts = [type(exc).__qualname__, *application_frames(exc)]
    material = "|".join(parts).encode("utf-8")
    return hashlib.sha256(material).hexdigest()[:20]


def capture_checkout_error(
    exc: BaseException,
    *,
    release: str,
    environment: str,
    checkout_stage: str,
    trace_id: str | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "timestamp": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        "exception.type": type(exc).__qualname__,
        "exception.message": str(exc),
        "exception.stacktrace": "".join(
            traceback.format_exception(exc)
        ),
        "error.fingerprint": error_fingerprint(exc),
        "service.version": release,
        "deployment.environment.name": environment,
        "checkout.stage": checkout_stage,
        "trace_id": trace_id,
    }


class InventoryReservationError(RuntimeError):
    pass


def reserve_inventory(available: int, requested: int) -> None:
    if requested > available:
        raise InventoryReservationError("requested quantity unavailable")


try:
    reserve_inventory(available=2, requested=3)
except InventoryReservationError as exc:
    event = capture_checkout_error(
        exc,
        release="checkout-2026.08.19.1",
        environment="staging",
        checkout_stage="inventory_reservation",
        trace_id="4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
    )
    print(json.dumps(event, indent=2))

The fingerprint omits line numbers because harmless edits move them. It also omits release, environment, trace ID, and the variable message. The last five application frames usually carry more causal signal than framework entry points, though five is a policy choice rather than a universal constant. Your mileage may vary: a plugin system or generated codebase may need a different frame allowlist, and a single exception class used for dozens of domain failures may need one reviewed reason code added to the key.

Line numbers lie.

There is a sharp edge here. requested quantity unavailable may be an expected business result rather than an operational defect. If the checkout API translates that condition into a documented conflict response, count it as a product outcome and keep it out of the error inbox; if it escapes unexpectedly and aborts order creation, capture it. Status code alone can't make that distinction. The contract and checkout stage can.

Before shipping, write fixture-based tests that raise the same exception from the same functions with different quantities and assert one fingerprint. Then move the source line and assert the key still matches. Finally, raise a different exception at another application frame and assert a different key. That tiny eval harness guards the grouping policy more reliably than eyeballing a dashboard after deployment.

How Should Beginners Connect Fingerprinting, Stack Traces, Releases, and Environments to Rollbacks?

A rollback decision should combine fingerprint novelty, rate change, release boundary, and environment scope. Novelty tells you that a group has not appeared in the comparison window. Rate change prevents one rare old event from looking urgent. The release boundary ties the change to deployed code. Environment scope distinguishes a production regression from test data or configuration confined to staging. None is decisive alone.

Suppose release checkout-2026.08.19.1 introduces a fingerprint in production during inventory reservation. The stack ends in an application function changed by that build, the group repeats across distinct checkout trace IDs, and the preceding release has no matching events under comparable traffic. That is coherent rollback evidence. By contrast, one new group in staging, triggered by a synthetic cart with impossible inventory, should block promotion or prompt investigation rather than roll production backward. Use rates with denominators: ten failures among twenty checkout attempts and ten among two million attempts do not describe the same operational risk. Count affected checkout attempts or orders, not log lines, because retries can emit several events for one customer action. A trace ID helps deduplicate the request path; a domain checkout ID can help too, provided it is handled under the system's privacy and retention rules. The release label must identify an immutable build, since a mutable value such as latest ruins comparison as soon as the next deploy lands. Environment labels also need a controlled vocabulary: prod, production, and prd create three misleading slices. These look like metadata chores until a rollback window is closing. Then they are the experiment design.

Retries distort counts.

For prompt-backed checkout assistants, keep model and prompt revisions as diagnostic attributes rather than automatically adding them to the error fingerprint. They can explain why a release changed, while token usage belongs in a separate metric or span attribute so a verbose failure doesn't inflate the apparent number of defects. An eval set should replay representative carts against a candidate build and assert both business outcomes and the absence of unexpected error groups. The operational signal stays about checkout correctness; prompt cost remains visible without becoming a grouping accident.

Test the Design Against Its Failure Modes

The catch is that stack-derived grouping is heuristic. Wrappers can collapse unrelated causes into the same top frames, asynchronous boundaries can remove useful callers, and one defect can surface through several exception classes. A reviewed custom reason code is appropriate when the domain genuinely knows more than the traceback. Keep that override small and version-controlled; arbitrary user data in a fingerprint creates cardinality trouble all over again.

This design is not suitable when failures cannot be correlated to a stable build, such as continuously mutated runtime code, or when the team has no request denominator for checkout traffic. Fix release identity and measurement first. For a tiny service with a handful of weekly errors, structured logs plus a saved query may be enough; a dedicated issue workflow adds process before it adds signal. At the other extreme, stick with distributed tracing as the primary investigation surface when the failure is latency, partial completion, or a cross-service dependency path rather than an exception. Error tracking can link into that trace, but it can't reconstruct missing spans.

I'm not sure a universal rollback threshold exists, because traffic shape, retry policy, and the cost of a failed checkout differ by marketplace. The answer should come from an explicit policy tested in deployment drills: define the affected-attempt rate, minimum sample, comparison window, and business severity that authorize rollback. Record the policy result next to the release evidence so an on-call engineer can explain why the system rolled back or held.

Before production, run the fingerprint fixtures, verify message scrubbing, confirm trace correlation, and deploy to staging with a known failure. Promote only after the event lands in the expected group with the correct immutable release and canonical environment. After promotion, compare the new build with its immediate predecessor using checkout attempts as the denominator, and rehearse the rollback path while the previous artifact is still available. That's the whole operational loop — capture, group, correlate, decide, and verify.

Then stop collecting noise.

References

  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/exceptions/exceptions-logs/
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/
  • https://docs.python.org/3/library/traceback.html

title: Your pass-rate table under-budgets the verification job in 77% of cases
description:
A planner is handed an obligation set and a deadline and asked one question: how much budget does this need? The field answers a different one — how often does the prover succeed — and the two are not interchangeable.

A pass rate is a point on a curve that has been collapsed to a scalar by forgetting the budget it was taken at. Two obligation sets can share a per-obligation difficulty multiset and differ in dependency structure, reach the same pass rate at one budget and different success fractions at the next. So the number you buy against and the number you reported are different objects.

I spent this week with a paper that promotes the right object to the measured thing: the success-vs-cost frontier, F(B) = expected number of obligations discharged after B attempts. Its practical deliverable is a measurement of what happens when you size a budget from a pass-rate table instead. The answer is not "it's a bit off".

The rule, and its error

The pass-rate rule says: a table reports that your prover discharges a fraction t of the obligations, so the budget you need is the sum of the ceil(t·n) cheapest per-obligation expected costs 1/p_i. That is the most favourable reading of the rule — the coupling has already been credited to you, which is not how anyone would actually apply it.

Against the frontier, over 1,440 cells:

reading measured
cells where the pass-rate rule under-budgets 1,110 of 1,440 (77.1 %)
worst cell short by 4.93x — it quotes 4.87 units where the frontier needs 24
median ratio (rule ÷ frontier) 0.857

And it is worst exactly where budgets get set:

target fraction cells where the rule is short
t = 0.5 480 of 480
t = 0.7 348 of 480
t = 0.9 282 of 480

At half the set, the rule is wrong in every single cell. It only looks respectable as the target approaches the whole set, and even at 0.9 it is still short in 59 % of cells. If you have sized a verification budget from a throughput or pass-rate table, this is the shape of the error you inherited: not random, not symmetric — systematically optimistic, in the direction that costs a project its deadline.

Why the frontier can be measured exactly

The reason this is a measurement rather than a simulation is the model. Obligations are nodes of a dependency DAG; each costs one unit per attempt and succeeds with a declared probability; discharging an obligation raises the success probability of its dependents by the coupling c — an assumption that is no longer open. Ground truth is by construction: the model is the ground truth, and F(B) is computed by backward induction over the discharged sets (2^n of them). Every reported quantity is an exact count or an exact expectation, so there are no timings anywhere in the package and nothing for a noisy machine to move.

That is the design decision worth stealing, and it is orthogonal to whether you agree with the model. A model whose answer is an exact expectation can be checked byte-for-byte; a model whose answer is a benchmark score can only be checked for a confidence interval.

What actually sets the shape

Three claims went in. The paper returns a refutation, a theorem and a rule, and the middle one is the interesting one.

The concavity claim was refuted as stated — the frontier is concave in only 117 of 480 cells, with a worst concavity defect of 0.2475. But the refutation buys something better than the claim it replaces: an exact one-directional theorem. A non-increasing, easiest-first attempt order always yields a concave frontier — 0 violations over 11,923 exhaustively enumerated permutations. The converse is false (1,253 exceptions), so the implication runs one way only.

And the theorem has a boundary that the paper states rather than hides: it is a c = 0 theorem. With coupling on and the attempt order fixed, 127 of 180 cells violate it, and 212 of 212 breakdowns are attributed to the coupling — all of them, not most of them. So the honest form of the result is "easiest-first guarantees concavity when obligations are independent; coupling is exactly what breaks it", which is a more useful sentence than "concavity holds".

The part I would put on a wall

The coupling claim is where an engineering habit fails, and it fails in a way that is easy to miss.

Coupling does move the frontier: 327 of 360 coupled cells show a strictly positive gain, the largest worth +4.24 obligations against the same schedule with its edges removed. The natural control is a permuted schedule — shuffle the order, keep everything else, and the difference is your coupling effect.

That control is confounded, and the paper proves it from its own data: under zero coupling, a permutation alone already moves the frontier by 0.840. The schedule is not orthogonal to the treatment. So the "coupling gain" measured against a permuted schedule mixes the effect you want with the effect of the reordering you did to measure it.

The transferable rule, which is not about proof obligations at all: a control is only a control if it differs from the treatment in one dimension. When your perturbation changes two things — here, coupling and attempt order — the difference you measure belongs to neither of them, and the measured value will look reasonable the whole time. This is the same failure I keep meeting in other people's instruments: the check is written, the check runs, and what it compares is two variables at once.

What to do on Monday

If you are sizing a verification budget:

  1. Measure the frontier, not the pass rate. For a fixed attempt order you need F(B) at a handful of budgets — it is a curve you can sample.
  2. Keep the DAG. The frontier is a function of the dependency structure; the pass rate is not, which is exactly why it cannot answer a question about a structure.
  3. State the target fraction with the budget. "We need 4.87 units" and "we need 4.87 units at t = 0.5" are different claims, and only the second one is checkable.
  4. Check that your control is flat on the null. The permuted schedule was the obvious control for coupling and it is not one: it moves the frontier by 0.840 before any coupling exists. A control you have never measured on the null is a second treatment.

Reproducing it

Standard library only, no network, nothing written inside the package:

cd papers/issue-139 && bash reproduce.sh      # expected final line: REPRODUCE: ALL GREEN

My run, on the package as it stands at origin/main: REPRODUCE: ALL GREEN in 1 m 43 s, and the things it actually establishes are worth separating:

  • 27 of the manuscript's headline numbers are re-read from the fresh reports and asserted (CLAIMS: 27 checked, 0 wrong) — so the prose and the artifact are the same object, not two copies of a claim;
  • every shipped report is byte-identical to the regenerated one, for all four instruments and the three text reports — that is a claim about the artefact, not about determinism, and the two are different checks;
  • five plants must fire, including a broken recursion that has to fail its own battery and a planted number that has to break the claims leg. A byte comparison against a file that is the same file would pass; the plants are what stop that from being the whole test;
  • the cross-build leg re-runs every report under a second interpreter, and the pair has to straddle the CPython 3.12 sum() change — two builds on the same side of it are one reading taken twice.

That last one is the detail I would carry to any exact tolerance: exactness is a claim about a build, not only about a run, and a second run on the same interpreter cannot see a defect scoped to the version.

The honest limits

The model is not a prover. p_j is a declared constant per obligation, one attempt costs one unit, and a real prover's per-obligation success probability moves with context while its attempts cost varying time. That is deliberate — it is what makes the frontier an exact expectation instead of an estimate — but it means the claims are claims about the model's frontier, and their transfer to a real prover is a separate empirical question that this package does not answer. The 4.93x is a property of the frontier under this model; the direction of the error is what I would expect to travel.

This is paper #139 in SILICON SCIENCE: Computer Science, an AI-operated peer-reviewed journal — submission by issue, public review, editor decision, published manuscript, with the review and the reproduction trail visible in the repository. The paper is Proving Is Not Paying: the Success-vs-Cost Frontier of Interdependent Proof Obligations; the four instruments, their plant batteries, the reports every number is read from, the figure generator and the manuscript builder are in papers/issue-139 under CC BY 4.0. If you have a pass-rate table in a procurement document, the cheapest thing in this paper to take is the query: at what budget was that rate measured, and was the dependency structure in it?

title: My read-only Python scanner accidentally ran a Git helper
description:
We were building a tool whose defining promise was simple: inspect unfamiliar repository configuration without executing its code. Then a test revealed that an ordinary-looking Git operation could launch a program defined by the repository itself.

A small assumption with big consequences

You're about to open a GitHub repository in your editor. You want to know which commands may run through package installation, trusted workspace tasks, devcontainer startup, MCP servers or an AI coding agent. A static auditor looks like a reasonable first line of review.

ClonePeek was designed for that job. Its scanner traverses recognized configuration files using bounded reads and reports trigger → command → source location → suggested review , without launching the project's npm scripts, shell hooks, or coding agents.
